en: The Scripture on the Arising of the World, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta et al. of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Continent of Jambudvīpa. Chapter One: The Continent of Jambudvīpa.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Karīra stone cave.
At that time, after their meal, all the bhikṣus gathered in the hall where the Dharma is regularly preached.
Once they were seated, each gave rise to this thought and they deliberated together, saying:
"It is unprecedented that these elders have come here.
How did this world, the lands, the heavens, and the earth where sentient beings dwell, come to be established?"
How does it disintegrate?
How, having disintegrated, is it re-established?
And how, having been established, does it attain stability?
At that time, the World-Honored One was alone in a quiet chamber;
his divine ear, which was pure and surpassing that of humans, heard all the bhikṣus gathered after their meal in the Hall of Constant Discourse, engaging in such rare conversation.

Having heard this, the World-Honored One emerged from meditation in the late afternoon, rose from his stone chamber, and proceeded to the Dharma Hall. He took the seat regularly prepared before the great assembly of bhikṣus and sat upright and composed.
Thereupon the World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], asked intentionally: "Monks,
as you sit gathered here, what have you been discussing until now?"
At that time, the bhikṣus together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable World-Honored One!
We bhikṣus have gathered here in this Dharma hall after our meal.”
The great assembly deliberated in detail and spoke thus:
"It is unprecedented that these elders should say:
'How is it that the world is established in such a manner?'"
How does the world thus disintegrate?
How, after having disintegrated, does the world re-establish itself?
And how, once established, does the world remain stable?
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
We have recently gathered here to discuss and deliberate upon this very matter.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, you bhikṣus!”
"You are indeed able to act thus, practicing with faith in accordance with the Dharma.
O sons of good family!
It is because of your faith that you have left your homes to renounce the world."
If you are able to gather together in one place and engage in such discourse in accordance with the Dharma, it is truly inconceivable. You bhikṣus!

When you are assembled and seated, you should cultivate these two kinds of practice as your respective tasks, without giving rise to indolence: namely, discussing the meaning of the Dharma and noble silence.

If you are able to do so, you should listen to this meaning as taught by the Tathāgata: how the world is established, how the world is disintegrated, how the world, having been disintegrated, is established once more, and how the world, having been established, attains stability.
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha in unison, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time."
Sugata! Now is precisely the right time.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to explain this meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus, we bhikṣus, having heard what the World-Honored One says, shall uphold it accordingly.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in due order."
Then, the bhikṣus spoke to the Buddha in unison:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣu!

Just as the place traversed by one sun and moon illuminates the four continents, so too, the area illuminated by a thousand suns and moons within such a system of four-continent worlds is called a ‘small thousandfold world-system’ (sāhasracūdikalokadhātu).”
O Bhikṣus! Within a thousandfold world system, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, and a thousand Sumeru Kings;
four thousand small continents, four thousand great continents, four thousand small seas, four thousand great oceans, and four thousand lineages of nāgas.
...four thousand families of great nāgas, four thousand families of garuḍas, four thousand families of great garuḍas,
four thousand families dwelling in evil realms, four thousand families of great beings dwelling in evil realms,
four thousand minor kings, four thousand great kings, seven thousand kinds of great trees, and eight...
There are a thousand various great mountains; ten thousand various great hells; a thousand kings of Yama;
a thousand Jambudvīpas; a thousand Aparagoyānīs; a thousand Pūrvavidehas; a thousand Uttarakurus;
a thousand Cāturmahārājika heavens; a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens; a thousand Yāma heavens; and a thousand Tuṣita heavens.
The gods, the thousand gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, the thousand gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, the thousand Māra gods,
and the thousand Brahmā-world gods. Monks!
Within the Brahma-world, there was a Brahmā King whose power was most supreme and whom none could subdue; he ruled over a realm of a thousand sovereign Brahmās and declared:
"I am able to create, I am able to transform, and I am able to manifest illusions."
He said, "I am like a father.
Having uttered such arrogant words regarding various matters, he immediately gave rise to conceit.
The Tathāgata is not like this. Why is that?
All worlds arise and are established according to the power of their respective karmas.
"O monks! This thousandfold world-system, which is like a *cūḍa*—*cūḍa* meaning 'topknot' in the language of Sui—is called a small thousandfold world-system (*sāhasracūdika-lokadhatu*). O monks!"
The totality of one thousand such Cakravāḍa worlds is called the second-order intermediate thousandfold world system (*dvisāhasra madhyama lokadhātu*). O bhikṣus!

When a thousand of these second-order intermediate thousandfold world systems are taken as a single unit and multiplied again by a thousand, this is called a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasro lokadhātu*).

"O monks! This trichiliocosm is established simultaneously; having been established simultaneously, it then dissolves and disintegrates; having dissolved and disintegrated simultaneously, it then establishes itself once more; and having been established simultaneously, it attains stable abiding."
When such a world has been completely incinerated, it is called "dispersed and destroyed.
When it has completely arisen, it is called "established.
When it has completely subsisted, it is called "securely abiding."
This is the fearless single Buddha-field where sentient beings dwell. "O Bhikṣus!
Now this great earth has a thickness of four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas, and its circumference is immeasurable."
In this way, the great earth rests upon the water; the water rests upon the wind; and the wind relies upon space. O bhikṣus!
Beneath this great earth, there is a mass of water sixty hundred thousand yojanas thick, its circumference being immeasurable.
Beneath that mass of water lies a mass of wind, thirty-six hundred thousand yojanas thick and immeasurable in circumference. O monks!
This great ocean, at its deepest point, is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep and immeasurable in circumference.
"O bhikṣus!
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, enters eighty-four thousand yojanas into the waters of the ocean and rises above the waters of the ocean for another eighty-four thousand yojanas."
Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, has a level and even base; its lower roots extend down and rest upon the great golden wheel. O Bhikṣus!

Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, stands within the great ocean; it is narrow at the bottom and broad at the top, gradually widening as it rises. It is straight and not crooked, with a massive and solid body, exquisite and extraordinary, most excellent and worthy of being beheld. It is composed of four precious substances, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Upon Mount Sumeru grow all kinds of trees; these trees are lush and verdant, emitting various fragrances whose scent wafts afar, pervading all the mountains. It is the dwelling place of many sages and worthies, as well as the most majestic and virtuous devas of supreme excellence.

“O Bhikṣus! On the upper portion of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there are peaks that protrude from its four sides and curve over the great ocean; each is seven hundred yojanas high, exquisite and lovely, composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate—which serve as their adornments.”
"O Bhikṣus!
Beneath Mount Sumeru, there are three distinct tiers that serve as the dwellings of various deities.

The lowest tier is exactly sixty yojanas in both length and breadth. It is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls and courtyards, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets of bells, and sevenfold rows of tāla trees, which are majestic and lovely to behold. These trees are all composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and emerald."

Each wall-enclosure has four gates; at each gate, there are battlemented towers, multi-storied pavilions, carriage sheds, defensive watchtowers, palaces, halls, corridors, gardens, groves, and ponds, all fully adorned.
From each and every pond, wondrous flowers emerge, scattering various fragrances.
There are groves of trees, complete with all manner of stalks and leaves, and all kinds of flowers and fruits, which likewise emit various exquisite and sublime scents.
Furthermore, there were various birds, each emitting exquisite sounds; their calls mingled together in a manner that was harmonious, elegant, pure, and refreshing.

The second terrace was equal in length and breadth, measuring forty yojanas. It featured sevenfold walls and courtyards, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells. There were also seven rows of *tāla* trees, all perfectly level and uniform on every side, majestic and lovely. These were likewise adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
All manner of adornments were fully present: gateways, pavilions, towers, palaces, gardens, ponds, fruit trees, and various birds.

Its uppermost terrace was perfectly square, measuring twenty yojanas in length and breadth. It featured sevenfold walls and courtyards, and even the birds all produced exquisite sounds; nothing was lacking.
"O monks! On the lower tier there dwells a yakṣa named Pāṇi;
on the second tier there dwells a yakṣa named Mālādhara."
Within the upper tiers, there dwell yakṣas named Constantly Drunk.
"O bhikṣus! Halfway up Mount Sumeru, at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas, are the palaces where the Four Great Heavenly Kings reside."
Upon Mount Sumeru, there are the palaces of the Thirty-three Heavens where Śakra resides;
twice as high above the Thirty-three Heavens are the palaces where the Yāma devas reside;
and twice as high above the Yāma heavens, again, are the palaces where the Tuṣita devas reside.
Twice as high above the Tuṣita Heaven is the palace where the gods of Nirmāṇarati dwell;
twice as high above the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is the palace of the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin;
and twice as high above the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is the palace where the gods of Brahmakāyika dwell.
Between the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations and the Brahma-body Heaven, there are the celestial palaces of Māra Pāpīyas;
above the Brahma-body Heaven, there is the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
and above the Ābhāsvara Heaven, there is the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Twice the height of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven above is the Bṛhatphala Heaven;
twice the height of the Bṛhatphala Heaven above is the Avṛha Heaven;
the Bṛhatphala Heaven is above, and the Avṛha Heaven is below.
Within that interval, there are separate celestial palaces where beings dwell, known as the Non-conceptualizing Beings (asaṃjñisattva);
above those who are even less coarse is the Heaven of No Affliction (avṛha);
and above those who are even less afflicted is the Heaven of Good Vision (sudṛśa).
Twice the height of Sudarśana is the Abhāsvara Heaven;
twice the height of Abhāsvara are the celestial palaces of the Akaniṣṭha devas. O bhikṣus!

Above Akaniṣṭha, there are further heavens named the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; all of these are called abodes of the devas.
"O bhikṣus! Such are the locations and such are the realms where sentient beings dwell;
these sentient beings, whether coming or going, being born or passing away, reach their ultimate limit therein."
In this world, all sentient beings undergo birth, old age, and death; they abide within such paths of existence and do not transcend them—this is called the Saha World, the fearless land.
It is likewise in all other worlds throughout the ten directions. "O Bhikṣus!

To the north of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a continent named Uttarakuru. Its land is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly square on all four sides; the faces of the people of that continent correspond to the shape of the terrain."
"O bhikṣus!

To the east of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a continent named Pūrvavideha. Its land is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is circular like the full moon; the faces of the people on that continent likewise resemble the shape of the terrain."
"O Bhikṣus!

To the west of Sumeru, the king of mountains, there is a continent named Aparagoyānī. Its land is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its shape is like a half-moon; the faces of the people on that continent likewise resemble the shape of the land."
"O Bhikṣus!

On the southern side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a continent named Jambudvīpa. Its land is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, like the carriage of a Brahmin. Furthermore, the faces of the people therein resemble the shape of the terrain."
"O Bhikṣus!
The northern face of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is composed of celestial gold and illuminates the continent of Uttarakuru.
Its eastern face is composed of celestial silver and illuminates the continent of Pūrvavideha."
The western face of the heavens is composed of crystal and illuminates the continent of Aparagoyānī.
The southern face of the heavens is composed of blue lapis lazuli and illuminates the continent of Jambudvīpa. "O bhikṣus!

On the continent of Uttarakuru, there is a great tree named Āmra; its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and breadth, it extends twenty-one yojanas into the earth, it rises one hundred yojanas high, and its branches and leaves hang down and cover fifty yojanas.
"O Bhikṣus!

On the continent of Pūrvavideha, there is a great tree named Kadamba; its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and breadth, it extends twenty-one yojanas into the earth, it rises one hundred yojanas high, and its branches and foliage spread out and cover fifty yojanas."
"O Bhikṣus!
On the continent of Aparagoyānī there is a great tree named Tiṇḍuka; its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and breadth, and its branches and leaves extend downward to cover fifty yojanas."
Beneath that tree there is a stone ox, one yojana in height; for this reason, it is named Godānī, which in the Sui language means "Ox-Gift.
O Bhikṣus!

In this Jambudvīpa, there is a great tree called Jambu; its trunk is seven yojanas in both length and breadth, and its branches and leaves extend downward and outward to cover an area of fifty yojanas.

Beneath this tree, there is a mass of Jāmbūnada gold twenty yojanas high; because this superior gold originates from beneath the Jambu tree, it is named Jāmbūnada, and the Jāmbūnada gold derives its name from this.
"O Bhikṣus!

In the abodes of the nāgas and garuḍas, there is a great tree called Kūṭaśālmali; its trunk is seven yojanas in both length and breadth, and its branches and leaves extend downward and outward to cover fifty yojanas."
"O Bhikṣus!

In the realm of the asuras, there is a great tree named Supuṣpaka (Good Day Flower). Its trunk is seven yojanas in both length and breadth, and its branches and leaves extend downward to cover an area of fifty yojanas."
"O Bhikṣus!

Among the Trāyastriṃśa devas, there is a great tree named Devacāra. Its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and breadth, it extends twenty-one yojanas deep into the earth, it rises a hundred yojanas high, and its branches and foliage spread out and cover fifty yojanas."

“O Bhikṣus! Beneath Mount Sumeru, there is another mountain called Khadiraka, forty-two thousand yojanas in height and as wide at its summit; it is majestic and lovely, composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearl, musaragalva, and agate.”
"O Bhikṣus!

Between Mount Sumeru and Mount Khadiraka, the distance is eighty-four thousand yojanas. All around, immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, along with various exquisite fragrant substances, completely cover the surface of the water."
"O Bhikṣus!

Outside of Khadiraka, there is a mountain named Īṣādhara, twenty-one thousand yojanas high and as many yojanas wide at the summit; it is majestic and beautiful, composed of the seven precious gems, including agate."

Between Mount Khadiraka and Mount Īṣādhara, the distance is forty-two thousand yojanas; all around, immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, along with various exquisite fragrant substances, completely cover the surface of the water.
Outside Mount Īṣādhara is a mountain named Yugandhara, twelve thousand yojanas high and as wide at the summit; it is majestic and lovely, composed of the seven precious substances, including agate.

Between the two mountains, Īṣādhara and Yugandhara, the expanse is twenty-one thousand yojanas wide; it is completely covered by immeasurable quantities of *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, as well as various exquisite fragrant substances that blanket all the waters.

Outside the Gandhamādana Mountains there is a mountain named Sudarśana, six thousand yojanas high and as wide at its summit; it is majestic and lovely, composed even of the seven treasures such as agate and so forth.

The distance between Yugandhara and Mount Sudarśana is twelve thousand yojanas; all around, immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, along with various exquisite fragrant substances, completely cover the waters.

Outside Mount Sudarśana is a mountain named Aśvakarṇa (Horse-Ear), three thousand yojanas high and as wide at its summit; it is majestic and lovely, composed of the seven precious substances, including agate.

Between that Mount Sudarśana and Mount Aśvakarṇa, the distance across is six thousand yojanas; all around, upon the waters, there are immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, as well as various exquisite fragrant substances.

Beyond the Horse-Headed Mountain lies a mountain named Nimindhara, one thousand two hundred yojanas in height and of equal width at its summit; it is majestic and lovely, composed of the seven precious substances, including agate.

Between the two mountains, Aśvakarṇa and Nimindhara, the expanse is two thousand four hundred yojanas wide; it is surrounded by immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, as well as various exquisite fragrant substances, which completely cover the waters.
Outside Mount Nimindhara is a mountain named Vinataka, six hundred yojanas high and as wide at its summit; it is majestic and lovely, composed of the seven precious substances, including agate.

Between the two mountains, Nimiṃdhara and Vinataka, the width is one thousand two hundred yojanas; its circumference is immeasurable, and four kinds of variegated flowers, as well as various exquisite fragrant substances, completely cover all the waters.

Outside Mount Vinataka there is a mountain named Cakravāḍa (translated in the Sui language as "Circular Wheel"), which is the Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*). It is three hundred yojanas high, and its width at the summit is likewise; it is majestic and lovely, composed of the seven precious substances such as agate and so forth.

Between the two mountains, Vinataka and Cakravāḍa, the distance is six hundred yojanas; it is surrounded by immeasurable quantities of four kinds of variegated flowers and various exquisite fragrant substances, which completely cover the waters.
Not far from Mount Cakravāḍa, there is also a level expanse where green grass spreads everywhere;

this is the great ocean. To the north of the great ocean stands a king of trees called the Jambu tree. Its trunk has a circumference of seven yojanas and its roots extend twenty-one yojanas into the earth. It rises one hundred yojanas high, and including its branches and leaves, it extends fifty yojanas in all four directions, covering the area. On its periphery is an open space where green grass spreads everywhere.
Next, there are groves of āmra trees, jambu trees, tāla trees, and nāda trees, each fifty yojanas in length and breadth; between them are open spaces where various green grasses grow.

Next there are a male grove named Tree Forest and a female grove named Tree Forest, as well as the Śāṇḍana Forest and the Cāndana Forest; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with open spaces at their edges covered in lush green grass.

Next there were groves of harītakī fruit trees, bhallātaka fruit trees, āmalaka fruit trees, and āmrātaka fruit trees, each also fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with open spaces at their edges covered in lush green grass.

Next there are the Kṣudraka tree groves, the Bilva fruit groves, the Panasa fruit groves, and the pomegranate fruit groves; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with open spaces at their borders covered in lush green grass.

Next there are the forests of Udumbara trees, Mango trees, sugarcane, small bamboo, and large bamboo, each also fifty yojanas in length and breadth; at their edges there are open spaces covered with lush green grass.

Next there are forests of reeds, forests of rushes, forests of *kara*, forests of *mahākara*, and forests of *kāśamanta*, each also fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth, with open spaces at their borders covered with lush green grass.

Next, there are groves of atimuktaka flowers, campaka flowers, pāṭala flowers, and rose-apple flowers, each also fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with open spaces at their edges covered everywhere with green grass.
Furthermore, there are various ponds covered all over with *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are various ponds filled with venomous snakes, each also fifty yojanas in length and breadth; between them are open spaces entirely covered with green grass.
Next, there is a sea named Ucchanaka, twelve yojanas wide.
The water was clear and cool, its flavor exceedingly sweet, light, soft, and limpid.

It was surrounded on all sides by sevenfold terraces, interspersed with the seven precious gems; sevenfold railings and sevenfold networks of bells; and outside these, seven rows of *tāla* trees encircled it. All was exquisitely wonderful and majestic, adorned with the seven treasures such as agate and the rest.

Extending throughout the four directions, there were various stairways and paths, all of which were perfectly majestic and composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, agate, and other such precious substances.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers covering the surface of the water; those that were fire-colored immediately manifested flames of fire,
those that were gold-colored immediately manifested golden light,
and those that were blue immediately manifested blue light.
Those that were red manifested red light;
those that were white manifested white light;
those of the color of *pāṇḍu* manifested the light of *pāṇḍu*.
"The flowers are like chariot wheels and their roots are like chariot axles; these roots exude a sap that is white in color like milk and sweet in taste like honey. O Bhikṣus!"
In the ocean of Ucchanaka, there is a road traversed by the wheel-turning sage kings (cakravartin), which is twelve yojanas wide.
When a wheel-turning sage king appears in Jambudvīpa, this sea-road naturally emerges, becoming level with the surface of the water.
"O bhikṣus!
Beyond the ocean of Ucchanaka, there is a mountain named Uccakalā.
O bhikṣus!"

This Mount Kūṭaka is magnificent and well-proportioned, exquisite and beautiful to behold; all kinds of trees, leaves, flowers, fruits, and fragrances, as well as various grasses, birds, and beasts—all things produced in the world—are fully present within that mountain, none lacking.
"O bhikṣus!
Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is thus upright, exquisite, and beautiful to behold; you should all maintain this well. O bhikṣus!"
Next there is another mountain named Suvarṇapārśva (Golden Flank).

Within this mountain are eighty thousand caves, in which eighty thousand nāga-elephants dwell. They are all white in color like the kumuda flower, with seven limbs touching the ground; they all possess supernatural powers and travel through the air.
Its head is red in color, resembling the indragopaka insect; it is endowed with six tusks, which are slender and sharp, inlaid with gold of various colors.
O bhikṣus!
Beyond the Golden Flanks lies the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), five hundred yojanas in height, and likewise in breadth and thickness.
That mountain is exceptionally sublime, composed of four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On the four sides of that mountain, four golden peaks protrude beyond its perimeter, each twenty yojanas in height.
Furthermore, there are lofty peaks interspersed with various jewels, rising majestically and prominently to a height of one hundred yojanas.
Upon the summit of the mountain is a lake named Anavatapta, where the Naga King Anavatapta dwells.
The lake is fifty yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are cool and refreshing, sweet, light, and delicious, pure and free from turbidity.

It was surrounded on all sides by seven layers of brickwork, seven layers of wooden planking, seven rows of railings, and seven layers of bell-nets; it was magnificent and exquisite, composed of the seven treasures such as agate and the rest.

Furthermore, there were various flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—of diverse colors: blue, yellow, red, and white. Each flower was as large as a chariot wheel; beneath them were lotus roots as thick as chariot axles, with sap as white as milk and a flavor as sweet as honey.
"O bhikṣus!
Within this Lake Anavatapta, there is the palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta; its hall has five pillars and is exquisitely beautiful and lovely."
"The Dragon King Anavatapta, together with his retinue, sports therein, enjoying the five celestial sensual pleasures with ease and sovereignty. O Bhikṣus!"
To the east of Lake Anavatapta is the Gaṅgā River, which issues from the elephant’s mouth and flows into the eastern ocean together with five hundred rivers.
To the south of Lake Anavatapta is the Sindhu River, which issues from the bull’s mouth and flows into the southern ocean together with five hundred rivers.
To the west of Lake Anavatapta is the Vakṣu River, which issues from the Horse’s Mouth and flows into the western ocean together with five hundred rivers.
To the north of Lake Anavatapta is the Sītā River, which issues from the Lion’s Mouth and flows into the northern ocean together with five hundred rivers.
“Monks! For what reason is this nāga named Anavatapta? Monks!”
There are three causes and conditions.
What are the three? O monks!

Within Jambudvīpa, there are various abodes where nāgas dwell; with the exception of the Nāga King Anavatapta, when all other nāgas experience pleasure, hot sand immediately falls upon their bodies, and at that moment, they lose their celestial forms and manifest the appearance of snakes.
"Other nāgas experience these various sufferings from time to time, but the Nāga King Anavatapta does not; this is called the first causal condition, O bhikṣus!"

In Jambudvīpa, with the exception of the Nāga King Anavatapta, when the other nāgas sport and enjoy themselves, a hot wind comes and blows upon their bodies; they immediately lose their celestial forms and manifest the appearance of snakes, undergoing such suffering as this.
For the Naga King Anavatapta, such a thing does not occur; this is called the second causal condition. Monks!

When the various nagas within Jambudvīpa are sporting and enjoying themselves, the Garuḍa King flies into their palaces. Upon seeing the Garuḍa King, the nagas give rise to fear in their hearts. Because of that fear, they immediately lose their celestial forms and manifest the appearance of snakes, fully experiencing manifold sufferings.
For the Naga King Anavatapta, such a thing does not exist.
Should the Garuda King conceive such a thought as:
"I now wish to enter the inner palace of the Naga King Anavatapta," [it would be impossible].
"Because that garuḍa’s retribution is inferior, it immediately undergoes suffering for itself and can never enter the palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta.
O Bhikṣus!"
This is the third causal condition.
For this reason, it is called Anavatapta. "O bhikṣus!
Not far from the southern face of the Snowy Mountains is a city named Vaiśālī.
To the north of Vaiśālī are the Seven Black Mountains; to the north of the Seven Black Mountains is the Fragrant Mountain.
Within Mount Gandhamādana dwell immeasurable and boundless kinnaras, who are constantly engaged in the sounds of song, dance, and music.
That mountain abounds with various kinds of trees, each emitting diverse fragrant incenses; it is the dwelling place of deities of great majesty and power.
"O Bhikṣus!

Within that Fragrant Mountain there are two precious caves: the first named Variegated (Citra) and the second named Well-Variegated (Sucitra). They are exquisite and lovely, composed of the seven treasures including agate; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, soft and smooth, such that touching them is like the touch of kāñcanatiktaka cloth."
"O bhikṣus!

There is a gandharva king named Anupama (Without Parable), who dwells together with five hundred kinnarī women in two caves called Citra and Sucitra. There he fully experiences the five desires, enjoying himself and sporting as he walks, stands, sits, and lies down."
"O Bhikṣus!
To the north of the two caves, there is a great king of śāla trees named Supratiṣṭhita, surrounded on all sides by a separate grove of eight thousand śāla trees."
Beneath that well-established śāla grove lived a nāga-elephant, also named Well-Established, who dwelt and roamed therein.
Its color was exceedingly bright white, like a kumuda flower; its seven limbs touched the ground, and it moved through the air. The protuberance on its crown was as high as an indragopaka insect.
Its head was crimson in color and it possessed six tusks; these tusks were slender and sharp, inlaid with golden sand.

Furthermore, it had eight thousand other dragon-elephants as its retinue; they were all white in color like *kumuda* flowers, their seven limbs touching the ground, and their tusks were likewise entirely inlaid with gold.

To the north of the well-situated Śāla grove, for the sake of the great nāga-elephant king Supratiṣṭhita, there arose a lake named Mandākinī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal in all dimensions. Its waters were cool, sweet, clear, and free from all turbidity or impurity; even the lotus roots were as large as chariot axles, and when broken, they yielded a sap white as milk and as sweet as honey.
"O Bhikṣus!
Surrounding the side of the Mandākinī Pond, there are further eight thousand ponds encircling it on all four sides; each one is exactly like the Mandākinī, without any difference."
“Monks! When that Nāga-elephant king, Supratiṣṭhita, intends to enter the Mandākinī pool to sport, he immediately calls to mind his retinue of eight thousand nāga-elephants.”
At that time, those eight thousand dragon-elephants also gave rise to this thought:
"The Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita has turned his mind toward us; we shall now go to the place of King Supratiṣṭhita."
When the elephants had arrived, they all stood with their heads bowed before the great dragon-elephant king, Sunābha.
At that time, knowing that the elephants had assembled, the great dragon-elephant king Sunābha immediately set forth toward the Mandākinī pond.
Eight thousand dragon-elephants surrounded him on all sides as they followed in his train.
The elephant king Supratiṣṭhita walked with a composed and steady gait;
among the dragon-elephants, some held white parasols to shade him from above, while others used their trunks to hold white mani-whisks to brush his back.
There were various *nāga* deities who sang, danced, and performed as entertainers, leading the way before him.

At that time, the great *nāga* elephant king Supratiṣṭhita arrived and entered the Mandākinī pool; emerging and submerging himself, he bathed, frolicked, and played with joy, experiencing every pleasure according to his heart's desire.

Among them were some elephant-lords washing their trunks; some grinding their tusks; some rubbing their ears; some pouring water over their heads; some sprinkling their backs; some massaging their flanks; some washing their thighs; some washing their feet; and some bathing their tails.
Some elephant-lords plucked lotus roots, washed them clean with their trunks, and held them up to their mouths.
Others plucked *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers and fastened them upon the head of the Elephant King, Supratiṣṭhita.

At that time, the Great Nāga Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, within the Mandākinī pool, bathed at will, frolicked with joy, and enjoyed himself in sovereign bliss; he ate the lotus roots offered by other nāga elephants and adorned his head with various flowers such as blue lotuses (utpala).
When this was finished, they emerged from that pond and stood upon the bank.

Then, eight thousand nāga-elephants dispersed into eight thousand ponds, bathing at will and sporting freely to enjoy their pleasures. Having done so, each ate lotus roots; when they had finished eating, they also adorned themselves by fastening various flowers, such as *utpala* and others, upon their heads. They then gathered together once more before King Susīma, surrounding him on all four sides and remaining there in respectful attendance.
At that time, the Great Naga Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, preceded and followed by those eight thousand naga elephants, returned to the Supratiṣṭhita Śāla Grove.
As the Elephant King proceeded, various dragon-elephants followed him as before, some holding white parasols and others grasping white whisks; likewise, the gods played music to lead the way.

At that time, the Great Naga Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, having reached the great forest of Supratiṣṭhita Sāla trees, lay down and rose as he pleased beneath the king of trees, experiencing all manner of peace and happiness; likewise, eight thousand naga elephants each went to those eight thousand trees, moving, standing, lying down, and rising with sovereign ease and happiness.

In that forest there were *sāla* trees; some had trunks with a circumference of six *vyāmas*, while other *sāla* trees had trunks with a circumference of seven, eight, nine, or ten *vyāmas*. There were even *sāla* trees whose trunks measured twelve *vyāmas* in circumference, yet only this king of *sāla* trees, Supratiṣṭhita, had a trunk measuring sixteen *vyāmas* in circumference.
Within those eight thousand *sāla* groves, whenever there were withered or yellowed leaves or fallen foliage, a wind would immediately arise to blow them outside, so as not to defile the groves;
and as for all the excrement and urine of the eight thousand dragon-elephants, various *yakṣas* would sweep them up and cast them away.

“Monks! When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in Jambudvīpa, among his eight thousand elephants, the smallest one goes before the Wheel-Turning King every morning at dawn to provide service and attend to him; it is for this reason that the Elephant Treasure (hastiratna) receives its name.”
That Great Nāga Elephant King, Suvilokita, every fortnight at dawn, would go to where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was staying; he would stand before him and wait to receive his commands.
"O Bhikṣus!

The elephant king Supratiṣṭhita possesses such supernormal powers and such majestic virtue; although he was born among the animals as an elephant, he belongs to the lineage of nāgas and thus possesses such great power and majesty."
"You monks, you should remember and uphold this.
Chapter Two: On Uttarakuru, Part One. 'O monks!'"

In the continent of Uttarakuru there are immeasurable mountains. Within those mountains are various kinds of trees; these trees are lush and verdant, emitting all manner of fragrances, the scent of which wafts everywhere, pervading the entire continent.

Various kinds of grasses grow there, all of a deep azure-blue color, curling to the right like the feathers of a peacock; their fragrance is like that of the vārṣika flower, and they are as soft to the touch as kācilindika cloth. They are four finger-widths in length, bending down when one steps upon them and returning to their original state when the foot is lifted.
There are also various fruit trees of diverse colors, with stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits of many kinds, emitting all manner of fragrances that waft everywhere.
Various birds each sing their own songs; their calls are harmonious and elegant, their voices subtle and exquisite.

Within those various mountains, there are diverse rivers flowing and dispersing in a hundred channels, descending smoothly and flowing gradually with steady motion; they are neither sluggish nor rapid, and are free from waves.

Their banks are not deep, being level and shallow enough to cross easily; the water is clear and limpid, covered above by various flowers, and half a yojana wide, filled throughout with flowing water.

On both banks of the various rivers, there are diverse groves that grow along the water; their branches and leaves cast a dense shade, while various fragrant flowers and diverse fruits abound. Lush green grass carpets the ground, and flocks of birds sing in harmony.

Furthermore, on that riverbank, there were various exquisite boats, adorned with diverse colors, wonderful and lovely to behold; they were all fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.

“Monks! The continent of Uttarakuru is level and even; it is free from thorns, dense thickets, pits, chasms, latrines, filth, impurities, gravel, and potsherds. It consists entirely of gold and silver; it is neither cold nor hot, and its seasons are harmonious.
The ground is always moist and lush, covered with green grass, and various groves of trees have branches and leaves that are perpetually flourishing, bearing flowers and fruit.”
"O Bhikṣus!

In the continent of Uttarakuru, there is further a forest named Anvaya (Abiding). Its trees are all six krośas high—one krośa being five li—and their leaves are densely layered and joined together in succession, like thatch covering a house, so that raindrops do not leak through. The people there dwell beneath these trees."

There are various fragrant trees, some six krośas in height, others five krośas, and some four, three, two, or one krośa; even the smallest tree is half a krośa in height. They all possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, and from these trees, various fragrances flow forth according to one's wishes.

Furthermore, there are *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, each six *krośas* high, down to five, four, three, two, and one *krośa*; the smallest of these are half a *krośa*. All of them possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, from the sides of which various garments spontaneously emerge and hang suspended among the trees.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of necklaces-trees; these trees are also six *krośas* in height, down to five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*. They all possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, from the sides of which various necklaces flow forth according to one's wishes, hanging down and remaining suspended.

There are also garland-trees; these trees likewise reach a height of six *krośas*, down to five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, and even as little as half a *krośa*. They possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, from the sides of which various forms of garlands emerge according to one's wishes and hang upon the trees.

Furthermore, there are vessel-trees; these trees are also six *krośas* high, down to five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*. They likewise possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. From the side of these fruits, various vessel-shapes emerge according to one's wishes and hang from the trees.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of diverse fruit trees; these trees are also six *krośas* in height, or even five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*. All of them possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. From the branches of these trees, all manner of fruits emerge according to one's wishes, remaining upon the trees.

Furthermore, there are trees of music; these trees are likewise six *krośas* high, with others ranging down to five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, and even as small as half a *krośa*. They possess various branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, from which various musical instruments emerge according to one's wishes and hang amidst the trees.
That land also possesses natural non-glutinous rice that does not require cultivation; it is fresh, pure white, and free of husks or chaff.

When they wish to cook it, there are other fruits called *dun-chi* which serve as cauldrons; by burning *huo-zhu* (fire-jewels), flames emerge naturally without the need for firewood or charcoal, cooking all manner of food and drink according to their desires.
Once the food is cooked, the jewel-flames subside.

“Monks! On the continent of Uttarakuru, there are four great lakes surrounding its four sides; each lake is named Anavatapta. They are each fifty yojanas in length and breadth. Their waters are cool, soft, sweet, light, fragrant, pure, and unclouded.”
It was surrounded on all sides by seven layers of brick walls, seven layers of wooden planks, and seven layers of railings; seven-layered nets of bells hung down all around.

Furthermore, there were seven rows of *tāla* trees encircling it on all four sides, beautiful with their variegated colors, composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
On each of the four sides of the pond there are stairways, and each individual stairway is likewise composed of the seven treasures, variegated with diverse colors;

furthermore, there are various flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers—in blue, yellow, red, white, as well as pale green and azure hues. Each flower is as large as a chariot wheel, and their fragrance is pervasive, subtle, and most excellent.
There are also lotus roots as thick as chariot axles; when broken, they exude sap the color of milk, which is sweet and delicious to eat, its flavor like honey.

“Monks! On the four sides of Lake Anavatapta there are four great rivers, each one yojana in width, covered with various flowers. The water flows smoothly and directly without meandering; it is neither swift nor sluggish, free from waves, surges, or collisions. Their banks are not high; they are level, shallow, and easy to enter.”
On both banks of the various rivers, there are diverse groves whose interlacing branches cast a covering shade and emit manifold exquisite fragrances.

Various kinds of grasses grow along their sides; they are green and soft, curling to the right. To speak briefly, they reach a height of four finger-widths; when one steps down, they sink, and when one lifts the foot, they return to their original state.
There are also various birds that utter diverse sounds.

On both banks of the river there were also various boats, multicolored and delightful, even composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva and agate; they were soft to the touch, like kācilindika cloth.

“Monks! In the continent of Uttarakuru, at midnight, great dense clouds arise from among the four lakes of Anavatapta, spreading everywhere until they completely cover the continent of Uttarakuru, as well as all its mountains and seas. Only then does it rain the water of eight meritorious qualities, for a duration like the time it takes to milk a cow, falling to a depth of four finger-breadths. Wherever it falls, it immediately sinks into the earth and does not flow away.”

Returning at midnight, the rain ceased and the clouds dispersed, leaving the sky pure and clear. A wind rose from the ocean, blowing this sweet moisture—cool, refreshing, and soft—which brought peace and comfort upon contact. It moistened the continent of Uttarakuru, making it everywhere temperate, fertile, and lush.
“Just as when a skilled garland-maker or a garland-maker’s apprentice has finished making a garland and sprinkles it with water, that garland, being sprinkled, becomes lustrous and bright. O monks!”
The continent of Uttarakuru is likewise always moist, delightful, lustrous, and glossy, as if someone were constantly anointing it with clarified butter. Monks!

On the continent of Uttarakuru, there is another lake named Suprabha. This lake is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are cool, refreshing, soft, pure, and free from turbidity. It is paved with bricks of the seven precious gems, and even the roots of its lotuses have a flavor as sweet as honey.

"Monks! To the east of Lake Sudarśana, there is another grove, also named Sudarśana. This grove is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of bell-nets, and seven rows of tāla trees. It is of various delightful colors, composed entirely of the seven treasures, including *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*."

On each side, there are various gates, and at every gate there are defensive towers, variegated and delightful, composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, ruby, musaragalva, and agate.
"O Bhikṣus!

That Subhavyūha Garden is level, upright, and majestic; it is free from thorns, hills, mounds, pits, gravel, tiles, rubble, as well as privies and other various impurities, containing instead an abundance of gold, silver, and various kinds of rare jewels.
Its seasons are harmonious, being neither cold nor hot."
There are always springs and streams flowing and overflowing on all four sides; the leaves of the trees are lush and flourishing, and the flowers and fruits are fully ripened.
There are various fragrances that waft sweetly with the wind;
furthermore, there are various birds of diverse species that constantly utter exquisite sounds, harmonious, elegant, pure, and refreshing.

There are grasses of green color, curling to the right in elegant spirals, soft, fine, and smooth like peacock feathers; their fragrance resembles that of the *bālisika* flower, and their touch is like that of *kācalindika* cloth; when stepped upon with the foot, they sink and rise in accordance with the movement of the foot.
Furthermore, there are various trees, each possessing diverse roots, trunks, flowers, leaves, and fruits, all of which emit manifold fragrances that universally permeate that land.
"O Bhikṣus!

Within the Subhavyūha Garden, there is also a grove named Sthāvara. Its trees all rise to a height of six krośas; their leaves are densely layered so that raindrops do not fall through, overlapping like the thatch upon a grass-roofed house, and people dwell and lodge beneath them.

Furthermore, there are fragrant trees, karpāsa trees, garland trees, wreath trees, vessel trees, and fruit trees. There is also naturally ripened non-glutinous rice and cooked rice, pure and exquisite."
"O Bhikṣus!

That Caitraratha Garden is without self and without owner, and it has no guardian. When the people of Uttarakuru wish to enter this garden to sport at will and experience various pleasures, they may proceed through its four gates as they please. Having entered the garden, they sport, bathe, and indulge in pleasure according to their desires; when they wish to leave, they leave, and when they wish to stay, they stay, moving with complete freedom according to their hearts."

"O Bhikṣus! For the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, to the south of the Sudarśana Lake, there is another grove called Samantabhadra. This grove is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, and so forth, up to the pure, exquisite, and delicious cooked rice."
"O Bhikṣus!

This Universal Virtue Garden (Samantabhadra-udyāna) is likewise without a guardian. Whenever the people of Uttarakuru wish to enter the Universal Virtue Garden to bathe, play, and enjoy pleasure, they may enter through any of its four gates as they please. Having entered, they bathe, play, and enjoy themselves; once they have finished enjoying themselves, they may depart whenever they wish, or remain whenever they wish."

“O Bhikṣus! For the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, to the west of Lake Suprabha, there is another grove called Supuṣpa. This grove is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings; briefly described, it is exactly like the Suprabha grove without any difference, and likewise has no guardian.

When the people of Uttarakuru wish to enter the Saumanasa Garden to bathe, sport, and enjoy themselves, they enter through whichever of its four gates they please; having entered, they bathe, sport, and experience pleasure. Once they have enjoyed themselves, they may leave whenever they wish, or remain as long as they wish.

“Monks! For the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, to the north of Lake Sudarśana, there is another grove called Nandana, exactly one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and so forth, until: it has no guardians.”

When the people of Uttarakuru wish to enter the Nandana Grove to bathe, play, and enjoy pleasure, they may enter through any of its four gates as they please. Having entered, they bathe, play, and experience delight; once they have enjoyed themselves, they may depart whenever they wish to go, or remain whenever they wish to stay. A brief description is as previously given for the Sudarśana Grove and others.

"O Bhikṣus! For the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, to the east of Lake Sudarśana and bordering the Garden of Sudarśana, there is a river named Easy Access Road. It flows gradually downstream, without waves, neither slow nor swift, covered everywhere with various flowers, and two and a half yojanas in width."

"O Bhikṣus! The River of Entering the Path is easy to traverse. On both its banks stand various kinds of trees, their branches and leaves forming a dense canopy that emits all manner of fragrances, which universally perfume the entire area. Various kinds of grasses grow there; briefly described, they are so soft to the touch as to be like kācilindika cloth. They rise to a height of four finger-breadths, and when stepped upon by the feet, they sink or rise according to the foot, following it upward or downward.
Furthermore, there are various fruit trees of diverse colors, fully endowed with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits."
Furthermore, various fragrances waft everywhere,
and diverse birds each sing in harmonious chorus.

On both banks of the river are many exquisite boats, variegated and delightful, fashioned from the seven treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate— adorned and embellished with these precious materials.

“O Bhikṣus! For the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a great river to the south of Lake Sudarśana called Śubhavati. It flows gradually downstream; a brief description of it is entirely like that of the River Easy-to-Enter.”
All the various groves of trees here are no different from those [in the other realms], even down to the boats, which are composed of variegated colors and are as soft as kācilindika cloth.
"O Bhikṣus!
To the west of Lake Sudarśana, for the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a great river named Samtāna; [the description] continues as before in brief, flowing down gradually."
"O Bhikṣus!

To the north of Lake Sudarśana, for the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a great river named Oghavatī. It flows gradually downward; to speak briefly, its two banks have boats adorned with the seven precious gems, as soft as kācilindika cloth."
In this regard, there is a summary verse (*uddāna*):
“Subhūti, Samantabhadra, and others, Sukusuma, Nanda, and Sukha,
Supraveśa and Suvapu, Tulyaratha, Īśvara, and Sindhu.”

"Monks! When the people of Uttarakuru wish to enter those rivers—the Easy-to-Enter Way, the Well-Bodied, the Equal-Cart, and the Majestic Lord—to bathe, play, and enjoy various pleasures, they all go to both banks of those rivers, take off their clothes, place them on the shore, and each sit in a boat. They row into the water, bathe their bodies, and enjoy themselves in play."
Having finished bathing, whoever was first to emerge from the water would take the upper garment that was there, put it on, and depart, without seeking out their own original garment.
Why is this? Because the people of Uttarakuru have no sense of "I" or "mine," and they possess nothing to guard.

Furthermore, these people proceed to the base of the various fragrant trees; having reached the trees, they naturally bend their branches downward and droop them, emitting exquisite fragrances for those people so that they may reach them by grasping with their own hands.

Those people take various kinds of incense from the trees and smear it upon their bodies; they then each proceed to the *karpāsa* trees, and upon arriving, those trees likewise bend their branches downward as before, producing various garments that reach the hands of those people for them to grasp.

That person further takes various kinds of exquisite garments from the tree, puts them on, and departs; proceeding further, he goes beneath the *mālā-vṛkṣa* (garland-tree). Upon arriving there, the branches of the garland-tree likewise all bend downward, yielding for those people various kinds of exquisite garlands that can be grasped by their hands.

Those people take various kinds of necklaces and ornaments from the trees and fasten them upon their bodies. They then proceed further to the *mālya-vṛkṣa* (garland trees). Upon reaching those trees, the branches naturally bend downward for them, and various exquisite, precious garlands flow forth, allowing the people to grasp them with their hands.

Having taken these wonderful garlands from the branches and bound them upon their heads, they proceed further to the *bhājana-vṛkṣa* (vessel trees). Upon reaching those trees, the branches likewise naturally bend downward, reaching their hands; they take whatever vessels they desire according to their wishes, and carrying them, they proceed to the fruit trees.

At that time, those fruit trees also bent their branches downward for the sake of the people, producing various kinds of excellent and sweet fruits within reach of the hand. Those people, according to their hearts' desire, would take the ripe fruits from the trees and eat them to their satisfaction; some among them would even squeeze out the juice, collect it in vessels, and drink it.

When the eating and drinking were finished, they proceeded once more to the Grove of Musical Instruments. Upon reaching that grove, for the sake of those people, the branches of the musical instrument trees all bent downward, producing various kinds of musical instruments within reach of their hands.

Those people, at the trees, each take whatever musical instruments they require according to their needs; these are exquisite in form and harmonious in sound. Having taken them, they embrace them and roam to the east and west, playing them when they wish to play, dancing when they wish to dance, and singing when they wish to sing, enjoying all manner of pleasures according to their inclinations.
"When these matters have been concluded, each may go or remain according to their own preference. (From the *Qishi jing*, Scroll One).

This scripture is titled the *Qishi yinben jing* in the Song Canon, translated by Jñānagupta; it was relegated to the position of a later scripture and included in the "Qu" (取) case. In the Dan Canon, it is titled the *Qishi jing* and is promoted to the position of a primary scripture.

Now, having consulted the *Kaiyuan lu*, the edition from the Danzang is deemed the correct one; therefore, the title here has removed the two characters "yinben" (original source) and has been advanced to "Chenghan" (Case of Clarification).
The Scripture on the Arising of the World, Volume Two, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Section on the Continent of Uttarakuru, Part Two.

“O monks! The people of Uttarakuru have hair that is deep blue-black in color and reaches a length of eight finger-breadths. All are of one kind, with a single form and a single color; there are no distinct physical features by which their differences can be known.”

"O Bhikṣus! The people of Uttarakuru all possess clothing; there are none who are naked or partially exposed. They treat kin and strangers with equal impartiality, without favoritism or aversion. Their teeth are all even and closely set, neither missing nor sparse; they are exquisite, pure, and clean, white as a conch shell, brilliant and lovely."

"O Bhikṣus! When the people of Uttarakuru feel hunger or thirst and require food and drink, they simply gather it; there is no plowing or sowing. There is naturally occurring non-glutinous rice, pure, fresh, and white, devoid of husks or chaff. Having taken it, they place it in a *dun-hi* fruit-vessel. They then take a fire-gem and place it beneath the vessel. Through the power of the beings' merit, the fire-gem spontaneously emits flames at the appropriate time. Once the food and drink are cooked, the flames extinguish themselves."
When that person obtained the rice and wished to eat, he prepared the vessels and sat down upon his seat.

At that time, if people came from the four quarters wishing to eat together with him, he would immediately provide them with food; yet the rice was never exhausted. Even until the last person had finished eating, the vessel of rice provided remained constantly full.

When those people eat this naturally ripened non-glutinous rice, which is free of husks and chaff, it is pure, fragrant, and delicious, replete with every flavor; no soup or broth is required. The color and form of the rice are like the taste of the *sudhā* nectar of the devas, and its appearance is as pure white and radiant as a cluster of flowers.

Once that person has eaten, their body becomes full and robust, without decrease or deficiency; it remains serene and unchanged, free from aging or transformation. This food continues to benefit that person until their physical form, strength, tranquility, and eloquence are all fully perfected.

“Monks! When the people of Uttarakuru feel lustful attachment toward a woman, they turn their eyes to gaze upon her according to their desire. Once she perceives this, she immediately follows after him. When the man leads her beneath a tree, if the woman he has taken with him is his mother, paternal aunt, sister, or a relative, the branches of the tree do not bend downward as they normally do; its leaves wither and fall out of season, failing to provide a canopy, and it produces neither flowers nor fruit, nor does it provide a bed or bedding for them.”

If she is not their mother, aunt, sister, or other such relative, the tree immediately lowers its branches and droops its twigs to provide shade; its trunk and leaves become lush and flourishing, and its flowers and fruits fresh and radiant. It also produces for that person hundreds of thousands of kinds of couches, mats, and bedding, and they together enter beneath the tree to enjoy themselves as they please in pleasure and delight.
“Monks! The people of Uttarakuru remain in the mother’s womb for only seven days; on the eighth day, they are immediately born.
Once the birth is complete, the mother places the newborn—whether male or female—at a crossroads and departs, leaving them behind.”

As people traveling east, west, south, and north pass back and forth upon that road, they see these men and women and feel compassion for them; for the sake of nourishing them, each places a finger into their mouths, from the tips of which flows naturally a most excellent and sweet milk that feeds the men and women, enabling them to survive.

Having drunk this milk for seven days, those men and women regained their own bodies of a single species, identical in size and form to those they had previously possessed; the men returned to follow the men, and the women returned to follow the women, each departing together with their respective companions.
“Monks! The people of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan and do not die prematurely; when their lives come to an end, they all attain rebirth in the higher realms.
For what reason and by what causes and conditions do the people of Uttarakuru obtain this fixed lifespan, such that after their lives end, they all again attain rebirth in the higher realms?”
"O bhikṣus!

There may be some persons in the world who are exclusively devoted to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and are reborn in hell."

Furthermore, there may be someone who has never killed living beings, has not stolen the property of others, has not engaged in sexual misconduct, has not spoken falsely, has not been double-tongued, has not used harsh speech, has not engaged in frivolous chatter, and has been without covetousness, malice, or wrong views. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their body breaks up and life ends, they proceed toward the good realms and are reborn among humans or devas.
For what causes and conditions do beings descend to lower births?
It is because of such things as killing and wrong views.
For what causes and conditions do they ascend to higher births?
This is because of [the practice of] non-killing, right view, and so forth.
Furthermore, some people may think:
"I should now practice the ten wholesome actions; by reason of these causes and conditions, when my body perishes, I shall attain rebirth in Uttarakuru."
"Once born there, one will dwell for a lifespan of a thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Having made such a vow, that person practices the ten wholesome actions and, upon the dissolution of the body, is reborn in Uttarakuru. There, they likewise obtain a fixed lifespan, fulfilling exactly a thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
"Monks! By this cause and condition, the people of Uttarakuru obtain a fixed lifespan. Monks!"
For what reason do they all attain rebirth there?
O monks! Because the people of Jambudvīpa receive the ten wholesome courses of action from others, they attain rebirth in the realm of Uttarakuru immediately upon the end of their lives.

Because the people of Uttarakuru have long possessed the ten wholesome courses of action and practice according to the Dharma within Uttarakuru, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall all be reborn in the higher realms among the devas.
"Monks! By this cause and condition, the people of Uttarakuru are reborn in superior realms. Monks!"

When the life of a person in Uttarakuru comes to an end and they relinquish their lifespan, there is not a single person who grieves, laments, or weeps; rather, they are collectively carried to a crossroads and abandoned there before departing.
“Monks! Among the people of Uttarakuru there is such a custom:

when the lifespan of any sentient being comes to an end, there is a bird named Ucchunga-ma (translated in the Sui language as ‘High-Flying’), which flies swiftly from the great mountains and arrives; it seizes the hair of the deceased with its beak, takes their corpse, and casts it away onto another continent or island.”
Why is this? Because the people of Uttarakuru possess pure karmic conduct and delight in cleanliness.
Because their minds are joyful, they do not allow the wind to carry foul and impure odors to where they dwell.
"O Bhikṣus!
When the people of Uttarakuru are about to discharge their excrement or urine, the earth cracks open for them; once they have finished, the earth closes back up as it was before."
Why is this? Because the people of Uttarakuru delight in purity and cleanliness, and they take pleasure in mental joy.
Furthermore, for what reason is that place called the continent of Uttarakuru?
"O Bhikṣus!

Among the four continents within the four quarters of the world, that continent of Uttarakuru is the most superior, the most exquisite, the highest, and the most excellent compared to the other three continents; therefore, that continent is called Uttarakuru. The correct pronunciation of 'Uttarakuru' is *Uttarakurau*; in the Sui language, it means 'elevated and superior,' signifying that it is elevated and superior to all other regions."
Chapter Three: On the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings. From the *Sūtra on the Arising of the World*: "O Bhikṣus!

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world within Jambudvīpa, this Jambudvīpa naturally possesses seven kinds of auspicious treasures, and the body of the Wheel-Turning King further possesses four kinds of supernormal powers and virtues."

What are the seven treasures? First, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth, the divine jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the treasurer treasure; and seventh, the military commander treasure. These are the seven treasures.
"Monks! What is meant by a Wheel-Turning Sage King being endowed with the precious wheel? Monks!"

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King emerges from Jambudvīpa, having been consecrated with water as a Kṣatriya sovereign, on the morning of the full moon on the fifteenth day when he observes the fast, he bathes himself until pure. He wears garments of unspun white cotton, lets his hair hang down, and adorns himself with mani-jewels and various necklaces. Standing atop a multi-storied pavilion, he is surrounded by his kinsmen and ministers before and behind him.

At that time, before the king, the precious golden wheel suddenly appeared in response; its diameter was seven cubits, and it was fully endowed with all characteristics—the thousand spokes, hub, and rim—spontaneously perfected and not fashioned by any craftsman.
At that time, the consecrated Kṣatriya wheel-turning sage-king had this thought:
"I have heard it said in the past:

'If a consecrated Kṣatriya king, on the morning of the full moon on the fifteenth day when he has observed the fast, having bathed and purified himself, wearing unwashed white cotton garments and various necklaces and ornaments, stands upon a pavilion surrounded by his kinsmen and ministers before and behind him—at that moment, a divine golden wheel-treasure suddenly appears before the king, with a thousand spokes, hub, and rim, complete in all its characteristics, appearing spontaneously and not fashioned by a craftsman; the wheel is seven cubits in diameter, golden both inside and out. When such an auspicious omen is obtained, he then achieves the merit of a wheel-turning king.'"
"I have now obtained this; it must surely be that I am a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

At that time, the consecrated Kṣatriya Wheel-Turning Sage King, desiring to test that divine wheel-treasure, commanded the fourfold army—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—to be fully prepared.

Once the fourfold army was fully equipped, the king proceeded to where the divine golden wheel was located; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground before the golden wheel, extended his right hand to touch the precious wheel, and spoke these words:
"O divine golden wheel, if I am truly a Wheel-Turning King, may you subdue those places not yet subdued by me."
At his voice, that divine wheel-treasure immediately turned, for the purpose of subduing those not yet subdued. Monks!

At that time, having seen the wheel-treasure turn in this manner, the consecrated Kṣatriya king ordered his chariot to be prepared and set out toward the eastern direction; thereupon, the wheel-treasure and the fourfold army all followed at once.
"O Bhikṣus!

Before the wheel-treasure, there further appear the bodies of four great devas who lead the way. To whatever region the divine wheel-treasure arrives and halts, the Wheel-turning Sage King and his fourfold army all remain and lodge in that place."

"At that time, all the kings of every land in the eastern direction each took golden vessels filled with silver grain and silver vessels filled with golden grain; having prepared these, they all went together before the Wheel-Turning King and addressed him, saying:
'Welcome, O Heavenly King!'"

Welcome! These offerings now presented are the property of the Heavenly King. In the eastern regions, the people enjoy abundance, joy, and peace, free from all fear; the households are numerous and exceedingly delightful.

We pray that Great Heaven will look upon us with compassion and accept our offerings; have pity on us, these minor kings, for today we serve Your Majesty with single-minded devotion, without a second thought.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King addressed the various kings, saying:

"If you can be thus sincere in heart, you should each, within your own realms, govern and transform according to the Dharma to nurture all living beings, ensuring that nothing unlawful occurs within your kingdoms."
Why is this? If any unlawful or evil matters should manifest and spread within my realm, you shall be punished for your crimes without exception.

I now instruct you all to personally abstain from taking life and to teach others not to kill; do not take what is not given, and do not engage in sexual misconduct, false speech, or even wrong views—none of these should be committed.

If you can refrain from taking life, teach others not to kill, do not take what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, speak truthful words, and maintain right view, then I shall know with certainty that you kings, together with your entire nations, have been subdued.

“At that time, the kings of the various kingdoms in the eastern direction, having heard such an exhortation from the Wheel-Turning King, all simultaneously undertook the practice of the ten wholesome courses of action.”
Having received [the wheel], they each governed their respective realms according to the Dharma.

By the sovereign power of the Cakravartin King, wherever he turned, the Wheel Treasure followed him. Thus, having subdued all the kingdoms of the eastern direction, this celestial golden wheel treasure of the Holy King traveled extensively as far as the eastern ocean; thereafter, it returned and proceeded in succession through the south, the west, and even the north, leading the way along the path traversed by the ancient Cakravartin Kings.

When the Wheel-Turning Sage King and his fourfold army proceed in succession, there are first the bodies of the Four Great Kings who precede the wheel-treasure. Wherever this wheel-treasure halts, the Wheel-Turning Sage King and his fourfold army will immediately halt and lodge in that direction.

"At that time, all the kings of every land in the northern quarter also each brought vessels of natural gold filled with silver grain and vessels of natural silver filled with gold grain, and together they came to the place where the wheel-turning king was."
Having arrived, he knelt on his right knee and spoke these words:
"Excellent, O Deva, that you have come!
Excellent, O Deva, that you have come!"

"Under the power of the Heavenly King, we of the northern region have seen our people flourish, enjoying abundance, joy, and peace; free from all fears, it is most delightful. We pray that Your Majesty will remain here to carry out your governance and transformation; we, your subjects, shall follow in obedience, never daring to harbor divided hearts."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King commanded the various kings, saying:
"If you are able to do so, each of you shall govern and transform your respective realms in accordance with my instructions; do not allow anything within your borders to be contrary to the Dharma."
Why is this? If there should be any who act contrary to the Dharma or commit evil deeds within my realm, I shall punish you.

Furthermore, you must not kill living beings yourselves, nor incite others to kill; do not take what is not given; abandon sexual misconduct, false speech, and even wrong views—you must sever all such things.

If you abstain from taking life, and so forth, up to practicing right view for both yourselves and others—if you are able to do thus, I shall know with confidence that your lands have already been well-subdued.
At that time, all the kings raised their voices in unison and addressed the Wheel-Turning King, saying:
"As Your Majesty commands, we, your subjects, shall carry it out.
Then, the kings of the northern regions, having heard such instructions from the Wheel-Turning King, each and every one of them received and followed the practice of the ten virtuous actions.
Having received them, they uphold and maintain them all in accordance with the Dharma, each governing and transforming their respective realms according to the Vinaya.

By the sovereign power of the Wheel-Turning Sage King, wherever he travels, the wheel-treasure follows him. This golden wheel-treasure, in this successive manner, subdues the northern regions, reaching as far as the shores of the northern ocean; having completed his circuit, it returns to its original place.

At that time, the Wheel-Treasure selected the most supreme, majestic, and exquisitely beautiful site within Jambudvīpa. Upon this site, it demarcated a boundary measuring seven yojanas in width from east to west and twelve yojanas in length from south to north. Once these measurements had been established as the boundaries, the various devas immediately descended from the sky during that night and constructed a palace for the Wheel-Turning King, which was completed in an instant.
Once it was accomplished, it was of exquisite color and dignified appearance, adorned with the four jewels—namely, celestial gold, celestial silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
For the sake of the noble king, this precious wheel-jewel remained suspended motionless in the air above the palace gate, as steady as a wheel fixed upon its axle.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King experienced immeasurable great joy and exultation, and he thought to himself:
"I have now obtained the precious wheel-treasure!"
"Monks! A wheel-turning sage king possesses such a divine golden wheel-treasure, naturally complete in all its aspects. Monks!"
Furthermore, what kind of white elephant-treasure (*hastiratna*) does a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) possess, which he ought to fulfill? O monks!

When this Wheel-Turning King sits in his main hall during the first watch of the day, the elephant-treasure named Uposatha—translated in the Sui language as "Pure and Even"—immediately appears before the king. Its physical form is sublime; its color is pure white like the *kumuda* flower. Its seven limbs touch the ground, and it possesses great supernormal power, traveling through the air. Its head is crimson-red like the *indrāyudha* insect. It has six tusks, all of which are slender and sharp. Each tusk is fully adorned with various colors inlaid like golden grains.
Having seen the elephant-treasure, the Wheel-Turning Sage King thought to himself:
"Although this white elephant has appeared, I do not yet know if it has been tamed, whether it is capable of enduring various tasks, or if it will become a noble mount."

At that time, within a single day, the elephant-treasure was thoroughly tamed; it became fit for harnessing in all matters, just like other elephants that have been perfectly trained for immeasurable thousands of years—stately, virtuous, pleasing, and compliant.
In this way, indeed, this precious white elephant becomes temporarily tamed within a single day and is capable of performing all tasks; it is just so.

Then, in order to test the elephant, at dawn when the sun first rose, the Wheel-Turning King mounted this precious elephant and traveled in circuitous rounds, traversing all the coastal regions to the very limits of the earth.
Having completed his circuit, the Wheel-Turning King returned to his palace and partook of light food.
For this reason, at that time, the king rejoiced within his heart, leaping for joy with delight:
"For my sake, such a precious elephant has been born."
"O bhikṣus! A wheel-turning sage king possesses such white elephant-treasures as these, naturally and spontaneously complete. O bhikṣus!"
What is meant by the Cakravartin King being endowed with the horse-treasure? Monks!

At the first watch of the day, while the Cakravartin King is seated upon his main throne, there appears before him the horse-treasure named Bhalluka (translated in the Sui language as "Long-haired"). It is blue in color with a glossy body; its mane and tail are lustrous, its head is black, and its mane flows down. Possessing supernormal powers, it travels through the air.
At that time, having seen the horse-treasure, the Wheel-turning King thought to himself:
"Although this horse has appeared, it is not yet known whether, when trained, it will be capable of enduring all tasks; can it become a fine mount for me?"

At that time, within a single day, the horse-treasure was thoroughly tamed and became capable of enduring all tasks, just like other horses that have been perfectly trained and well-accustomed for countless thousands of years.
In this very way, when this horse is being trained, it becomes capable of performing all tasks within a single day; it is just so.

Then, wishing to test the horse, at the break of dawn when the sun first rises, the Wheel-Turning King mounts this precious horse, traverses the entire earth, and returns to his own palace before the Wheel-Turning Sage-King even begins to take his meal.
For this reason, he gave rise to great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking:
"I have now obtained the treasure of the dark-blue horse! O bhikṣus!
