The wheel-turning sage-king is thus fully endowed with such horse-treasures.
"Monks, what is meant by the wheel-turning sage-king being fully endowed with the jewel-treasure?"
"O Bhikṣus!

A wheel-turning sage king possesses a maṇi-jewel, the color of lapis lazuli, complete with eight facets, not fashioned by a craftsman, exceptionally beautiful and sublime, naturally emitting pure radiance."
At that time, having seen the jewel-treasure, the Wheel-turning King thought to himself:
"This maṇi-jewel is perfect in all its characteristics; I should now suspend it within the palace so that it may manifest its radiance."

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test this maṇi jewel, arrayed his fourfold army—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry. Having fully prepared these four forces, at midnight, when a light rain fell from the heavens and thick clouds shrouded the sky in darkness, and as flashes of lightning appeared, the Holy Wheel-Turning King took this precious jewel and suspended it atop a banner, then went out to roam within the park.
For what reason?
Because he intends to wander about and examine the qualities of the jewel. O bhikṣus!

This maṇi jewel atop the high banner shines universally throughout the four directions; the fourfold army is clearly visible in its entirety, its radiance pervading everywhere like the sun illuminating the world.

At that time, all the brahmins, householders, and others in that land, thinking that the light of the sun had already appeared, were startled awake and rose together to attend to their various affairs.
For these reasons, the Wheel-Turning Sage King experienced great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking:
"This treasure has been born for me!"
"Monks! A wheel-turning sage king is thus fully endowed with such precious jewels. Monks!"
What is meant by the Cakravartin King’s possession of the Woman-Jewel? Monks!

In the world of a Cakravartin King, a Woman-Jewel is born who is neither coarse nor delicate, neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark; she is most excellent and most wondrous, her deportment is graceful and beautiful, her physical appearance is perfect, and those who behold her find it pleasing to look upon without ever growing weary.

Furthermore, this Woman-Jewel is cool to the touch when it is hot and warm to the touch when it is cold; her body emits a wondrous fragrance like that of sandalwood, and from her mouth there constantly issues the scent of the utpala lotus.

For the sake of the Wheel-Turning King, she goes to bed late and rises early, acting with diligence, care, and reverence; in all her actions, she never fails to please the king’s mind. This woman harbors not even an evil thought in her heart, much less any transgression in her body or speech.
For this reason, the Wheel-Turning Sage King experienced great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking to himself:
"Has this maiden-jewel already been born for me!"
"Monks! A wheel-turning sage king is endowed with such female treasures as these. Monks!"
What is meant by the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s Jewel of the Treasurer being endowed with sovereign power?

Monks! When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, the Jewel of the Treasurer is born. He is immensely wealthy, possessing abundant riches and many merits; as a karmic reward, he has attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), through which he clearly perceives all hidden treasures (*nidhi*) within the earth, whether they have an owner or not. All such things are discerned by his vision, whether they be in water or on land, far or near. Whatever rare and precious objects exist therein, this Treasurer acts as their guardian, protecting and watching over them according to the Dharma so that they are neither destroyed nor lost. As for those things without an owner, he collects them at the appropriate time to provide for the needs and enjoyments of the Wheel-Turning King.
At that time, the treasurer went in person to where the wheel-turning monarch was, and upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
"Great Sage, Heavenly King!

As for whatever wealth, provisions, or treasures Your Majesty requires, please do not worry; by my power I am able to provide them, and I shall ensure that everything Your Majesty uses is fully supplied."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the Treasure of the Steward, boarded a boat and stayed in midstream, then commanded the Steward, saying:
"Come here, O Steward! I require wealth and treasures; you must prepare them with all speed!"
"You should quickly prepare everything!

The treasury minister replied, "I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me a brief moment to wait for the boat to reach the shore; I shall collect the treasures by the water's edge to provide for Your Majesty's use."
The King said to the treasurer:
"I have no need for wealth on the shore; you should simply prepare it for me right here.
The treasurer replied:
"I respectfully receive the Imperial decree and dare not disobey.

At that time, the treasury minister, having received the King's command, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ship, and plunged his hands into the great waters; his fingers were like crabs or turtles as he gathered the gold and silver, filling the various vessels. Then, on the ship, he held them up as an offering and addressed the King, saying:
"Great King, all this gold and silver is celestial treasure. The Devas provide these things for the King to serve as wealth and resources."
Then the Wheel-Turning King said to the treasurer:
"I have no need for wealth; I was merely testing you.
Having heard the King's words, the treasurer then withdrew the gold and silver and placed them back within the water.
For this reason, the Wheel-Turning Sage King experienced great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking to himself:
"I have now obtained the treasure of the minister-treasure!"
"Monks! A wheel-turning sage king is thus fully endowed with such treasury ministers.
"Monks! [he continued.]
What is meant by the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s possession of the full majesty of the military minister treasure? Monks!

By the power of the Wheel-Turning King’s merit, the treasure of a military commander is spontaneously produced—one who is skillful and versatile, adept at all strategic counsel, thoroughly understands military operations, and is perfected in divine wisdom.

The military forces required by a Wheel-Turning Sage King can all be fully provided; he may advance when he wishes to advance, march when he wishes to march, disperse when he wishes to disperse, and assemble when he wishes to assemble.
At that time, the military commander went in person to where the Wheel-Turning King was, and upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:

"If Your Majesty requires troops for training and service, please do not worry; I shall train the king’s cavalry and infantry for you, ensuring they all act according to your will and become disciplined, supple, and compliant."

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test this Jewel of the Military Commander, issued an order to the relevant officials to prepare the fourfold army—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.
When the King knew that the fourfold army was fully prepared, he addressed General Ratna, saying: "Bring forth your troops;

you shall serve as my commander-in-chief for the fourfold army. Instruct them to be compliant, so that they may advance well, retreat well, assemble well, and disperse well, acting in accordance with the Dharma and not deviating from it."
At that time, having heard these instructions from the Wheel-Turning King, the General-Treasure replied:
"Great King, I respectfully obey Your Majesty’s command; I dare not disobey."
He then took command of the fourfold army, arrayed their weapons, and instructed them in fleeing, marching, assembling, and dispersing.

Following the king’s commands, they would flee when told to flee, march when told to march, assemble when told to assemble, and disperse when told to disperse, acting with complete freedom according to his will.
For these reasons, the Wheel-Turning Sage King experienced great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking to himself:
"I have now obtained the treasure of the General of the Army!"
"O bhikṣus! A wheel-turning sage king possesses such a precious general of the army, endowed with full majestic power.
O bhikṣus!"
"If these seven treasures appear, only then may one be called a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
Monks! What are the four kinds of sovereign supernormal powers with which a Wheel-Turning Sage King is fully endowed?"
"O bhikṣus!
The lifespan of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is long and he dwells in the world for a great duration;
at all times and in all worlds, there is no human being capable of dwelling in such peace and security for a lifespan equal to that of a Wheel-Turning King."
This is called the first supernatural power of the Wheel-Turning Sage King: the perfection of longevity.

Furthermore, monks, the body received by the Wheel-Turning Sage King is free from much illness or affliction and is endowed with all the marks of excellence. His abdomen is level and full, being neither too thin nor too large. Cold and heat, coolness and warmth, are all harmoniously adjusted according to the season. His movements are light and agile; his food and drink are digested, and he dwells in peace, security, and happiness.
At all times and in all worlds, there is no other person born in the human world who is so free from illness and affliction as this;
this is called the second perfection of the physical power and supernormal faculties of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
"Furthermore, monks!

A Wheel-Turning Sage King is born with a physical appearance that is exceptionally handsome and extraordinary; he is always a sight for the world to behold without weariness. His physical body is pure, fully adorned, most excellent and most wondrous, without peer.

At all times and in all worlds, among those born as humans, there is none so handsome and extraordinary, nor one whom the world so tirelessly delights to behold, as is the one endowed with the marks of a Wheel-Turning King."
This is called the third supernatural quality of physical appearance possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Furthermore, monks, by reason of the power of his karma, the Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses great merit and retribution; all kinds of worldly assets are abundant and rich, and there is no rare and wondrous treasure that he does not possess in full.

At all times and in all worlds, among human beings, there has never been anyone born who possesses such wealth, pleasure, and sovereignty, with storehouses overflowing with resources, clothing, ornaments, and various exquisite treasures, comparable to that of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
This is called the fourth fruit of retribution and the perfection of supernormal powers of a Wheel-Turning Sage King. O Bhikṣus!
Only when one possesses these four kinds of supernormal powers without deficiency can one be named a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
“O Bhikṣus! Furthermore, this Wheel-Turning Sage King is loved and respected by all his subjects, who always rejoice in him with hearts as full of joy as a son loves his father;
likewise, all the subjects are cherished by the Wheel-Turning King, who constantly nurtures them with compassion as a father loves his son.”

“Monks! At times, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, mounting a great precious chariot, leaves the palace for excursions and sightseeing, traversing various excellent sites and even reaching the groves and gardens.”
At that time, all the people were able to see the Wheel-Turning Sage King face-to-face; filled with great joy, they all raised their voices in unison and said to the charioteer:
"O skillful charioteer, we pray that you hold the reins and proceed slowly and steadily, not moving too fast."
"Why is this? If you drive the chariot slowly and proceed at a gentle pace, it will allow us to behold the Wheel-Turning Sage King for a long time.
At that time, having heard these words, the Wheel-Turning King likewise commanded the charioteer, saying:
"O skillful charioteer, proceed slowly and with gentle steps;
be careful not to go too fast.
Why is this? If you drive the chariot steadily and advance gradually, it will allow me to travel for a long time and observe all the people everywhere."

"O Bhikṣus! At that time, when the people saw the Wheel-Turning King, each took whatever precious objects they possessed, knelt before the wheels of his chariot, and offered them to the Wheel-Turning King, saying:
'Great King, we, the people, now offer these to Your Majesty; these things belong to Your Majesty. We pray that Your Majesty will accept them and use them as you please.'"
"Why is this? Because such precious objects are intended solely for the use of the gods. "O Bhikṣus!"

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, this Jambudvīpa becomes pure, level, and even; it is devoid of thorns, dense forests, mounds, ruins, pits, latrines, foul-smelling impurities, stones, tiles, gravel, and saline wasteland—none of these things exist at all.
The seven treasures, such as gold and silver, are spontaneously and fully provided; it is neither cold nor hot, and the seasons are perfectly harmonized. Monks!

Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, this Jambudvīpa is naturally established with eighty thousand cities and towns, all of which are joyful and free from all fears; the population is flourishing, food and grain are abundant, and the settlements are numerous and most delightful.
"O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, this Jambudvīpa, over which he rules, consists of villages and cities with houses so closely packed that one could reach them by the flight of a cock; the people therein are peaceful and happy in an inconceivable way."
"O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, at midnight in this Jambudvīpa, great clouds arise from Lake Anavatapta, spreading across Jambudvīpa and all its mountains and seas. Rain falls in due season, covering Jambudvīpa everywhere; the depth of the rain is four finger-breadths, like the intervals between milk being drawn from a cow."

That water was sweet and possessed the eight meritorious qualities; it sank immediately upon reaching the ground and did not flow further, soaking into the earth so that no flood appeared. By the latter part of the night, the clouds and mists had vanished.

A cool breeze arises from the great ocean, blowing and dispersing its moisture; when the people of Jambudvīpa touch it, they all experience peace and happiness. Furthermore, that sweet rain saturates this continent, making it everywhere fertile, vibrant, bright, and lustrous.

It is just as when a master garland-maker or his disciple has finished crafting a garland and sprinkles it with water, causing it to become pleasingly moist and the colors of the flowers to shine with fresh brilliance; so it is here as well.
Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, all the lands of this Jambudvīpa naturally become fertile, lush, and moist;
just as if someone were to smear an object with clarified butter and oil, so too does that ground become rich, succulent, and well-watered.
"O bhikṣus!

Once a Wheel-Turning Sage King has appeared and dwelt for a long time in the world, passing through immeasurable years, during that interval he likewise experiences various human sensations of suffering."

For example, it is like a man of delicate constitution whose body is weak and tender; after eating fine food, he must engage in physical activity and exertion to experience a slight sensation of fatigue before the food can be digested.
In this very way, that wheel-turning monarch, having dwelt in the world for a long time, likewise experiences only slight contact with suffering amidst birth and death.
"O Bhikṣus!
When a Wheel-turning Sage King reaches the end of his lifespan and casts off this body, he will certainly be reborn in the heavens, dwelling together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
“O bhikṣus!

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King is about to pass away, in order to make offerings to that king, there shall naturally rain down from the sky all kinds of fragrant flowers—such as *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—as well as celestial powdered aloeswood, *tagara*, sandalwood incense, and various celestial flowers such as the *māndārava*.

Furthermore, there were celestial musical instruments whose sounds were subtle and exquisite, resonating spontaneously without being struck; there were also the voices of various devas singing praises in the void, for the purpose of making offerings to the body of this wheel-turning king and creating merit and benefit.

“O bhikṣus! At that time, the Woman-Jewel, the Treasurer-Jewel, the Military Commander-Jewel, and the others bathed the body of the Wheel-Turning King with various kinds of pure and exquisite fragrant waters.”
After washing it with fragrant liquid, he first wrapped his body in *karpāsa* cotton cloth;
then he further wrapped it with unwashed cotton cloth;
next, he again wrapped it in succession with five hundred pieces of exquisite, fine cotton cloth, layering them over the two previous cloths.
Having completed the wrapping, he further took a golden coffin and filled it with ghee and oil; he placed the body of the Wheel-Turning King inside the coffin.
He then took a silver outer casing and placed the golden coffin within it; once the silver casing was in place, he drove nails from top to bottom to ensure it was secure.
Furthermore, having gathered all kinds of fragrant wood and piled them into a great pyre, he then performed the cremation of the Universal Monarch’s body.

Once the cremation was complete, he collected the ashes and bones and, at a crossroads, erected for the Universal Monarch a *stūpa* (the Sui term *sōutōngbō*; the older term "tā" is an abbreviation and corruption) one *yojana* in height and half a *yojana* in width. It was adorned with various colors and composed of the four precious substances, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

That stūpa was surrounded by four courtyards extending fifty yojanas; it had seven layers of walls and seven layers of railings, as briefly described above, up to the point where various birds each sang their own songs.

At that time, the Jewel-Woman, the Jewel of the Treasury-Master, the Jewel of the Military Commander, and the others built a stūpa for the Wheel-Turning King. Once it was completed, they then provided supreme and exquisite offerings; to all who came seeking, they gave various provisions—namely, food to those needing food, drink to those needing drink, vehicles to those needing vehicles, clothing to those needing clothing, wealth to those needing wealth, and jewels to those needing jewels—bestowing them all in full until everyone was satisfied.

“Monks! After the death of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, within seven days of his passing, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, and the jewel-treasure will all naturally vanish and disappear.”
The Woman-Jewel, the Treasurer-General, and the Military Commander likewise passed away.
The four kinds of precious palaces gradually underwent transformation and reverted to being mere bricks and earth.
All the people, likewise, gradually diminished over time. Monks! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;
they thus undergo change and transformation, possessing no permanence. They are subject to destruction and dispersal, and lack any independent autonomy.
This is a phenomenon subject to decay; it lasts but a brief moment and does not endure for long. O bhikṣus!
You should abandon all conditioned formations (saṃskāra), you should distance yourselves from them, you should feel weary of them, and you should swiftly seek the path to liberation.
Chapter Four: On the Hells, Part One of the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of the World). "O Bhikṣus!

Outside of the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, all other great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, there is another mountain called Cakravāḍa—formerly translated as 'Iron Encircling Mountains' (*Lohakāla-parvata*). It is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height, and its length and breadth are likewise six million eight hundred thousand yojanas. It is dense, solid, and firm, composed of vajra, and is difficult to destroy."
"O Bhikṣus!
Beyond this Cakravāḍa mountain range, there is yet another great Cakravāḍa mountain, equal in height and breadth to the former, measured in yojanas.

Between these two mountains, there is profound darkness with no light at all; even the sun and moon, possessing such great majesty, power, and virtue, cannot illuminate that place to make light visible."
"O bhikṣus!
Between these two mountains, there are eight great hells.
What are the eight?"

These are the Sañjīva Great Hell, the Kālasūtra Great Hell, the Saṃghāta Great Hell, the Raurava Great Hell, the Mahāraurava Great Hell, the Tapana Great Hell, the Pratāpana Great Hell, and the Avīci Great Hell.
“Monks! These eight great hells each have sixteen minor hells surrounding them as their retinue.”
These sixteen hells are all five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
What are the sixteen? They are:

the Black Cloud Sand Hell, the Excrement and Filth Mire Hell, the Five Forks Hell, the Hunger Hell, the Thirst Hell, the Pus and Blood Hell, the Single Copper Cauldron Hell, the Many Copper Cauldrons Hell, the Iron Mill Hell, the Box Measure Hell, the Chicken Hell, the Ash River Hell, the Carving and Cutting Hell, the Sword-Leaf Hell, the Fox and Wolf Hell, and the Cold Ice Hell.
“Monks! For what reason and by what causes is it called the Saṃjīva Great Hell? Monks!”

All sentient beings within this Reviving Great Hell—whether those who have been born there, those currently existing there, those emerging from it, or those dwelling within it—all naturally possess iron melons upon their fingers; these are long, slender, and sharp, all like the points of blades.

Once those sentient beings have seen one another, their minds become turbid and disturbed. Because their minds are turbid and disturbed, each uses their own iron claws to tear at their own bodies until they are all rent asunder;
some tear at their bodies, tearing again and tearing yet more, even tearing them greatly; once torn, they tear again, even tearing them greatly;
having cut, they cut again, even cutting them greatly.
"O bhikṣus!
Those sentient beings, having thus torn themselves apart, perceive it in this way:
'I am now wounded; I am now dead.'"

Due to the retribution of his karma, at that very moment, a cold wind blew upon his body; in an instant, his muscles, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, blood, and marrow were restored, and having been regenerated, he returned to life.
Once they have regained their lives, by the causal conditions of their karma, they rise up and move here and there, saying to one another:
"O sentient beings, do you wish to have gained life that is superior to mine?"
"O monks! You should know that this is called 'reviving' only because it is described here in brief.

However, within that state there are further distinct karmic actions whereby one undergoes extremely heavy suffering, oppressed by pain and affliction, such that its bitterness and toxicity are unbearable. This continues until the evil and unwholesome karma—whether produced and created in a previous human life or a non-human life—is not yet exhausted, not yet extinguished, not yet eliminated, not yet transformed, not yet partially manifested, and not yet fully manifested; during that interval, as long as the retribution of life is not yet finished, one seeks death but cannot obtain it."
"Furthermore, monks!

All sentient beings dwelling in the Saṃjīva Great Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently being born, or are still residing there—will have fingers grow with blades made of pure iron or half-iron, which are extremely long, slender, and sharp."

Each looks upon the others, their minds becoming turbid and disordered; once their minds are thus disordered, they proceed to tear, rend, split, and hack one another until they die. Then a cold wind blows upon them, and in an instant they are restored to life.
"Monks! It is just so, it is just so.
Because it is described only in part, it is called 'living. Monks!"
Furthermore, there is another distinct karma, within which they undergo extreme suffering and affliction; because the suffering is not yet exhausted, they seek death but cannot obtain it.

Until all the evil and unwholesome karma created and performed—whether in a human body or a non-human body—in the past has been fully experienced, exhausted, extinguished, eliminated, and abandoned, they must undergo all such consequences in their proper sequence.
"Furthermore, monks!

When the sentient beings in the Saṃjīva Great Hell have exhausted their retribution for suffering after an immeasurable time, they emerge from this hell and run hither and thither, seeking other dwellings and houses, seeking places of refuge and protection, and seeking a place of reliance."
While seeking in this manner, due to his sinful karma, he immediately enters the Black Sand Small Hell of his own accord; that hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.

Once they have entered the prison, a great black cloud arises in the sky above, raining down flying sand. Blazing with fierce flames and extremely intense heat, it falls upon the bodies of the sentient beings in hell. It burns through the skin, burning the skin; it burns through the flesh, burning the flesh; it burns through the tendons, burning the tendons; it burns through the bones, burning the bones; and it burns through the marrow, burning the marrow. Emitting great smoke and flames that pierce through everything in a blazing conflagration, they undergo extreme suffering and distress; yet because the retribution for their karma has not yet been fully exhausted, they cannot seek death.

Even those evil and unwholesome karmas committed and created throughout past lives—whether as humans or non-humans—are not extinguished, not eliminated, not transformed, not altered, not departed from, and not lost; they must be experienced in succession over immeasurable periods of time.

“Monks! After those sentient beings have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from the Black Sand Hell and once again run about, seeking a house, seeking a dwelling, seeking rescue, seeking shelter, and seeking a place of refuge.”
While searching in this manner, he further enters the Small Hell of Hot Excrement and Mud, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once the sinner has entered, from his throat downward he is submerged in the excrement and mud; the excrement boils hotly, emitting both smoke and flames that burn the sinner’s hands, feet, ears, nose, head, eyes, and body, all of which are simultaneously scorched and ablaze.

Furthermore, whatever evil and unwholesome karma was generated or committed by them in the past—whether by humans or non-humans—that has not yet been exhausted or extinguished, not yet eliminated or transformed, and which they have neither parted from nor lost, will be experienced in succession.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within the minor hell of Excrement and Filth, there are iron insects called 'Needle-Mouths' that dwell amidst the excrement and mud, boring into the bodies of sentient beings and piercing every part of their limbs."

First it bores through their skin; once the skin is pierced, it next bores through their flesh; once the flesh is pierced, it next bores through their tendons; once the tendons are pierced, it next bores through their bones; and once the bones are pierced, it dwells within the marrow, consuming the vital essence of all sentient beings and causing them to experience intense and agonizing suffering throughout their entire bodies.
Yet their lifespan has not yet come to an end; until those evil and unwholesome karmas of theirs have been extinguished and exhausted, they must undergo them in this manner, in full succession.

"O bhikṣus! Those sentient beings within that hell, having endured painful suffering for immeasurable time, emerge from the minor hell of Excrement Mire and once again run about, seeking a chamber, seeking a house, seeking protection, seeking an island, and seeking a place of refuge."
At that time, they immediately enter the Five-Forked Minor Hell, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once those sinners have entered this hell, the hell-wardens seize them, lift them high, and hurl them down onto a ground of blazing, glowing-hot iron. As smoke and flames erupt intensely, the sinners lie there within it, unconscious and prostrate on their backs.
The hell-wardens then drove two red-hot iron nails into his two feet, which blazed with fierce flames;
they further drove two nails into his two hands, which likewise blazed fiercely;
then, driving an iron nail into the center of his navel, the flames became even more violent and intense.
Thereupon, the hell-wardens further impale his five limbs with five-forked stakes, causing him to experience extreme suffering and torment.

Thus it continues until his lifespan there has not yet ended and his evil karma is not yet exhausted; all the various evil karmas he previously committed while in human or non-human forms are experienced within this hell one after another.

"O Bhikṣus! Those sentient beings, having endured such agony for immeasurable time, emerge from the Five-Forked Minor Hell and once again run about, seeking rescue, seeking shelter, seeking an island, seeking refuge, seeking cover, and seeking protection; they then proceed once more to the Hungry Ghost Hell, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent."
Once the sinners have entered, the wardens of hell see those people coming from outside from afar and immediately go forward to ask them:
"Now that you have come here into this place, what do you desire?"
Those sentient beings all answered together, saying:
"O Benevolent One! We are hungry!"

At that time, the wardens of hell seize the offender and drag him onto a floor of blazing, glowing-hot iron. The offender, fainting and lying prostrate on his back, has his mouth pried open with iron tongs; they then take a ball of glowing-hot iron and cast it into his mouth.
His lips and mouth are instantly set ablaze; having burned his lips, it burns his tongue;
having burned his tongue, it burns his palate.
Having burned the palate, it then burns the throat;
having burned the throat, it then burns the heart;
having burned the heart, it then burns the chest.
Once the chest has been burned, it immediately burns the intestines;
once the intestines have been burned, it immediately burns the stomach;
once the stomach has been burned, it passes through the small intestine and exits from the lower part of the body.
The pellets remain fiercely hot and as red as before;
at that time, those sentient beings undergo extreme suffering and torment, yet their lives do not yet come to an end.
To speak briefly, up to this point: whatever was done by humans or non-humans in previous lives, they shall experience all such things in succession within this hell. "O Bhikṣus!

After those sentient beings have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from this minor hell of hunger and once again flee in haste; as briefly described before, they seek a place of refuge and protection.
Thereafter, they arrive at the Hell of Scorching Thirst, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.
Having entered this hell, the wardens of the prison see those people approaching from afar and immediately go forward to ask:
"What do you seek now?"
The sinner replied,
"O virtuous one!
I am now extremely thirsty."

Then, the wardens of hell seized the offender and dragged him onto a floor of blazing hot iron. Lying supine amidst fierce flames, he fell into a state of unconsciousness; thereupon, they took iron tongs and pried open his mouth, pouring molten red copper into it.
The lips and mouths of those sentient beings are completely scorched and withered at that very moment.

Once their lips and mouths are burned away, it next burns their tongues; thus it burns the palate and the throat, burns the heart and the chest, and burns the intestines and the stomach, passing straight through the small intestine and exiting from the lower part of the body.

At that time, those sentient beings each experience extremely heavy suffering and extreme pain; this suffering is particularly unique and inconceivable, yet their life spans have not ended nor reached exhaustion.

To speak briefly as before, up until: if there are evil karmas created by humans or non-humans that have not yet been extinguished or abandoned, one shall fully experience them in this sequential manner.
*Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World), Scroll Two. *Qishi jing*, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Four: On the Hells, Part Two.
"Furthermore, monks!

After those sentient beings within that hell have endured extreme suffering for immeasurable time, they then emerge from this Scorching Thirst Hell, which extends five hundred yojanas. They flee as before, and in brief, continue until they seek a place of refuge and protection."
He then proceeded to the Pus-and-Blood Hell; that hell was also five hundred yojanas in extent, filled everywhere with pus and blood reaching up to the throat, all of it boiling hot.
Once the sentient beings of hell have entered therein, they run to and fro, crisscrossing in the east, west, south, and north.
As those sentient beings run in this manner, their hands are burned and their feet are burned; their ears are burned and their noses are burned.
Once their hands, feet, ears, and noses have been burned, all their limbs and joints are likewise set ablaze.
When their limbs and joints are set ablaze, those various sinners undergo great suffering and affliction—severe, agonizing, and inconceivable.
"Furthermore, monks, as long as the evil and unwholesome karma created and performed by a person—whether human or non-human—is not yet exhausted, their life will not come to an end.
"Moreover, monks!"

In the Pus-and-Blood Hell there are further insects called "Most Fierce and Victorious"; these insects inflict great torment and harm upon the sentient beings who are undergoing punishment in that hell.
Entering from the outside of the body, it first breaks through the skin;
once the skin is broken, it next breaks through the flesh;
once the flesh is broken, it next breaks through the tendons.
Once the sinews have been torn apart, they next break the bones;
once the bones have been broken, they extract the marrow and eat it as they go.
At that time, those sentient beings undergo the most extreme suffering.

Furthermore, whatever evil and unwholesome karma has been created and performed by humans or non-humans, as long as it remains未尽 (unexhausted) and 未滅 (unextinguished), and their lifespan is not yet ended, they shall experience all of it in its entirety.
"Furthermore, monks!

All the sentient beings in the Pus-and-Blood Hell are so tormented by hunger and thirst that they sometimes scoop up such boiling pus and blood with their hands and place it in their mouths. Once it is in their mouths, their lips and mouths are instantly scorched;
when their lips and mouths are scorched, it immediately burns their palates."
Having burned the palate, it immediately burns the throat;
likewise, it burns the chest, the heart, the intestines, and the stomach.
Having burned the stomach, it passes straight through the small intestine and exits from below.
Those sentient beings, in this hell, undergo such severe and heavy suffering, yet their life-span has not yet ended.
Until the non-human and human karmic results of the evil and unwholesome deeds they previously committed are fully exhausted, they must experience them in this sequential manner.
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings within that hell, having endured extreme suffering for immeasurable time, subsequently emerge from this Pus-and-Blood Hell, which is five hundred yojanas in extent, and run as before, seeking a place of refuge and protection."
They then enter again into a copper cauldron hell, which is also five hundred yojanas in width.
Once the offenders have entered, the hell-wardens see them, immediately seize them, and hurl them into the cauldron with their heads all downward and their feet all upward.
When these sentient beings are within the cauldron, the fierce fires of hell intensely torment and press upon them.
As they rise with the boiling water, they are both scorched and boiled;
as they sink with the boiling water, they are likewise both scorched and boiled.
During the intermediate stage, it is both boiled and stewed;
as it moves back and forth in a crisscrossing manner, it is also both boiled and stewed;
when covered by froth and bubbles, it is likewise both boiled and stewed.
Whether they see it or not, they are boiled at all times.

It is like when in the world one boils small beans, large beans, or peas: they are placed inside a cauldron, filled with water, and set over a great fire; thereupon they boil and bubble, the broth and the beans mingling together.
When floating upward, it is both boiled and stewed;
when sinking downward, it is both boiled and stewed;
when staying in the middle, it is also both boiled and stewed.
When they move crosswise, they are both boiled and stewed;
when covered by froth, they are also both boiled and stewed;
whether seen or unseen, they are stewed at all times.
"O bhikṣus!
In this way, and in this very manner, in one of the copper cauldron hells, the wardens seize those offenders, turn them head-downward and feet-upward, and hurl them into the cauldron."

While inside the cauldron, they are tormented by the fierce fires of hell; as the boiling heat becomes intense, the offenders are driven by the surging waves, moving up and down, being boiled and seared as they go. Briefly stated, this continues whether they are seen or not; at all times, they are boiled in this same manner.
Those sentient beings, within this hell, undergo severe and agonizing suffering.
Even the evil karma they committed in the past, whether as humans or non-humans, they experience in its entirety within this hell, following such a sequence.

"O bhikṣus! After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from the small hell of the copper cauldron, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. As before, they run about, seeking a place where they might find rescue and protection."
At that time, they immediately enter the Minor Hell of Numerous Copper Cauldrons, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once the offenders have entered, the hell-wardens come to seize them; grasping the offenders, they cast them into the copper cauldrons with their feet upward and their heads downward. The fierce fires of the hell blaze intensely, boiling and pressing down upon them. When the boiling water surges upward, they are both seared and cooked;
when the boiling water subsides, they are likewise seared and cooked.
During the intermediate stage, they are both seethed and boiled;
whether covered from all sides or not, whether seen or unseen, they are entirely seethed and boiled.

It is like boiling beans: as they are heated and pressed by the fire and surge upward in a rolling boil, they are both seethed and boiled—briefly stated, this continues until, whether seen or unseen, they are entirely seethed and boiled.

"O monks! In this very way, within this minor hell of the Great Copper Cauldron, measuring five hundred yojanas, the sentient beings are seized by the wardens of hell by their two feet; they are made to stand upright with their heads downward and cast into the copper cauldron."

At that time, tormented and oppressed by the fires of hell, that person moves upward and downward, shifting back and forth; in brief, whether seen or unseen, they are all likewise boiled and scorched in this manner.
"O Bhikṣus!

Within this minor hell of the Copper Cauldron, five hundred yojanas in extent, the sentient beings there are further made into wardens by the jailers; with their iron claws, they fish out the offenders from one cauldron to another, boiling them in succession."

When they emerge from this cauldron and approach another cauldron, the pus, blood, skin, and flesh flow and scatter in all directions until they are entirely exhausted, leaving behind nothing but skeletal remains.
At that time, the sinner undergoes extreme suffering yet still does not die.
Until all the evil karma created within the bodies of humans and non-humans is exhausted and extinguished, they must suffer for it all within this hell.

“Monks! Those sentient beings within that hell, having endured such suffering for immeasurable time, emerge from the Small Hell of the Many Copper Cauldrons, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. They flee as before, seeking a place of refuge and protection.”
At that time, he immediately entered the Iron Mill Hell, which was also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once he had entered, the hell-wardens immediately came forward, seized the sentient beings undergoing punishment, and flung them face-up onto iron anvils. Intense, blazing flames erupted all at once, completely engulfing them; thereupon the sinners lay prostrate, fainting and unconscious.
At that time, the jailer took another large rock and pressed it down from above;
having pressed it, he pressed again, and thus further ground it;
having ground it, he ground it again, until it was finally reduced to fine powder.
Once it has been ground into powder, he grinds it again; having ground it, he grinds it yet again until it becomes a fine powder.
Taking that fine powder, he grinds it further; having ground it, he grinds it repeatedly until it becomes the finest of all powders, the most subtle and minute powder.

At that time, the body of the sinner—with its fat, blood, brain, and marrow flowing out from one side, while even the finest fragments of bone still remain—endures the most grievous suffering at all times until the retribution for his life has finally ended.

"Even for the deeds done in human or non-human forms, as long as those evil karmas have not been lost or extinguished, one shall experience their results in full, in this sequential order. O Bhikṣus!"

After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from the Small Hell of the Iron Mill, which is five hundred yojanas in extent; they run as before, seeking a dwelling, seeking a place of refuge and protection.
At that time, he immediately entered the Iron Box Hell (*ayaḥ-saṃghāta-naraka*), which was also five hundred *yojanas* in extent.

Having entered within, the hell-wardens seized the offender and placed him inside an iron box, ordering him to measure the fire. That box was fiercely hot, with blazing flames; as the hell-being measured the fire, his hands were burned, his feet were burned, his ears were burned, his nose was burned, and all his limbs were burned, until every part of his body was completely consumed by the flames.
While being burned, these sinners undergo extreme suffering and endure heavy agony, yet their life-span has not yet come to an end.

Furthermore, whatever evil and unwholesome karma they have created throughout all their bodies—whether as humans or non-humans—in the past, which has not been extinguished, has not vanished, has not departed, and has not been lost, they shall experience the full consequences of it in this sequential manner.

“Monks! After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from the Small Hell of the Caskets, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. Running away as before, they seek a dwelling, seek shelter, seek rescue, seek an island, and seek a place of refuge.”
At that time, he immediately entered the Kukkula (Chicken) Hell, which was also five hundred yojanas in extent.
Within that hell, only chickens were born, filling the entire place; from their bodies down to their knees and shins, everything was intensely hot, with blazing flames fiercely burning.

These sentient beings dwell within it, running hither and thither, their feet treading upon blazing flames. Looking in the four directions, they find no place of refuge. As the great fire fiercely blazes, it burns their hands and feet, burns their ears and noses; in this sequence, it burns all their limbs and joints, until their entire bodies, both large and small, are simultaneously engulfed in a pervasive conflagration.
At that time, the sinner undergoes extremely heavy suffering, with agonizing and bitter torment; yet, in that place, the retribution of their life-span has not yet ended.
Until the evil karma created by human or non-human bodies is extinguished and exhausted, they must experience all such consequences in this successive order.

“O bhikṣus! After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from this Chicken Hell and flee as before, seeking a place of refuge and protection.”
At that time, he entered the Hell of the Ash River; that hell was also five hundred yojanas in extent. O Bhikṣus!
At that time, the Ash River flowed with rapid currents, its waves surging and billowing, its roar thundering and shaking, as the boiling ash-water overflowed and filled both banks.
Once the sinners have entered, they float and sink along with the current; at the bottom of the Ash River are iron spikes, their points so fine and sharp as if freshly whetted.
On both banks of the river, there are further forests of swords, towering and densely packed, most terrifying to behold.
Within these sword forests, there are also various dogs; they are smoke-black in form, their fur and skin filthy and stained, and they are likewise most fearsome.
On the banks, there are furthermore numerous hell-wardens who guard that hell.
Moreover, on both banks grow countless śamala trees; these trees are thorny, all slender and long, with tips as sharp as if ground.
At that time, when the various sentient beings in hell have entered the river and seek to reach the opposite shore, they are suddenly submerged by great waves and sink to the bottom of the river.

There, all the iron spikes within the river pierce their bodies from below, penetrating them entirely so that they cannot move. While trapped therein, the offenders undergo immense and heavy suffering, as well as agonizing and poisonous torment.
After enduring this for a long time, they finally manage to float to the surface and cross from the River of Boiling Ashes to the other shore.

Having already stepped onto the shore, they enter again into the Forest of Swords. That forest is extremely vast, with branches and stalks growing densely together. As they pass through the woods, they encounter sharp blades; everywhere they go, they proceed without ceasing, cutting their hands and feet, cutting their ears and noses, cutting their limbs and joints, slicing through their entire bodies until there is no part that is not mangled.

At that time, those persons undergo bitter and poisonous suffering and experience extremely heavy agony; until all the evil karma they previously committed while in human or non-human forms is exhausted, their lives do not end, and they must endure it all within this forest.
"Furthermore, monks!
When the wardens on both banks of the Ash River see those offenders, they immediately step forward and ask:
'What do you desire now?'"
Then those sinners answered with one voice, saying:
"We are extremely hungry!
We are extremely hungry!"

At that time, the jailers immediately seized the offender and dragged him onto the ground; the earth was fiercely hot, with blazing flames burning intensely, and the offender lay there in a state of stupor, prostrate on his back.

Furthermore, using iron tongs, they pry open their mouths and place glowing iron balls inside; instantly these burn and scorch them, causing the lips and mouths of those sentient beings to blister and break. To speak briefly, this continues until the iron passes down through the throat and reaches the small intestine, passing straight through without obstruction.
At that time, that person undergoes severe and piercing suffering and experiences extremely heavy agony, yet their life does not yet end.
Until the evil and unwholesome karma they previously committed as a human or a non-human being is fully exhausted, they must experience it all in its entirety right here.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, upon both banks of this Ash River, there are dogs with bodies as black as smoke, filthy and terrifying. With glaring eyes, they howl and bark, emitting great and evil sounds; they devour the limbs and members of those hell-beings, gnawing at their flesh piece by piece until nothing remains."
That person remains therein, undergoing severe and piercing suffering, even up to the most extreme and heavy suffering, yet does not meet their end.
Until those evil and unwholesome karmas created in former lives—whether as a human or a non-human—are exhausted, they must experience all of them in full.

"O bhikṣus! Those sentient beings within that hell, already tormented by such a river of boiling, seething ash, are further distressed by dense forests of sharp iron thorns and blades, by the various hell-wardens, and by foul-smelling black dogs; beset by these manifold calamities and urgencies, they have no place of refuge."

He then ran back up toward a śalmali tree; the branches and stalks of that tree were composed entirely of iron thorns, their tips fine and sharp as if newly whetted, all pointing downward, piercing and lacerating his body.
When they wish to descend from the tree, the heads of these iron thorns turn upward.
While those sentient beings are upon the śālmali trees, there are also crows called "iron-beaks" that fly onto the trees and peck at those offenders.
First it pecks at his head, breaking through and sinking into the cranial bone to devour his brain.
At that time, the person undergoes extreme suffering and agonizing pain; unable to endure it, he immediately falls back into the river of boiling ashes.
Thereupon, that person is once again swept away and submerged by the waves until they reach the bottom of the river.
Having reached the bottom, they are further pierced and lanced by iron spikes.
Once they have been pierced, iron spikes cover their entire bodies; unable to move further away, they remain therein and undergo extreme, most violent, and cruel suffering that they cannot endure.
Having suffered for a long time, his strength being fully exhausted, he manages to rise and cross over from the Ash River, running toward this shore.
Once he has reached this shore, he enters the Forest of Blades.

Upon entering the Forest of Blades, they are further cut by the blade-edges; their bodies are sliced, their hands and feet are severed, and eventually all their limbs and joints are completely cut apart. Within that place, they undergo full measure of suffering, yet their lives do not yet end.
To speak briefly, even those evil karmas committed in the past in human or non-human forms that have not yet been extinguished or exhausted must all be experienced in succession.
"Furthermore, monks!
When the various wardens on this shore of the Ash River see the sentient beings undergoing punishment in hell coming from the opposite shore, they immediately step forward and ask:
"For what reason have you come so far?"
"What do you wish to obtain?
Those sentient beings each replied,
"We are parched with thirst."
Then, the wardens of the prison immediately seized those sentient beings again, flung them onto a floor of blazing, glowing-hot iron, and forced them to lie on their backs.
As they lay on their backs, flames erupted violently from their bodies; the wardens then used iron tongs to pry open their mouths and poured molten, glowing red copper into them.

At that time, those sentient beings in the hells, having drunk the molten copper, have their lips and mouths burned, continuing through until the small intestines, passing straight through without obstruction, and exiting from the lower part of the body.

At that time, that person undergoes extremely heavy suffering; until their lifespan is exhausted and comes to an end, they must fully experience all the evil karma they previously committed in human and non-human forms that has not yet been extinguished.
"Furthermore, monks! Those sentient beings within that hell undergo this retribution for immeasurable time;

their suffering and affliction are long-lasting. Then a wind arises, named 'Conjunction' (*saṃyoga*), which blows those sentient beings of the hell to the shore. In this manner, they gradually manage to emerge from that Ash River Hell (*kṣāranadī-naraka*). Having emerged, they run about, seeking a place of refuge and protection."
At that time, he immediately entered the Chakche (Cutting) Hell, which was also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once the offenders had entered, the hell-wardens seized them and cast them down upon a floor of blazing, glowing red-hot iron; they even forced them to lie prostrate on the ground. Grasping great iron axes—blazing, fiercely hot, and terrifying in their radiant glare—they hacked at those sentient beings suffering in the hell: hacking hands, hacking feet, and hacking both hands and feet; hacking ears, hacking noses, and hacking both ears and noses; hacking limbs, hacking joints, and hacking both limbs and joints. In this manner, they hacked the entire body in succession.
At that time, those sentient beings undergo extremely heavy suffering, yet their lives do not yet end.
Until such time as the evil and unwholesome karma they have created—whether in human or non-human form—is fully exhausted, they must experience all of it in this successive manner.
"Furthermore, monks!

After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from the Khadira-chedana (Small Chopping) Hell. Having emerged, they run about, seeking a place of refuge, even seeking a house, seeking a dwelling, seeking shelter, seeking an island, and seeking a place of protection."
At that time, he immediately entered the Sword-Leaf Hell, which was also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Having entered it, due to the fruit of his evil karma, a wind suddenly arose that blew iron leaves like sharp swords, falling from the sky and slicing through all parts of the offenders' bodies—namely, cutting off their hands, cutting off their feet, and cutting off both hands and feet; cutting off their ears, cutting off their noses, and cutting off both ears and noses; cutting off their limbs and joints, and cutting off both limbs and joints.
At that time, the offenders undergo extreme suffering and agonizing pain, yet their lives do not come to an end; the details are as described above.
Until the evil karma created by them—whether in human or non-human form—is extinguished and exhausted, they must fully experience all such sufferings within this hell.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, due to the fruit of their evil karma, iron-beaked crows suddenly fly into that Sword-Leaf Small Hell. They alight upon the shoulders of those sentient beings, treading on them with their feet and covering their heads with their wings; they then peck out the pupils of the eyes of those offenders with their iron beaks and carry them away in their beaks."

At that time, the offenders undergo extremely heavy suffering; their pain and distress are so intense as to be inconceivable, yet their life spans have not yet come to an end, as briefly described above.
"Furthermore, monks! Whatever evil karma has been committed in the form of human or non-human bodies, one shall experience all of it in this very sequence."

After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they finally emerge from the Sword-Leaf Minor Hell. Having emerged, they run about, seeking a dwelling, seeking shelter, seeking an island of refuge, seeking a place of reliance, and seeking a place of protection.
At that time, they further enter the Fox-Wolf Hell, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once these sentient beings have entered this hell, due to the fruit of their evil karma, foxes and wolves are born within the hell. Fierce, blazing, and extremely cruel, they glare with bared fangs and roar; the sounds they emit are most terrifying. They gnaw upon the bodies of the various sentient beings in the hell, devouring all their flesh and sinews; they trample them with their feet and seize them with their mouths, tearing them into pieces to eat.
At that time, the offenders undergo extremely heavy suffering; their pain and distress are so acute and piercing that their lives do not yet end, as briefly described before.
The evil karma created by human and non-human beings is experienced in its entirety within this realm, following such a sequence.
"Furthermore, monks!

After those sentient beings within that hell have endured such suffering for immeasurable time, they emerge from the minor hell of Foxes and Wolves. Having emerged, they run away, seeking a room, seeking a house, seeking shelter, seeking an island, seeking a place of refuge and protection, and seeking a place of reliance."
At that time, they further enter the Hell of Cold Ice; that hell is also five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once these sinners have entered that hell, due to the retribution of their evil karma, a cold wind suddenly arises from the four directions, blowing a freezing chill that is coarse, harsh, and intensely toxic, striking the bodies of the sentient beings in that hell.
Wherever it touches, the skin immediately bursts open;
once the skin has burst, it next tears through the flesh;
once the flesh has been torn, it next breaks through the tendons.
Once the tendons have been torn asunder, they next break their bones;
once the bones have been broken, they next break their marrow.
When the marrow is being broken, those sentient beings undergo extreme suffering, most piercing suffering, even great suffering that is unbearable, and therein their life-span comes to an end.
This constitutes the first Great Hell of Saṃjīva and its sixteen other minor hells.

"Furthermore, monks, the second Great Hell, Kālasūtra, is likewise surrounded by sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in extent; beginning with Kālasūtra-saikatā and ending finally with the sixteenth, named Śīta-hima-naraka, they form a single retinue."
"O bhikṣus!
For what reason and by what causes is this hell named the Great Hell of Black Ropes? O bhikṣus!"

Regarding all the sentient beings within that great hell of Black Rope—those who are born, those who exist, those who emerge, and those who dwell there—they experience the fruition of their past unwholesome karma. Consequently, coarse and massive black ropes suddenly appear in the void; blazing and fiercely hot like dark clouds, they emerge from the sky, filling it with gloom and descending to touch the earth.

In this very way, for all sentient beings within that great Black Rope Hell, because they have obtained the retribution for their unwholesome karma from previous lives, great black ropes emerge from the midst of space, blazing with fierce heat, just so.
These Black Rope whips fall upon the bodies of the sentient beings who have fallen into hell; as they land on their bodies, they immediately burn the offenders in all their limbs.
First they burn the skin;
once the skin is burned, they next burn the flesh.
Once the flesh has been burned, next the sinews are burned;
once the sinews have been burned, next the bones are burned;
at the time the bones are burned, it penetrates all the way to the marrow.
The marrow then flows out and is consumed by the fire; as the marrow burns, it emits great, fierce flames.
At that time, the sinner undergoes piercing pain and most grievous suffering, yet because of their karmic offenses, their life does not yet end.

Furthermore, all evil and unwholesome karma created throughout past lives—whether as humans or non-humans—that has not yet been extinguished, transformed, eliminated, or brought to an end, is experienced entirely within this hell.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, regarding all those sentient beings within the great hell of Black Rope—those who are born, those who exist, those who dwell, and those who are manifested—due to the ripening of the unwholesome fruits of their past lives, the hell-wardens seize these offenders and cast them onto a ground of blazing, glowing-hot iron. The flames are fierce and intense, scorching their entire bodies. They force the offenders to lie prostrate and, using hot iron cords, measure out various sections across their bodies. Once measured, they use glowing, fiercely radiant hot iron axes to hack at the limbs and members of those beings in that hell, cutting them into two parts, three parts, four parts, five parts, or even ten parts; or into twenty parts, fifty parts, or even a hundred parts."

It is, for example, like a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice who takes various pieces of timber, places them on level ground, and uses a marking line to measure them out lengthwise and crosswise. Once the measurements are complete, he then uses a sharp axe to cut along those lines, dividing them into two parts, or three, four, five, or even ten parts, or twenty parts, or even a hundred parts.

"In this way, monks, it is so for all sentient beings within that great Black Rope Hell. The wardens seize the offenders and cast them down upon the ground of blazing hot iron; they force them to lie on their backs and, using black iron cords, measure out and mark the body before hacking it apart with iron axes into various segments, just as described."
At that time, the offenders suffer such piercing pain and affliction that they undergo extreme agony, yet their lives do not come to an end.
As long as those non-human karmic debts have not been exhausted, they must fully experience all the consequences of the unwholesome deeds they committed in the past within this hell.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, among all the sentient beings within that great Black Rope (Kālasūtra) Hell—whether they be born there, transformed there, or even those who dwell there—the hell-wardens seize them and cast them upon a ground of blazing, hot iron. They force them to lie prostrate on the ground, measure their bodies with black iron cords, and having measured them, they saw through their bodies at the marked lines using iron saws that are fiercely burning and intensely hot. They saw again and again, from small saws up to large ones; then they break them again and again, from small breaks up to great breaks. They cut or slice them, and having cut or sliced them, they cut and slice them yet again, slicing them into the finest pieces."

For example, suppose there is a skilled sawyer in the world or a sawyer’s apprentice who takes various pieces of timber, places them on level ground, and uses black cords to mark them out with longitudinal and transverse lines. Having completed the marking, he then uses a sharp saw to cut along those lines; having cut once, he cuts again, continuing until the wood is greatly reduced. Next, he breaks it into smaller pieces, breaking them again and again until they are greatly shattered. He further slices and chops them, and having already sliced and chopped them, he slices and chops them yet again, reducing them to the finest fragments.
"Thus it is, thus it is, O bhikṣus!

Regarding all those sentient beings within that great hell of Black Rope—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or even remain there—the wardens seize them and cast them down upon the ground of blazing, hot iron. They force them to lie prostrate on the ground, measure them with black iron cords, and then cut their bodies apart with iron saws of fierce, blazing flames. Having sawed once, they saw again; from small saws to large ones, having split them, they split them again; from small splits to large splits, having sliced them, they slice them again; from small cuts to large cuts, having severed them, they sever them again."
At that time, even as that person undergoes such extremely severe suffering, their life does not yet come to an end.
To speak briefly as above, they must fully experience within it all the evil karma created while in human or non-human form.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, all those sentient beings within the Great Black Rope Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or even dwell there—are handed over by the various hell-wardens to one another, using great iron mallets that are blazing with fierce, hot, and dazzling flames, so that each may strike the others.
While they were striking one another, their hands were burned and their feet were burned, their hands and feet being burned all over;
their ears were burned and their noses were burned, their ears and noses being burned all over;
their limbs were burned and their joints were burned, their limbs and joints being burned all over.
At that time, even as that person undergoes extremely severe and agonizing suffering, their life does not yet come to an end.
To speak briefly as above, they must fully experience all the karmic actions performed in the past, whether in human or non-human forms.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, for all those sentient beings within the great Black Rope Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or even reside there—the fruit of their evil karma causes great black ropes to emerge from the sky, blazing with smoke and flames, extremely fierce and hot, until they fall upon the bodies of the sentient beings in that hell."
When the Black Rope [hell] touches them, it immediately binds the bodies of the offenders; having bound them, it binds them again, even until they are tightly bound;
having bound them, it binds them yet again, even until they are firmly secured.
Once they have been bound and strangled, a wind arises again that blows them apart.
When the ropes are loosened, the skin of those sentient beings' bodies is all flayed;
once the skin is flayed, the flesh is likewise stripped away.
Once the flesh has been stripped away, they next extract the sinews, even breaking through the bones;
once the sinews and bones are shattered, they blow out the marrow, which departs with the wind.
At that time, the sinner undergoes even the most severe and grievous suffering, yet his life does not end.
To speak briefly as above, he experiences all these things in succession until his evil and unwholesome karma is fully exhausted.
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings within that hell undergo long-lasting suffering for immeasurable time; they then emerge from the Great Black Rope Hell. Having emerged, they run about, seeking a dwelling, seeking a house, seeking shelter, seeking an island, seeking a place of refuge, and seeking a place of protection."
At that time, they further enter the Black Sand Hell, which is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Once the offenders have entered, the description is as briefly stated above, continuing in succession until they enter the sixteenth hell, the Cold Ice Hell.
Having entered these various hells, they undergo manifold sufferings until their lives come to an end.

"Furthermore, monks, within the Great Universal Hell (Mahāniraya), there are also sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounding one another. Starting from the Black Sand Hell (Kālasūtra) and briefly described down to the very last, which is named the Cold Ice Hell (Himapaṭala)."
"Monks! For what reason and by what cause is that great hell named Saṃghāta? Monks!"

All sentient beings within that hell—whether they are born there, have been born there, emerge from it, are manifested there, or even dwell there—exist due to the fruit of the evil karma of those sentient beings.
There are two great mountains named White Sheep’s Mouth, blazing fiercely with intense heat and radiant, flaming splendor.

At that time, the hell-wardens drive and compel the offenders into the interior of these mountains; once they have entered between the mountains, the two peaks close together, goring one another, striking one another, and grinding against one another.
Then those two mountains, having thus joined together, struck, collided, and rubbed against one another, returned to their original places.
It is like the two named Vikhaṇḍa and Rāvikhaṇḍa— these being names for lightning— which, having joined, struck, collided, and rubbed against each other,
each returns to its original place once they have finished striking and rubbing.

"In this way, monks, in this very manner, those two mountains come together and collide, strike and grind against one another; having rubbed and ground each other to the utmost, they each return to their original places, just so."

When all the sentient beings within that hell are crushed and ground by the closing impact of the mountains, their bodies are entirely drenched with flowing pus and blood until nothing remains but shattered bones.
At that time, even while undergoing such extremely severe and grievous suffering, the person’s life does not yet come to an end.
As briefly described above, they must experience [all these torments] in succession; this is how it should be understood.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, regarding all those sentient beings within the Saṃghāta Great Hell—both those who have been born there and those who dwell there—the wardens seize those sentient beings of the hell and cast them upon great, blazing, hot iron that is fiercely flaming, radiant, and terrifying."

They force him to lie on his back, then take another large iron [plate], also extremely fierce and blazing, and cover him with it; they grind him in this manner, just like the method of grinding used in the world for millstones.
Having ground it, he grinds it again, grinding it yet more;
having pulverized it, he pulverizes it again, pulverizing it yet more;
having rubbed it, he rubs it again, rubbing it yet more finely, until it finally becomes fine dust.
Once it has been turned into dust, it is further reduced to fine particles; thus, through successive stages, it becomes the most subtle atom (*paramāṇu*).
When it is ground into powder, all its constituent parts become pus and blood, which flow and scatter until they are entirely gone, leaving only the skeletal dust remaining in that place.
At that time, that person continues to experience even the most severe and agonizing suffering, yet their life does not come to an end.
The details are as described above; this sequence should be understood accordingly.
"Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!"

Furthermore, all those sentient beings within that Saṃghāta Great Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or are dwelling there—the hell-wardens seize them and hurl them into a great iron vat of intense heat; this vat is ablaze, radiating a constant, fierce glare.

Once they have been placed in the vat, just as in the worldly method of pressing sugarcane and sesame seeds, so too are they pressed; having been pressed, they are pressed again, until finally they reach the great pressing.
Once they have been crushed, one sees only pus and blood flowing to one side, while all their skeletal remains are reduced to fine powder.
At that time, the offender undergoes extremely severe suffering.
To summarize what has been said above: even before their lives have ended, they must fully experience all the consequences of their actions. "Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, regarding all those sentient beings within the Saṃghāta Great Hell—whether they are being born, already born, or currently dwelling there—the hell-wardens seize them and hurl them into iron mortars. These mortars are ablaze with fierce, blazing flames; furthermore, red-hot iron pestles, also extremely fierce and glowing, pound those offenders."
Having pounded it, he pounded it again, until he pounded it greatly;
having ground it, he ground it again, until he ground it greatly.
Once it had been pounded and ground, it finally became a fine powder.
Having ground these things into powder, he grinds them further and further until they become most minute.
While grinding them into powder, he sees only pus and blood flowing down on one side, while on the other side there still remain fragments of pulverized bone.
At that time, the offenders undergo extremely severe and heavy suffering.
To speak briefly as above, even until their lives have not yet ended, they fully experience all manner of sufferings.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, as for all those sentient beings within that Saṃghāta Great Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or are dwelling there—at that time, a great iron elephant will spontaneously appear in the sky above, blazing fiercely and powerful, with its flames shining resplendently in every direction."
With his two feet, he tramples the bodies of those sentient beings in hell from head to foot, crushing them in succession.
First he tramples their skulls, then the other parts; having trampled them once, he tramples them again, and so on until he tramples them most violently.

When the elephants trample upon them, the bodies of those sentient beings in that hell burst open, and their pus and blood gush forth, scattering in all directions; only the crushed bones remain piled together on one side.
At that time, the offenders undergo great and heavy suffering.
Briefly described as above, their lives do not yet come to an end.
In this manner, they experience [the suffering] in full succession within those realms.
"Furthermore, monks!
Moreover, those sentient beings within the Saṃghāta Great Hell undergo long-lasting suffering for immeasurable periods of time."
When this suffering has ended, they emerge from the Saṃghāta Great Hell; having emerged, they run straight ahead in flight, seeking a place of refuge and protection.

At that time, he further enters the Kṛṣṇabāluka (Black-Sand) minor hell, which is five hundred yojanas in extent; having entered there, he further enters various other minor hells, continuing in this manner until he reaches the Arbuda (Icy) hell, where he fully experiences suffering.
"Furthermore, monks! They enter again into the Raurava Hell.
Within this hell there are also sixteen subsidiary hells, each five hundred *yojanas* in extent, which serve as its retinue, ranging from Kālasūtra down to the final Śīta Hell."
"O bhikṣus!
For what reason and by what cause is this hell named Raurava?
O bhikṣus!"

Thus, all the sentient beings within the Great Hell of Screaming—whether those who have been born there, those currently existing there, or even those dwelling there—are at once driven and coerced by the hell-wardens to enter an iron city. That city is ablaze with glowing, fierce iron flames, its radiance intensely brilliant and scorching.

At that time, the offenders within the Iron City undergo extremely severe suffering; because they are overwhelmed by these manifold agonies and find them unbearable, they constantly cry out, and for this reason it is called the Hell of Wailing (Raurava).

Furthermore, within that hell, the buildings are made of iron; the chambers, carriages, and litters are likewise all of iron. The towers, pavilions, gardens, and ponds are entirely composed of fiercely burning, glowing embers, radiating intense light and penetrating through from top to bottom. The hell-wardens drive the suffering sentient beings into these structures; oppressed by various agonies beyond endurance, they immediately cry out, and for this reason it is called the Hell of Wailing (Raurava).
The sinner undergoes great and heavy suffering therein; briefly described as above, their life has not yet ended.
If those evil and unwholesome karmas have not been exhausted, they will continue to experience them in this manner, in full succession.

“O Bhikṣus! Those sentient beings within that hell endure suffering for a long duration throughout immeasurable time before they finally emerge from this Raurava Hell. Having emerged, they run away—in brief, as described previously—seeking a place of refuge and protection.”

He then proceeded again to the various minor hells, such as Kṛṣṇābhra and others, extending for five hundred yojanas. Having entered them, he underwent all manner of punishments just as before; to speak briefly, he eventually entered the Cold Ice Hell at the very end, where he fully experienced manifold sufferings until his life finally came to an end.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Screaming Great Hell, there are also sixteen minor hells as its retinue, each measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, ranging from the Black Sand Hell to the final Cold Ice Hell."
"Monks! For what reason and by what cause is this hell named 'Great Wailing' (Mahāraurava)? Monks!"

All sentient beings within that Great Screaming Great Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently being born, or are dwelling there—the hell-wardens seize them and likewise hurl them into the iron city. It is fiercely burning and intensely hot, with flames blazing upward and downward in piercing intensity. The offenders therein undergo extreme suffering; because they are so oppressed by manifold afflictions that it is unbearable, they consequently let out great screams.
For these reasons, that hell is named Great Screaming (Mahāraurava).

Within that hell, the dwellings are likewise made of hot iron; the rooms, houses, carriages, pavilions, and towers are all entirely of iron. Blazing coals burn fiercely, filling the place with intense heat. The sinners within undergo extreme suffering, as briefly described before, yet their lives are not yet ended.
In this manner, they experience [the sufferings] in full succession. "O monks!

Furthermore, those sentient beings in that hell endure long-lasting suffering for immeasurable time before finally emerging from this Great Howling Great Hell. Having emerged, they run away—and so on, as briefly described—seeking a place of refuge and protection."

Thereupon, they proceeded again to the minor hells such as Kālamegha and others; having entered them, they underwent suffering until, finally reaching the寒冰 (Cold Ice) Hell, they experienced all manner of torments before their lives came to an end.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Hell of Heat and Torment, there are also sixteen minor hells as its retinue. Each of these hells is, as before, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, extending from the Black Sand Hell down to the final Cold Ice Hell."
"O bhikṣus!
For what reason and by what causes is this hell named the Great Hell of Burning Torment (Tapana)? O bhikṣus!"

Within this Great Hell of Burning Heat, all sentient beings—whether born there, currently existing there, or even dwelling there—are seized by the various hell-wardens and cast into cauldrons of blazing, glowing-hot iron.
