With their heads downward and their feet upward, they are tossed about as the waves surge and boil in a state of constant, fierce heat.
Within it, the sinners are seared and boiled, undergoing extreme heat and affliction; therefore, it is named the Hell of Heat and Affliction (Tapana).

Furthermore, within that prison there are many iron cauldrons, iron jars, iron basins, iron vases, iron boilers, and iron tripods, as well as various iron griddles, all of which are blazing and intensely hot.
The sinners within are burned and boiled; for this reason, it is called the Hell of Tormenting Heat.
Within this hell, even as they undergo the most severe and grievous suffering, their lives do not yet come to an end.
Until that person’s evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted, they must undergo all these sufferings in successive order.

"O Bhikṣus! Those sentient beings within that hell endure long-lasting suffering for immeasurable time; only then do they emerge from the Great Hell of Burning Torment. Having emerged, they even run and flee, seeking a place of refuge and protection."

At that time, they further enter the minor hells such as Kṛṣṇa-saikatā, and so forth, briefly described down to the Arbuda hell, where they undergo all manner of sufferings until their lives come to an end.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Hell of Intense Heat (Pratāpana), there are also sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, beginning with the Minor Hell of Black Sand (Kālasūtra) and ending finally with the Hell of Cold Ice (Himā).
"Monks! For what reason and by what causes is this hell named the Great Hell of Intense Heat? Monks!"

The various sentient beings within that Great Hell of Intense Heat—those who have been born there, those currently existing there, and even those dwelling there—the hell-wardens seize them, turn them head-downward and feet-upward, and hurl them into cauldrons.
The cauldrons therein are fiercely hot, with boiling water and fire both ablaze; they strike against the offenders, who are tossed up and down as they boil.
At that time, they undergo extreme heat-affliction, great heat-affliction, and immense heat-affliction; therefore, it is named the Hell of Great Heat-Affliction.

Furthermore, within that hell, all the iron cauldrons, iron basins, iron pots, iron tripods, and iron pans are likewise ablaze with extreme and fierce heat; moreover, the sinners are cast into their midst.

At that time, the sinner is either boiled or seethed by the fires of hell, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions; being afflicted again and again, he experiences extreme and intense torment. For this reason, it is called the Hell of Most Fierce Heat and Extreme Affliction.
Within it, the offenders undergo extreme suffering, as briefly described previously.
Until their lives end, they experience all these various sufferings in this successive order. "O Bhikṣus!"

The sentient beings within that hell, having endured various sufferings throughout an immeasurable period of time on this long and distant path, finally emerge from such a Great Hell of Intense Heat, Blazing and Fierce. Having emerged, they run away—in brief, they do so desiring a place of refuge, protection, and sanctuary.

Thereupon, they again proceeded to the minor hells such as Kṛṣṇa-abhra and so forth, continuing even unto the final Cold Ice Hell; as long as their life-span was not yet exhausted, they underwent various sufferings in succession, just as described before.
*Sūtra on the Arising of the World*, Scroll Three.
*Sūtra on the Arising of the World*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Four: On the Hells, Part Three. "Furthermore, monks!

Within that great Avīci Hell, there are also sixteen minor hells as its retinue, surrounding it on all sides; each of these hells is five hundred yojanas in extent, beginning with Kālasūtra and ending finally with the Śīta (Cold Ice) Hell."
"O bhikṣus!
For what reason and by what cause is this hell named Avīci?
O bhikṣus!"

All the sentient beings within this Avīci Great Hell—those who have been born there, those currently existing, those emerging, and those remaining—due to the fruit of their own evil karma, naturally give rise to various hell-wardens. Each of these wardens seizes the body of a sentient being from that hell with both hands and hurls them onto a floor of blazing hot iron. There, flames shoot straight upward in intense fury; the beings are forced face-down upon the ground, whereupon the wardens take sharp knives and, starting from the ankles, cut through and pull out their tendons. They continue pulling them up by the hand until reaching the tendons of the neck, drawing them all out in succession until they pierce through the heart and marrow, causing suffering beyond description.

Having been dragged in this manner, they are made to drive iron chariots, galloping and racing along; these chariots are extremely hot, with blazing flames fiercely burning, intensely and violently, as they carry them across immeasurable *yojanas*.

Wherever they travel, the path consists entirely of perilous roads of glowing, molten iron; having gone, they must go again, never pausing for even a moment at the will of the hell-wardens, and wherever they desire to go, they are sent there immediately.
Wherever they go and wherever they arrive, the hell-wardens drag them along, never letting them go.
As they travel in this manner, through whatever places they pass, the wardens consume and incinerate the flesh and blood of the offenders' bodies until nothing remains.
By reason of these causes and conditions, they undergo severe and piercing suffering, extremely heavy and intense suffering, and suffering that the mind finds unpleasant;

yet their lives do not come to an end. Until those evil and unwholesome karmas are exhausted—until they have been extinguished, dispersed, transformed, and shifted—they must experience in full all that was done in the past, whether in human or non-human forms.
"Furthermore, monks!

All sentient beings within this great Avīci hell—whether born there, existing there, manifested there, or dwelling there—due to the retribution of their unwholesome karma, a great mass of fire suddenly arises from the eastern direction, blazing with a crimson hue, possessing immense and fierce flames, and glowing with intense radiance.

In this same manner, in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as the four intermediate points and the zenith and nadir, there likewise arise great masses of fire, blazing forth with light and flames of intense radiance."

At that time, the sinner is surrounded on all four sides by these great masses of fire which gradually close in; because they touch his body, he experiences various sufferings, even undergoing most severe and agonizing pain, yet his life does not yet end.
Briefly stated as above, all these sufferings are experienced in full within that hell.
Furthermore, monks, among the sentient beings born, existing,

and even dwelling within this Great Avīci Hell, due to the fruit of their evil karma, great flames of light emerge from the eastern wall and shoot directly toward the western wall, where they remain upon arrival.
From the western wall, a great flame of light issued forth, shooting directly toward the eastern wall, where it reached and remained;
from the southern wall, a great flame of light issued forth, shooting directly toward the northern wall;
and from the northern wall, a great flame of light issued forth, shooting directly toward the southern wall.
Shooting from below upward and from above downward;
intersecting crosswise and shooting back and forth, the blazing light was magnificent and resplendent as surging flames clashed together.
At that time, the hell-wardens cast the sinners into six kinds of great masses of fire.
These sinners continue to undergo extremely severe and agonizing suffering, yet their lives do not come to an end.
To speak briefly, until that unwholesome karma is finished and exhausted, one must undergo its full retribution in the interim.
"Furthermore, monks!

All those sentient beings within this Avīci Great Hell—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or even remain there—suffer for a vast duration due to the fruit of their evil karma, enduring long-lasting torment throughout immeasurable time.

At that time, they saw the eastern gate of the hell suddenly open of its own accord. Having heard the sound of it opening and seeing the gate open, these sentient beings ran toward it; they ran and ran again, running with great speed, each saying:
"Once we have reached that place, we shall surely be liberated."
‘If we were to reach that place now, it would be most auspicious.
As those beings ran in this manner—running, running again, and running with great speed—the flames on their bodies grew even more fiercely blazing.
It is like a powerful and strong man in this world who, carrying a great torch, runs against the wind; that torch then burns even more fiercely, its flames becoming increasingly intense and blazing.

In this way, as those sentient beings run and run with such great speed, the various limbs and joints of their bodies burn even more intensely; when they lift their feet, their flesh and blood disperse, and when they set them down, the flesh and blood are restored.
Furthermore, as those sentient beings run about in this manner and are about to reach the gate, by the power of their sinful karma, the gate closes upon them once again.
At that time, within that hell, upon a ground of glowing, blazing flames and hot iron, the sinners faint and fall prostrate, collapsing face-downward.
Once overturned, it immediately burns their skin;
once the skin is burned, it next burns their flesh;
once the flesh is burned, it next burns their tendons.
Once the tendons have been burned, he next burns the bones;
once the bones have been burned, it penetrates to the marrow.
When it reaches the marrow, only smoke is seen emerging.
After emerging, they emerge once more, and from it, smoke, sparks, and fire burst forth.
Within this, the offenders undergo the most severe sufferings in succession, yet their lives do not end.
As briefly described before, until those evil and unwholesome karmas—committed in former lives as humans or non-humans—are fully exhausted, they must endure them all therein.
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings within this Great Hell of Avīci—whether they have been born there, are currently existing there, or even reside there—who, due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, have endured various sufferings for immeasurable time along the long and distant path, find that the four gates of the hell open once again."
When the gates open, the sentient beings within that hell hear the sound and see them opening; they run toward the gates.
They run, they run further, and they run even more swiftly, thinking to themselves:
"We shall surely attain liberation from this place now; our suffering will certainly come to an end at this very moment."
As that person runs thus with great haste, his body becomes even more fiercely ablaze.
It is like a strong man holding a torch of dry grass and running against the wind; once the torch is lit, it burns with ever-increasing intensity.
In this way, in this manner, those beings run and run again, even running with great speed; as they run thus, that person's body becomes increasingly ablaze.
When they wish to lift their feet, the flesh and blood disintegrate; when they wish to set them down, the flesh and blood regenerate.
Upon reaching the gate of the hell, the gate closes once more.
Those sentient beings run headlong across this blazing ground of hot iron; unable to escape, their minds become frantic and confused, and they fall face-down upon the earth.
Once he has fallen to the ground, the skin of his body is completely scorched;
once the skin is burned, next his flesh is burned;

once the flesh is burned, his bones are burned, penetrating even to the marrow. Smoke and flames blaze intensely together; the smoke billows forth and the flames glow fiercely. As smoke and flames mingle, the torment of heat is doubled, and that person undergoes extreme and severe suffering therein.

To speak briefly as before: until one’s lifespan has reached its end, and until those evil and unwholesome karmas have been extinguished, abandoned, transformed, and dispersed—even including all that was created and done in former lives as humans or non-humans—one must experience the consequences of it all.
"Furthermore, monks!
All sentient beings within this great Avīci hell, even those who remain there, are burned by the blazing fires of hell due to the power of the retribution for their unwholesome karma."

At that time, all forms seen by the eye are those which the mind does not delight in; those things which the mind would delight in do not appear before it. It is constantly oppressed and distressed by forms that are not favored by the mind, forms that are unlovely and unwholesome. Likewise, all sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental objects conceived by the mind are things that the heart and mind do not find pleasing.
Things that are not pleasing to the mind and not lovely phenomena constantly manifest before them; whatever objects they encounter are all unwholesome.

Because of these causes and conditions, those people constantly undergo extremely heavy, coarse, and harsh suffering and affliction. Because their appearance is foul, so too is their touch, continuing until their lifespan has reached its end.
If evil and unwholesome karma has not yet subsided or been extinguished—whatever was created in the past in human or non-human forms—all such evil karma will be experienced in its entirety.
"Furthermore, monks!
For what reason and by what cause is the Avīci hell named 'Avīci'? Monks!"
Within this Avīci Great Hell, at all times, there is not even for a moment a brief experience of peace or joy, not even for as long as the snap of a finger; therefore, this great hell is named Avīci.
In this manner, they experience suffering in its full extent. O monks!

These sentient beings in this Great Hell undergo long-lasting suffering for immeasurable periods of time until they finally emerge from this Avīci Great Hell. Having emerged, they run; having run, they run again; they run even further, running as fast as they can, seeking a house, seeking shelter, seeking an island, seeking a place of refuge, and seeking a place of protection.

At that time, they further enter the various minor hells, such as Kṛṣṇasāra, which are five hundred yojanas in extent; having entered them, they proceed, in brief, until they finally reach the sixteenth cold hell, where they fully undergo all manner of suffering before eventually passing away from that place.
In this regard, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If a person creates karma through body, speech, and mind, And having done so, enters into the evil realms,
They shall thus dwell in the Saṃjīva Hell, The most terrifying place that makes one's hair stand on end."
Having passed through countless billions of years, though dead, they must instantly revive again;
as enemies and foes each seek retribution from one another, sentient beings thus slaughter one another.
If one gives rise to an evil mind toward one's parents, or toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas,
all such persons shall fall into the Black Rope Hell, where they undergo suffering that is most severe and intense.
Those who teach others to practice correctly yet lead them astray, and who inevitably destroy the friendships of others—
these too fall into the Black Rope Hell.
Those who delight in committing the three kinds of heavy evil karma and fail to cultivate the sprouts of the three kinds of roots of goodness, [shall likewise suffer].
These deluded people shall certainly enter the Saṃghāta Hell and suffer for a long time.
Whether they kill sheep, horses, or various oxen, or various kinds of beasts such as chickens and pigs,
and further kill other insects and ants— those people shall fall into the Saṃghāta Hell.
The signs of fear in the world are manifold; by these, sentient beings are oppressed and afflicted.
They shall fall into the Grindstone Mountain Hell, where they undergo the suffering of being crushed, pounded, and ground.
Because of the fetters and latent tendencies of greed, hatred, and delusion, they pervert the correct principle and cause it to become otherwise;
by judging what is right as wrong and acting contrary to the Dharma and Vinaya, they are wounded by the wheel of swords.
Relying on power and status to plunder others, taking from both the strong and the weak,
if one inflicts such various oppressions, one shall be trampled by an iron elephant.
Those who delight in killing and harming sentient beings, whose hands and bodies are smeared with blood and whose minds are cruel,
and who constantly perform such impure deeds— they shall be born in the place of Wailing.
Because they have afflicted and vexed sentient beings in various ways, they are burned and boiled in the Raurava Hell;
within it there is also the Mahāraurava Hell, which results from a mind of deceit, crookedness, and guile.
Enshrouded by the dense forest of various views, Sunk in the increasingly thick net of craving,
Constantly performing such most base deeds, They shall fall into the Great Howling Hell.
When one arrives at such a place of Great Screaming, a blazing iron city that makes the hair stand on end,
the iron halls and iron houses therein set all who enter them ablaze.
If one performs various worldly activities, one will constantly afflict and disturb sentient beings;
such persons shall be born in the Hell of Torment and suffer that torment for immeasurable time.
If one constantly vexes and offends the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, one’s parents, elders, and the aged,
causing them displeasure, they shall all fall into the Hell of Tormenting Heat.
Those who do not delight in cultivating pure karma for rebirth in heaven, but instead constantly distance themselves from their beloved kin,
and take pleasure in performing such deeds— they shall enter the hell of burning heat.
Those who direct evil toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as toward virtuous people, their parents, and others,
or who even harm other honorable ones, will fall into the hell of Heat, where they are constantly scorched by blazing flames.
Constantly and frequently committing various evil deeds, Never once giving rise to a single virtuous thought—
Such a person goes straight to the Avīci Hell, Where they shall undergo immeasurable suffering and affliction.
If one proclaims the True Dharma as non-Dharma, and proclaims all that is non-Dharma as the True Dharma,
thereby failing to increase virtuous deeds, such a person shall enter the Avīci Hell.
The Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra hells constitute two; together with the Saṃghāta, Raurava, and others, they form five;
with Tapana and Pratāpana, they total seven; and the Avīci hell is the eighth.
These eight are called the great hells, Fierce and blazing, their agonizing pain is difficult to endure;
Because they are produced by those who have committed evil deeds, Within them there are sixteen minor hells.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
You should know that within the space between those worlds, there are yet ten other locations of hells."
What are the ten?
They are the Arbuda hell, the Nirarbuda hell, the Aṭaṭa hell, the Hahava hell, the Huhuva hell, the Utpala hell, the Padma hell, the Puṇḍarīka hell, the Mahāpuṇḍarīka hell, and the Kūmuda hell.
"Monks! Between those [two], there are these ten kinds of hells. Monks!"
For what cause and for what reason is the Arbuda hell named "Arbuda"? Monks!
Because the physical forms of all the sentient beings in the Arbuda hell are like bubbles of foam, it is therefore called "Arbuda."
"Furthermore, what is the reason why the Nirarbuda hell is named 'Nirarbuda'?
Monks! The bodies of all those sentient beings within that Nirarbuda hell are like lumps of flesh; therefore, it is named 'Nirarbuda'."
"Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is the hell named A-hu?
Monks! When the sentient beings in the A-hu hell are oppressed by intense and piercing suffering, they cry out and say: [A-hu!]"
"Ahu, ahu! What great suffering!
For this reason, it is called the A-hu Hell.
"Furthermore, by what cause and by what condition is the Hu-hu-pa Hell named Hu-hu-pa?"
"O Bhikṣus!
When those sentient beings within the Hu-hu-pa Hell are oppressed by its extreme sufferings, they cry out and say:
'Hu-hu-pa! Hu-hu-pa!'"
For this reason, it is called Huhuva.
Furthermore, by what cause and by what condition is the hell named Aṭaṭa so called?
"O monks! Those sentient beings within that Aṭaṭa Hell have their bodies so tormented by extreme suffering that they can only utter: 'Aṭaṭa, aṭaṭa.'"
However, because the sound of their tongues cannot issue forth from their mouths, they are called Aṭaṭa.
Furthermore, by what cause and by what condition are the Kukkula hell-beings named Kukkula?
"O Bhikṣus!
Within the Saugandhika Hell, the fierce flames have the color of the saugandhika flower; therefore, it is named Saugandhika."
"Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is that hell named Utpala? O Bhikṣus!
Within that Utpala Hell, the color of the fierce flames is like that of an utpala flower; therefore, it is named Utpala."
"Furthermore, for what cause and for what reason is the Kummuda hell named Kummuda?
Monks! Within that Kummuda hell, the color of the fierce flames is like that of the kummuda flower; therefore, it is called Kummuda."
"Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is the hell named Puṇḍarīka?
O monks! Within the Puṇḍarīka hell, the color of the fierce flames is like that of the puṇḍarīka flower; therefore, it is called Puṇḍarīka."
"Furthermore, for what cause and for what reason is the hell named Paduma?
O monks! Within that Paduma hell, the color of the fierce flames is like that of a paduma flower; therefore, it is called Paduma."

“Monks! Suppose there were twenty *droṇas* of sesame seeds in the kingdom of Kośala, heaped high and not leveled, and a man were to take out a single sesame seed from among them once every hundred years.
Proceeding in this manner, after a full hundred years have passed, one takes another seed and casts it aside. Monks!

When those twenty *khāris* of sesame seeds in the kingdom of Kośala have been thus cast away until they are exhausted, the lifespan in the Arbuda hell is still not yet finished, according to my reckoning.
Furthermore, calculating roughly by these numbers: twenty such lifespans in the Arbuda hell constitute one lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell;
twenty lifespans in the Nirarbuda hell constitute one lifespan in the Ababa hell;
and twenty lifespans in the Ababa hell constitute one lifespan in the Ahaha hell.
Twenty *huhuva* lifespans constitute one *aṭaṭa* lifespan;
twenty *aṭaṭa* lifespans constitute one *kukula* lifespan;
twenty *kukula* lifespans constitute one *utpala* lifespan.
Twenty *utpala* lifespans constitute one *kumuda* lifespan;
twenty *kumuda* lifespans constitute one *puṇḍarīka* lifespan;
twenty *puṇḍarīka* lifespans constitute one *padma* lifespan.
Twenty *paduma* lifespans constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). "O Bhikṣus!
In the region where the Paduma Hell is situated, if sentient beings remain even a hundred yojanas away from that location, they will still be reached by the flames of that hell."
Sentient beings dwelling within fifty yojanas of that place will all become blind and lose their sight due to the smoke of that fire;
sentient beings dwelling within twenty-five yojanas will have the flesh and blood of their bodies scorched, burned, and shattered.
"O Bhikṣus!
Because the bhikṣu Kokālika gave rise to a mind of slander toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—a turbid and evil mind—he was reborn immediately after death in the Padma Hell."
Having been born in that place, a great hot flame issues from his mouth, more than ten cubits in length; upon his tongue there naturally appear five hundred iron plows, which constantly plow it.

"O monks! Elsewhere, I have never before seen such a form of self-harm as this: namely, giving rise toward fellow practitioners of the holy life to a mind of defilement and turbidity, a mind of injury and affliction, a mind of poisonous malice, a mind of non-benefit, a mind devoid of compassion, and a mind devoid of purity."
"Monks! Therefore, you should give rise to acts of loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind toward all those who practice the holy life.
As I see it, one who gives rise to loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind day and night will always experience peace and happiness."

Therefore, all you bhikṣus, you should all act exactly as I have seen and taught: you must constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness throughout the day and night; you should always train yourselves in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"While people in this world are still alive, An axe naturally grows upon their tongues.
That which they call 'speaking various poisons and evils' In turn brings ruin and harm to their own bodies."

To fail to praise those who deserve praise, and to speak in praise of those who do not deserve it—this is called a dispute within the mouth; because of such disputes, there is no experience of happiness.
If a person wins wealth through gambling, this is but a minor dispute in the world;
yet to give rise to a turbid mind toward one who practices purity is called a great quarrel of the mouth.
In this way, there are thirty-six hundred thousand *Nirarbuda* hells,
as well as the various *Atata* hells, and those who fall into the *Padma* hell;
they reach such states because they reviled the noble ones, due to having committed evil through the actions of speech and mind.
“Monks! In the midst of the world-systems, there are further winds called ‘Tormenting Heat. Monks!”

If those winds were to come to this realm of the four continents, all sentient beings within these four continents—whether born or dwelling there—would have every part of their bodies completely shattered, destroyed, and annihilated without remainder.
"Just as, for example, when reeds or rushes have been cut down and are not watered, they will all wither and perish without remainder; even so, monks!"

In the midst of the world system, there are winds known as "Scorching Torment. When they arrive here within the realm of these four continents, all sentient beings inhabiting these four continents will simultaneously be completely withered and destroyed, leaving nothing behind; it is just like this.
"However, because it is obstructed by the two mountains—the Inner Iron Ring Mountain and the Great Iron Ring Mountain—that wind does not reach this place. O bhikṣus!"
Those Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains are able to provide such supreme benefit, acting as a supportive basis for all sentient beings within these four continents and four worlds.
"Furthermore, monks!

In the intermediate space between worlds, there are winds that blow upon those beings being burned and boiled in hell, scattering their flesh, fat, marrow, and various impurities; the stench and filth of these odors are most terrifying and loathsome."
"O Bhikṣus!

If that wind were to come into this world-system of four continents, all sentient beings within the four continents, even those who are stationary, would become utterly blind and lose their sight, because the stench of its odor is so extremely violent and intense."
However, because they are obstructed by the two mountains, Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa, which block their path, they do not come here. "O bhikṣus!

Those two great mountains, the inner Cakravāḍa and the Mahācakravāḍa, provide such supreme benefit for all sentient beings of this world-system of four continents, as they serve as the basis for the karmic activities upon which those beings rely."
Furthermore, monks!
Between the worlds, there is yet another great wind called Saṃghāta. Monks!

If that wind were to come to this world-system, it would be able to lift up from the ground all four great continents, the eighty-four thousand other minor islands, as well as the various great mountains and Sumeru, the king of mountains, by a distance of one *krośa*.

Having lifted them, it could cause them to be scattered and destroyed; even at distances of two, three, four, five, six, or seven *krośas*, once they have been raised, it could cause them to be dispersed and destroyed;
and even if they were lifted to a height of one *yojana*, their dispersion and destruction would be just as previously described.
In this manner, [the wind] lifts up and destroys objects two, three, four, five, six, and seven *yojanas* in size, causing them all to disperse;
even up to one hundred *yojanas*, once lifted up, they are dispersed and destroyed;
and for two, three, four, five, six, or seven hundred *yojanas*, once lifted up, they are likewise dispersed and destroyed as described before.
Even up to one thousand yojanas, two, three, four, five, six, or seven thousand yojanas, having lifted them up, he disperses and destroys them. O monks!
It is, for example, like a strong man who takes a handful of wheat bran, raises it high, crushes it into fine powder, and scatters and casts it into the air until not a single remnant remains.
"Thus it is, thus it is, O bhikṣus!

In that world-system, there is a most powerful and violent wind named Saṃghāta. If this wind were to come here to these four continents, at that time it would lift up all four great continents of this world-system, as well as the eighty-four thousand other minor islands, all the mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, tossing them up to a distance of one krośa, dispersing and destroying them;
briefly described as before, even if they were lifted as high as seven thousand yojanas, they would likewise be dispersed and destroyed."
"O bhikṣus!
It is solely because they are obstructed by the two mountains—the Inner Iron Ring Mountain and the Great Iron Ring Mountain—that they do not come here.
O bhikṣus!"

The majestic power of those two mountains, the Inner Iron Ring and the Great Iron Ring, provides great benefit; it is through such power that they perform the function of providing a refuge for all sentient beings within these four continents and four worlds.
"Furthermore, monks!

To the south of Jambudvīpa, beyond the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), there is the palace residence of King Yama, six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides. It is surrounded on every side by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells, with seven rows of *tāla* trees outside them."
It was of variegated colors, beautiful to behold, and composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
In each of the four directions there are various gates; at every gate, there are defensive watchtowers, battlements, palaces, gardens, and lotus ponds.
Within these gardens and ponds, there are various kinds of trees, each with diverse foliage, exquisite flowers, and beautiful fruits, which fill and spread everywhere.
Various kinds of incense waft far on the wind,
and various birds each sing in harmonious chorus.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!
Due to the fruit of his evil and unwholesome karma, that King Yama has red molten copper liquid spontaneously appear before him during the three periods of the night and the three periods of the day.

At that moment, the king’s palace immediately transformed into iron, and all the previously existing objects of the five sensory pleasures that had appeared before his eyes vanished and were no longer seen.
If he was within the palace, he was born right there inside the palace.
At that time, King Yama, having seen this event, became terrified and uneasy; his hair stood on end, and he immediately went outside.
If he was outside the palace, he would likewise be born outside.
At that time, King Yama felt fear arise in his heart; trembling and ill at ease, the hairs on his body all stood erect at once, and he immediately fled back inside.

Then, the jailers seize King Yama, lift him high and drag him down, placing him upon a ground of glowing iron. That ground is fiercely burning, extremely intense and powerful, with blazing and radiant flames. Having dragged him down and made him lie prostrate, they immediately use iron tongs to pry open his mouth and pour molten copper into it.
At that time, King Yama’s lips and mouth were scorched;
once his lips and mouth were scorched, his tongue was scorched next;
once his tongue was scorched, his throat was scorched in turn.
After burning the throat, it further burns the large and small intestines, gradually incinerating them until they exit through the lower orifice.
At that time, King Yama reflects thus:

"Because all these sentient beings committed evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind in the past, they now all undergo such various, manifold, and immeasurable sufferings and unpleasant experiences."
Just as it is with the sentient beings within the hells, so too is it now with this body of mine and other beings who have performed similar actions together with King Yama.

Alas! May it be that from this moment forth, after I have cast off this body, whenever I obtain another body, we may both meet and take birth together in the human realm. May I, at that time, attain faith and understanding within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; having attained faith and understanding, may I further attain full perfection of faith and understanding there, shave my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and, possessing right faith and understanding, go forth from the household life into homelessness.

At that time, having already gone forth, not long after my ordination, for what purpose did I, a son of good family, attain right faith and understanding, go forth from the home life, and personally realize through direct experience the ultimate goal of the unsurpassed holy life within this very life?
Having fully realized this, may I declare:
"Birth and death are now exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has all been accomplished; there will be no further existence in future lives."
"O monks! At that time, King Yama further gave rise to such habitual virtuous thoughts.

Immediately at that moment, the palace where King Yama dwells was restored as the seven precious jewels, with all manner of things produced therein, just like the fivefold sensual pleasures of the devas manifesting in full perfection."
At that time, King Yama again had this thought:
"All sentient beings obtain happiness through good conduct of body, speech, and mind; may they each individually receive such peace and joy."
"Just as, for example, there are various yakṣas dwelling in the sky—namely myself and other kings of Yama, along with all sentient beings who have accumulated similar karma.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. "O bhikṣus!"
There are three celestial messengers in the world.
What are these three?
They are namely old age, sickness, and death.

"O monks! There is a certain kind of person who, through his own negligence, engages in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind; such persons practice evil in body, speech, and mind."
Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they go to the evil realms and are born within the hells.
The hell-wardens immediately arrive at that time, driving those beings before King Yama and saying:

"O Heavenly King, these beings, while formerly in the human world, were wanton and self-indulgent; they failed to harmonize their conduct and gave rein to their body, speech, and mind to perform unwholesome deeds."
Because they committed evil deeds through their body, speech, and mind, they have now been born here.
We only pray that the Heavenly King will kindly instruct them and sternly rebuke them.
Then King Yama asked the sinner: "O virtuous man!

When you were formerly in the human world, the first divine messenger gave you excellent instruction and stern rebuke; how could you have failed to see the appearance and birth of that first divine messenger?"
He replied, "Great King!
I truly did not see it."
Then King Yama spoke again:
"O man! Did you not see that when you were formerly in the world as a human being, you were sometimes a woman, or..."
Having become a man, the signs of old age appear;
when one is a mahallaka, the teeth fall out and the hair turns white, the skin becomes lax and wrinkled, and dark spots cover the body like sesame seeds.

The shoulders droop and the back bends, the gait is lame and faltering, and the feet no longer support the body, leaning to the left or right; the neck grows thin while the skin becomes loose. The two...
The limbs hang loosely like the dewlap of an ox; the lips and mouth are parched and withered; the throat and tongue are dry and rasping;
the body is bent and weak; the vital energy is faint and feeble; the labored breathing produces sounds like those of a saw being dragged;
he leans forward as if about to fall, walking while leaning on a staff; his prime has declined, and his flesh and blood are utterly exhausted and emaciated.
Emaciated and frail, they tread the path toward future lives; their movements are sluggish and heavy, and they no longer possess a robust form.
Even their bodies and minds are in a state of constant trembling, and all their limbs and joints are so weary and lax that they can hardly be controlled.
“Did you see it? That person replied, “Great King!”
"I truly saw it.
Then King Yama spoke to him again, saying:
"You foolish man, you possess no wisdom."
Having previously seen such appearances as these, why did you not reflect in this way:
"This body of mine also possesses these qualities and is subject to these conditions; I too have not yet escaped from such phenomena"?
I now possess such a nature of aging and have not yet escaped it.
I should perform subtle and wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, so that I may obtain the retribution of long-term benefit, peace, and happiness?
At that time, that person replied again:
"Great Deva!
I truly did not think in such a way."
"Why is this? Because their minds were unrestrained and they practiced heedlessness.
Then, King Yama spoke again:
"You foolish person, if it is as you say, it is because you yourself were indolent and practiced negligence that you did not cultivate wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.

By these causes and conditions, you shall experience great suffering and affliction for a long night, devoid of peace and happiness; therefore, you must fully undergo this retribution for negligence and receive such evil karmic fruits, just as all other negligent sentient beings receive their retributive punishments."

Furthermore, you people, this retribution of suffering—the fruit of evil karma—is not created by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brothers, nor by your sisters, nor by the king, nor by the various devas, nor was it created by your ancestors of the past. It is you yourselves who committed these evil deeds, and now you have gathered together to undergo this retribution.
"At that time, King Yama, having thoroughly instructed and rebuked him with this first divine messenger, further instructed and thoroughly rebuked him with the second divine messenger."
He said to them:
"O people, do you not see that the second divine messenger has appeared in the world?
They replied:
"Mahādeva, I truly did not see it.
The king spoke again:

"Did you not see that when one was formerly in the world as a human being—whether in a female body or a male body—the four great elements were in harmony, yet suddenly fell into discord? Overcome by the suffering of illness, bound by severe affliction, one might lie upon a small bed or a large bed, defiling one's own body with excrement and urine, wallowing therein without any autonomy."

Whether sleeping, lying down, rising, or sitting, he must rely on others for support; he requires others to wash and wipe him, to hold and carry him, and to provide him with drink and food. Do you see this?
That person replied:
"Great King! I truly saw it."
The King spoke again, saying:
"Fool! You see things in this way; [yet it is not so]."
If one is skillful and wise, how could they not reflect in this way:
"I too now possess such qualities; I too now possess such circumstances; I have likewise not yet escaped from such afflictive states; and I myself am subject to such afflictive conditions."

Since one has not yet escaped [saṃsāra], one should reflect for oneself: "I should now also perform various wholesome karmas—whether wholesome karma of body, speech, or mind—so that in the long night of the future, I may obtain great benefit and great peace and happiness."
That person replied: "No, Great King!
I truly did not entertain such a thought."
"Because you act with negligence due to a lazy mind.
The King spoke again, saying: "Fool!"

Since you now act with heedlessness, being lazy and indolent, and do not perform wholesome deeds—whether by body, speech, or mind—how can you obtain benefit and the retribution of peace and happiness for the long night?
Therefore, you should practice wholesome deeds.

If you act with negligence, then because of that negligence, this evil karma of yours was not created by your father, nor by your brothers, nor by your sisters; it was not created by the king or the gods, nor by your ancestors of the past, nor was it produced by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
"Since you yourself committed these evil deeds, you must now undergo this retribution yourself.
At that time, King Yama, having thus instructed him with the second divine messenger and rebuked him, further instructed and rebuked him with the third divine messenger.
He spoke thus:
"You foolish person!
When you were formerly a human being among men, did you not see the third divine messenger appear in the world?"
He replied, "Great King!
I truly did not see it."
Then King Yama spoke to him again, saying:
"You foolish man!

While you were in the world, did you not see that whether it was the body of a woman or the body of a man, when their life ended according to its time, they were placed upon a bed, covered with cloth of various colors, and carried out from the village, further adorned all around with various kinds of canopies, awnings, and parasols?"

Surrounded by his retinue, he cast off his necklaces and ornaments; raising his hands and disheveling his hair, he smeared his head with dust and ashes. In extreme grief and anguish, he wailed and wept, sometimes crying out: "Alas!"
Some said, "A great many. Others said:
"O my nurturer!
he cried out at the top of his voice, beating his breast in mournful agony, uttering various words that were choked with sorrow and piercingly bitter.
Do you see all this?
He replied, "Great King! I truly saw it."
Then King Yama spoke to him again: "Fool!
Since you previously witnessed such things as these, why did you not reflect upon them in this way: "
"I too now possess such a nature; my body also possesses such a condition.
Since I have not yet escaped from such a state, I too shall die; I am subject to death and have not yet attained liberation from it."
I should now perform various wholesome deeds—whether wholesome deeds of body, speech, or mind—for the sake of attaining great benefit and peace for myself throughout the long night.
At that time, that person replied:
"Great Deva!
I truly did not have such a thought."
"Why is this? Because of negligence.
Then, King Yama spoke to him again, saying:
"O foolish man!
Since you are now a practitioner of heedlessness, because of this heedlessness you do not perform wholesome deeds, nor will it bring you benefit for the long night!"
For the sake of long-term peace and happiness, one should accumulate the remaining virtues of body, speech, and mind.
Therefore, you now possess such conditions as heedless conduct; because of this heedlessness, you have personally created these evil and unwholesome karmas.
This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by your brothers, nor by your sisters; it was not created by kings or gods, nor by your ancestors of old, nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
"This evil karma of yours was created by you yourself; because you accumulated it yourselves, you have obtained this retribution and must now experience it yourselves.
Then, King Yama, having fully instructed and rebuked those sinners with this third divine messenger, commanded them to be led away once the rebuke was complete.
At that time, the jailers seized the offenders by both feet and both arms, turned them head-downward with their feet upward, and flung them from afar into the various hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When sentient beings have committed evil deeds, After death they fall into the miserable realms.
When King Yama sees them arrive, He rebukes them with a heart of compassion:"
"When you were formerly among human beings, did you not see old age, sickness, and death?
These are the messengers of the gods who have come to inform you; why are you so heedless as to fail to perceive this?"
Though body, speech, and mind are stained by the various defilements, If one does not practice generosity and precepts to discipline oneself,
How can such a person be called "possessing consciousness," Yet fail to create the causes for benefit?
At that time, King Yama, acting in accordance with the Dharma, having thus rebuked the sinner, the man—
gasping for breath and his heart trembling with fear— shook his entire body and said to the King:
"In the past, because I followed evil companions, my mind took no pleasure in hearing the various wholesome teachings."
"Enshrouded and obscured by greed and hatred, you failed to cultivate your own benefit and thus brought harm upon yourself.
The King said:
"You did not cultivate the causes of goodness, but created only various kinds of evil karma. Today, O foolish man, you shall receive the fruit; because of that karma, you have come to this hell."
All such evil karmas as these were not created by father or mother,
nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor were they fashioned by kings or devas.

This is solely the result of what you yourself have done; because the seeds of your various evil karmas were impure, and since you yourself committed these various evil deeds, you must now share in the experience of their bitter fruits.
After that king had instructed and rebuked him in succession by means of these three messengers,
the Lord of the Dead, King Yama, then abandoned the sinner and allowed him to be led away.
Those who dwell within the realm of Yama immediately seize the transgressors before them and lead them away toward the abode of hell,
that most terrifying place where one's hair stands on end.
Facing one another on its four sides are four gates; the four cardinal and four intermediate directions are all perfectly symmetrical.
The surrounding enclosure walls are entirely of iron, and the railings on all four sides are likewise made of iron.
The ground is made of blazing, glowing iron; its fierce flames and smoke merge into a single mass.
Seen from afar, it is terrifying and shatters the heart; so fiercely burning and radiant, it cannot be approached.
Just as within a range of one hundred yojanas, A great fire blazes fiercely, completely filling it all;
The various classes of sentient beings burned therein All stem from evil causes created in the past.
Rebuked by the three celestial messengers, yet their minds remain heedless and lacking in self-awareness,
they now repent for the long night, all because of their inferior minds in the past.
All sentient beings possessed of wisdom, upon seeing the divine messengers come to guide them, should apply themselves with diligence and not be negligent;
this is the skillful teaching of the Holy Dharma King.
Having seen and heard this, one should be struck with awe;
among all states of birth and death, there is nothing that surpasses nirvana, wherein every variety of affliction is exhausted without remainder.
Upon reaching that security, there is happiness; thus one sees the Dharma and attains tranquility.
That is to say, having crossed over all terrors, one naturally becomes pure and attains nirvana.
*Sūtra on the Arising of the World*, Scroll Four;
*Sūtra on the Arising of the World*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Five: On the Various Nāgas and Garuḍas.
"Furthermore, monks, all classes of nāgas have four modes of birth."
What are the four? First, birth from eggs;
second, birth from a womb; third, birth from moisture; and fourth, birth by transformation. These are called the four modes of birth for nāgas.
"O bhikṣus!
The species of garuḍas are also born in four ways: namely, birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation; these are called the four modes of birth."
"O Bhikṣus!

Beneath the waters of the great ocean, there is the palace of the Nāga King Sāgara, measuring eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides. It is adorned all around with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings, further embellished by sevenfold nets of pearls interspersed with precious bells."

Furthermore, there were seven rows of *tāla* trees, their branches spreading lushly to provide shade and reflection, surrounding it on all sides. There were pavilions of exquisite color, adorned with various jewels—namely, the seven treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
In each of the four directions there are gates; at every gate, there are multi-storied pavilions, watchtowers, and defensive bulwarks, as well as gardens and various springs and ponds.
Within the gardens and ponds, there were various kinds of flowers and grasses, each arranged in orderly rows.
Furthermore, there were many trees with diverse branches and leaves, diverse flowers and fruits, and diverse exquisite fragrances that wafted far on the wind.
Various birds warble together with clear and resonant voices. Monks!

Between Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and Mount Khadiraka, there lies the dwelling place of the two great Dragon Kings, Nanda and Upananda. That place is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded by sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings—as described briefly above—up to the point where various birds each warble together in harmony.
“Monks! To the north of the great ocean, for the sake of the dragon kings and all the garuḍa kings, there grows a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali (in the language of Sui, ‘Deer Cluster’).”

The root of that tree has a circumference of seven yojanas and extends twenty yojanas into the earth; its trunk rises to a height of one hundred yojanas, and its branches and foliage cover an area of fifty yojanas.

Outside the grove, the park grounds are exactly five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls and moats, and so forth, up to the various birds each singing in harmony, as briefly described above.
"O bhikṣus! To the east of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali, there are the palatial residences where egg-born nāgas and egg-born garuḍas dwell."
Its palace is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, up to the various birds singing in harmony, as briefly described above.

To the south of the great tree Cūḍaśālmalī, there are palatial residences for the womb-born nāgas and womb-born garuḍas, each also six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, up to the various birds singing in harmony, as briefly described above.

To the west of the great *kūṭaśālmali* tree, there are the palatial residences of moisture-born nāgas and moisture-born garuḍas, each also measuring six hundred yojanas in length and breadth. They are surrounded by sevenfold walls, and so forth, until the various birds sing in harmony, as briefly described above.

To the north of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali, there are the palatial residences of the spontaneously born nāgas and spontaneously born garuḍas; these are also each six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, including the various birds singing in harmony, as briefly described above.

“Monks! When that king of the egg-born garuḍas wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, he immediately flies to the eastern branch of the great tree Jaṭāśamari. Having surveyed the great ocean, he then swoops down and fans the waters of the great ocean with his two wings, causing the water to part by itself for two hundred yojanas. Therein, he seizes the egg-born nāga in his beak and carries it out beyond the sea to eat it at his pleasure.”
"O bhikṣus!
The king of the garuḍas born from eggs can only capture and eat at will those dragons born from eggs; he cannot capture those born from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation."

“Monks! When the garuḍa king born from a womb wishes to seize a nāga born from an egg, he immediately flies to the eastern branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali. Looking down at the great ocean, he fans the waters with both wings, causing the water to part for two hundred yojanas. Thereupon, he seizes the egg-born nāgas in his beak and carries them out to sea, where he eats them at his pleasure.”

Furthermore, when the Garuḍa King born from a womb desires to seize a dragon born from a womb, he immediately flies to the southern branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali. Looking down at the great ocean, he fans the waters with his two wings until the sea opens up for four hundred yojanas. Thereupon, he seizes the womb-born dragon within it, carries him out over the ocean, and eats him at his pleasure.
"O Bhikṣus!

This garuḍa king born from a womb can only capture dragons born from eggs and dragons born from wombs for his use; he cannot, however, capture the two kinds of dragons born from moisture or by transformation."

“Monks! When the moisture-born king of the garuḍas wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, he immediately flies to the eastern branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali. With his two wings, he fans the waters of the great ocean until they part for two hundred yojanas. Having parted them, he seizes the egg-born nāgas and eats them at his pleasure.

Furthermore, when the moisture-born king of the garuḍas wishes to seize a womb-born nāga, he immediately flies to the southern branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali. With his two wings, he fans the waters of the great ocean until they part for four hundred yojanas. Having parted them, he seizes the womb-born nāgas and uses them as he pleases.”

Furthermore, when the King of the Moisture-born Garuḍas wishes to seize a moisture-born nāga, he immediately flies to the western branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali. With his two wings, he fans the waters of the great ocean until they part for eight hundred yojanas. He then seizes the moisture-born nāgas with his beak and eats them at his pleasure.
"O bhikṣus!

The various garuḍa kings born from moisture can only capture nāgas born from eggs, from wombs, or from moisture, taking them as they please and eating them at will; however, they cannot capture nāgas who are born through transformation."

"O Bhikṣus! When that *upapāduka* (miraculously born) king of the garuḍas wishes to seize an *aṇḍaja* (egg-born) nāga, he immediately flies to the eastern branch of the great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree. With his two wings, he fans the waters of the great ocean until they part for two hundred *yojanas*. He then seizes the egg-born nāgas with his beak and eats them at will.

Furthermore, when this *upapāduka* king of the garuḍas wishes to seize a *jarāyuja* (womb-born) nāga, he immediately flies to the southern branch of the great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree. With his wings, he fans the sea until the waters part for four hundred *yojanas*. Once the sea has parted, the *upapāduka* king of birds then seizes the womb-born nāgas with his beak and eats them at will."

Furthermore, when this king of *upapāduka* garuḍas wishes to seize a *saṃsvedaja* nāga, he immediately flies to the western branch of the great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree; fanning the ocean with his wings, the waters part for eight hundred *yojanas*, whereupon he instantly seizes the various *saṃsvedaja* nāgas and eats them at will.

Moreover, when this king of *upapāduka* garuḍas wishes to seize an *upapāduka* nāga, he again flies to the northern branch of the great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree; looking down at the great ocean, he fans the great sea with both wings, the waters parting for one thousand six hundred *yojanas*, whereupon he immediately seizes the various *upapāduka* nāgas and eats them at will.
"O bhikṣus! All those nāgas are entirely devoured by this king of the garuḍas. O bhikṣus!"
There are other nāgas whom the king of the garuḍas cannot seize; namely, the nāga king Sāgara, who has never been startled or disturbed by that king of the garuḍas;
furthermore, there are the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, these two nāga kings also cannot be seized by that king of the garuḍas;
and again, there are the nāga kings Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Anavatapta, whom the king of the garuḍas likewise cannot seize.
"O Bhikṣus!

There are other dragon kings who likewise are not seized and eaten by the Garuḍa king; namely, the Dragon King Mahācakra, the Dragon King Takṣaka, the Dragon King Karkoṭaka, the Dragon King Śveta, the Dragon King Vāsuki, the Dragon King Saṅkhapāla, the Dragon King Kamvala, the Dragon King Aśvatara, and so forth."
"O bhikṣus!
There are yet other nāgas who, within the domain of their respective abodes, likewise do not become food for the garuḍas."
“Monks! By what causes and conditions do these beings, having gone to such a destination, take birth among the nāgas? Monks!”

There are sentient beings who cultivate the causes for being a nāga, observe the precepts of a nāga, give rise to the mind of a nāga, and form the intention of a nāga; having performed such actions, because they have been brought to maturity by those causes and conditions, they are born among the nāgas.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes of the garuḍa, uphold the precepts of the garuḍa, give rise to the mind of the garuḍa, and discern the intention of the garuḍa; by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are born among such garuḍas.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes for being wild beasts, observe the precepts of wild beasts, give rise to the mind of wild beasts, practice the karma of wild beasts, and differentiate the intentions of wild beasts. Through such various cultivations of the causes of wild-beast precepts, they initiate karmic actions and perfect their mentalities. Due to these manifold causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among these various mixed species of wild beasts.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes of cattle, the precepts of cattle, the karma of cattle, the mind of cattle, and the intention of cattle; as briefly explained before, up to their discrimination based on these conditions, they are born among cattle.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes of chickens, the precepts of chickens, the karma of chickens, the mind of chickens, and the intention of chickens; as briefly described before, through such distinctions and these causal conditions, they are born among chickens.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cultivate the causes of an owl, receive the precepts of an owl, give rise to the mind of an owl, perform the deeds of an owl, and differentiate the thoughts of an owl. Because they have thus cultivated the karma of an owl, received its precepts, given rise to its mind, and differentiated its thoughts, after casting off this body, they are born among owls.

“Monks! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who cultivate the moon-vow, or cultivate the sun-vow, the constellation-vow, or the great-person vow; some cultivate the vow of silence, some cultivate the vow of the Mahādeva, some cultivate the vow of the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa), some cultivate the vow of entering the water, some cultivate the vow of making offerings to the sun, some cultivate the vow of serving fire, or they practice asceticism in various foul and turbid places. Having cultivated these, they form this thought:”

"May these various precepts I have cultivated—namely, the moon-precept, the sun-precept, the star-precept, the silence-precept, the Mahādeva-precept, the mahāsattva-precept, the water-precept, the fire-precept, the austerity-precept, the impurity-precept, and so forth—cause me, by means of them, to become a deva or to obtain the retribution of a deva."
"Having generated such perverse thoughts and vows, O bhikṣus!
Regarding these individuals who have given rise to perverse vows, I shall now declare their destination; they will certainly be reborn in two places:"
Whether they are born in hell or born as animals. "O bhikṣus!
There are some śramaṇas, brahmins, and others who hold such a view and speak thus:"
"The self and the world are eternal;
this alone is true, all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"'Both the self and the world are impermanent.
This is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:"
"Both the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal;
this is the truth, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘Both the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite;
this alone is the truth, all else is false. O bhikṣus!
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are finite.
This alone is true; all else is false."
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas, brahmins, and others who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are infinite."
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite."
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite."
"This alone is true; all else is false.
"Monks! There are some śramaṇas, brahmins, and others who hold such a view and speak thus:"
"Life is identical to the body;
this is the truth, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The life-principle is one thing and the body is another;
this is the truth, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is a life-principle and there is a body;
this is true, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak as follows:
"There is no life-principle and no body;
this alone is the truth, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is existence after the Tathāgata’s death;
this is the truth, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death;
this alone is true, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"Whether the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist after death—this alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"Regarding the Tathāgata after death, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
This is the truth; all else is false. "O Bhikṣus!"
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: "The self and the world are eternal.
This alone is true; all else is false."
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas will maintain the view of a self and the view of a world within the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*),
and they will maintain the view of a self and the view of a world apart from the conditioned formations.
For this reason, they hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are eternal.
This alone is true; all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: ‘The self and the world are impermanent.’”
If one were to say, "This alone is true,
all else is false," then those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas would hold the view of non-self and the view of no world regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
and they would likewise hold the view of non-self and the view of no world apart from conditioned phenomena.
For this reason, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are impermanent.
This is the truth; all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: ‘Both the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal.’”
"‘This alone is the truth; all else is false’—
such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas will maintain the view of a self and the view of a world within conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra),
and they will maintain the view of a self and the view of a world apart from conditioned phenomena."
For this reason, they speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are both eternal and impermanent;
this alone is the truth, all else is false."
“Monks! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: ‘The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.’”
If they say, "This alone is true,
all else is false," then those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas will maintain the view of a self and the view of a world within conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra),
and they will maintain the view of a self and the view of a world apart from conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal.
This alone is the truth; all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The self and the world are finite.'"
Regarding the claim that "this alone is true and all else is false," those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak thus:
"Life is finite and the person is finite; from the initial entry into the mother’s womb it is called life, and after death, when the body is encoffined and buried, it is called the person."

From the time of his initial birth, the Superior One has received four kinds of bodies; he has fallen seven times, transmigrated seven times, run seven times, and traveled seven times, thereby accomplishing life and entering the assembly of those who have attained life.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are finite.
This is the truth; all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: ‘The self and the world are infinite.’”
"This alone is true, all else is false"—thus do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak:
"The life-principle is infinite; the person is infinite."
From the initial conception within the mother’s womb it is called *jīva* (life); after death and burial, it is called *puruṣa* (person).

From birth, the superior person undergoes four types of embodiment, falling seven times, transmigrating seven times, running seven times and wandering seven times, thereby accomplishing life and entering the aggregate of life.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are infinite;
this is the truth, all else is false."
"Monks! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The self and the world are both finite and infinite.'"
"This alone is true, and all else is false.
Furthermore, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak thus:
"The life-principle (jīva) is both finite and infinite."
This person, from the initial moment of entering the womb while in the mother’s belly until death and subsequent burial,

is a superior person who, from the first reception of the four types of bodies, undergoes seven falls, seven transmigrations, seven runnings, and seven goings, thereby accomplishing life and entering the aggregate of life.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are both finite and infinite.
This alone is the truth; all else is false."
"Monks! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.'"
"This alone is true, all else is false.
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak thus:
"The world is neither finite nor infinite."

From the initial reception of the body, there are four types; having fallen seven times, transmigrated seven times, and run and wandered seven times, one achieves life and enters the aggregate of life.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.
This alone is the truth; all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The life-principle is identical to the body.'"
"Only this is true, and all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas perceive a self and perceive a life-principle within their own bodies,
and they likewise perceive a self and perceive a life-principle within other bodies.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"Life is identical to the body;
this alone is true, and all else is false."
"O bhikṣus! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The life-principle is one thing, the body is another.'"
"Only this is true, all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas perceive a self and perceive a life-principle within their own bodies,
and they likewise perceive a self and perceive a life-principle within other bodies.
Therefore, they speak thus: "The life-principle is one thing and the body is another.
This is the truth; all else is false."
"Monks! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The life-principle exists and the body exists.'"
"Only this is true; all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas perceive a self and perceive a life-principle within their own bodies,
and they likewise perceive a self and perceive a life-principle within other bodies.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"There is a soul and there is a body;
this alone is true, all else is false."
“Monks! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘The life-principle is not the same as the body.’”
"Only this is true, all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not perceive a self within their own bodies, nor do they perceive a life-principle;
nor do they perceive a self within other bodies, nor do they perceive a life-principle therein.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The life-principle is not the body.
This alone is true; all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'The Tathāgata exists after death.'"
"Only this is true, all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold such a view regarding the world:
that from one life one shall go to another life, and one shall likewise continue toward the cycle of saṃsāra.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The Tathāgata exists after death;
this is the truth, and all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death.’”
"Only this is true, and all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold such a view regarding the world:
that this present life-span continues until that [future state], after which the subsequent life-span is severed.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death.
This alone is true; all else is false."
“Monks! Among these, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: ‘After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he both exists and does not exist.’”
"Only this is true; all else is false"—thus do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold such a view regarding the world:
that when life is severed here, one goes to another place, proceeding through the cycle of transmigration.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The Tathāgata exists after death and does not exist after death.
This is the truth; all else is false."
"O monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus: 'After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he neither exists nor does he not exist.'"
"Only this is true, all else is false"—
those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold such a view regarding the world:
that when a person's life is severed and destroyed here, their life is likewise severed and destroyed as they move to another place.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he neither exists nor does he not exist.
This alone is the truth; all else is false."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
I recall that in the past there was a king named Ādarśamukha (Mirror-Face)."
On one occasion, King Ādarśamukha, wishing to observe those born blind for his amusement, issued a decree proclaiming throughout the kingdom that all men born blind should assemble.
Once they had assembled, he spoke to that group of blind men, saying:
"You who have been blind from birth, are you able to know the form and appearance of an elephant?
What is its shape like?"
Those who were born blind replied with one voice:
“O Heavenly King!
We are born blind; we truly cannot know the form and appearance of an elephant.”
The king spoke again:
"Since you have never known an elephant before, do you now wish to know its form and characteristics?
Then, those group of blind men answered in unison:
"O Heavenly King!
We truly do not know him.
If we were to receive the King's grace, we might perhaps come to know the physical characteristics of the elephant."
At that time, King Ādarśamukha immediately issued a decree, summoning an elephant trainer and addressing him thus:
"You should go quickly to my elephant stable, fetch an elephant, and place it before me to show to these blind men."
At that time, having received the king’s command, the elephant trainer immediately brought the elephant and placed it before the royal hall, saying to the blind men:
"This is the elephant."
Then, each of the blind men felt the elephant with his own hands.
At that time, the elephant trainer spoke again to the group of blind men:
"Having touched the elephant, report it to the King exactly as you have perceived it."

At that time, among the blind men, some touched the nose, some touched the tusks, some touched the ears, and some touched various parts of the body such as the head, neck, back, flanks, tail, and feet.
Then the king asked,
"O you who were born blind, have you now understood the form and characteristics of the elephant?
The men born blind answered the king in unison:
"O Great King!
We have now understood the physical characteristics of the elephant.
At that time, the king questioned them once more, saying:
"You blind ones, if you knew what an elephant is like, what would its characteristics be?
At that time, among the group of blind men, one who had touched the trunk spoke to the king, saying:
"O Great King!..."
The elephant’s shape was like a rope.
One who touched its tusks replied,
‘O Heavenly King!’”
"The elephant's shape is like a wooden stake.
When someone touched its ear, he replied,
"O Heavenly King!..."
"The elephant's shape is like a winnowing basket.
When someone touched its head, it replied,
"O Great King!"
The elephant’s shape was like a jar.
When someone touched its neck, it replied,
"O Great King!"
"The elephant is like a house rafter.
One who touched its back replied,
"O Heavenly King!"
"The elephant is like the ridgepole of a house.
One who touched its flanks replied, "O Heavenly King! [The elephant is like the ridgepole of a house]."
The elephant’s shape was like a grain basket.
When [the king] touched its thigh, it replied,
“O Heavenly King!...”
"The elephant's form is like a tree.
When someone touched its foot, it replied,
"O Heavenly King!"
"The elephant's shape is like a mortar.
When someone touched its tail, he replied,
"O Heavenly King!"
"The elephant is like a broom.
Then, each of the blind men replied,
"O Heavenly King!"
“The form of the elephant is like this,” [he said]. “O Great King! The form of the elephant is like this.
Having spoken thus, the king then addressed the assembly of blind men, saying:
"You do not even know whether this is an elephant or not an elephant, much less can you know the elephant's physical characteristics.
At that time, those blind men each held their own views and engaged in mutual contention; each covered his face with his hands, vying with one another and reviling one another.
When each had finished speaking,
King Ādarśamukha saw those blind men thus contending with one another and laughed with great joy.
At that time, the king spoke these verses:
"These blind men were born without eyes; they argue with one another over this matter at random.
Since no one has ever taught them, how could they know the parts of the elephant's body?"
“Monks! It is so, it is so.

All those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world are likewise; they are unable to know, as it truly is, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”

Since they do not know this as it truly is, you should know that for a long night they will continue to give rise to strife and contention, wandering through birth and death, mutually disparaging and mutually reviling one another.

Having already given rise to strife and contention, they persisted in their rivalry without ceasing; each used his own hands to shield his face, like a group of blind men who together cause one another distress and confusion.
In this regard, there is a verse:
"If one cannot know the Noble Truth of Suffering, Nor understand the cause that is the Accumulation of Suffering,
Then regarding all the various phenomena of suffering in the world— This is the state where suffering is extinguished without remainder."
Within this state, one does not yet know this Path; how much less could one know the practice that brings about the cessation of suffering?
Thus, their mind is not yet liberated, nor have they attained the state of liberation through wisdom.
Since they cannot discern and contemplate with clear insight, but only know how to move toward birth, old age, and death,
and have not yet attained liberation from the bonds of all Māras, how could they possibly reach the state of non-existence?

“Monks!
