If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who are able to know the noble truth of suffering as it really is, and who know as they really are the noble truths of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering, they should train themselves accordingly in this way.”

For a long night they have lived together in harmony, each rejoicing, free from contention, and pursuing a single training; like water and milk blending together, they dwell in one place, manifesting the noble Dharma taught by their Teacher and abiding in a state of peace and happiness.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
If one can know that all these existences are suffering, And the causes from which all such sufferings arise,
Having realized that everything is entirely suffering, One should cause it to be extinguished without remainder.
If one knows that this cessation arises through the Path, one will then reach the state where suffering is extinguished;
there, one can fully attain liberation of mind as well as the state of liberation through wisdom.
Thus one can reach the limit of all existences;
in this way, one does not arrive at birth, old age, or death, forever attaining liberation from the bonds of Māra, and eternally departing from all realms of worldly existence.
6. The Chapter on Asuras. *Qishi jing*, Chapter Six, Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."
To the east of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a distance of more than a thousand yojanas from the mountain, beneath the great ocean, lies the dwelling place of the asura king Vemacitra’s kingdom.

That place is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of city walls and seven tiers of railings, universally adorned, even with seven tiers of golden and silver bell-nets that embellish its perimeter.
Outside, there are seven rows of *tāla* trees of various beautiful colors, all composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
Each city wall is one hundred yojanas high and fifty yojanas thick.
On each of the four sides of the walls, with a distance of five hundred yojanas between them, a gate is placed; each gate is thirty yojanas high and twelve yojanas wide.
Within each and every gate, there are various defensive watchtowers, battlements, gardens, and ponds; within each of these gardens, there are various kinds of fruit trees.
Each of those trees has various kinds of leaves, various kinds of flowers, and various kinds of fruits; each of those fruits has various distinct fragrances, the scent of which wafts far.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of birds of diverse species, each singing in harmony and producing all manner of sounds, their voices plaintive and elegant. O Bhikṣus!

Within that great city of the Asuras, a separate palace-city was established for the Asura King Vemacitrin; it is named the Palace City of Śamāpāti. It is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold city walls composed entirely of the seven treasures, standing one hundred yojanas high and fifty yojanas thick.
At each of the four sides of the city, at a distance of five hundred yojanas from one another, a gate was established; each gate was thirty yojanas high and twelve yojanas wide.
Each of these gates also features watchtowers, battlements, and pavilions, as well as gardens, ponds, and various flower-filled pools.
Furthermore, there are diverse fruit trees, each with its own variety of leaves, flowers, fruits, and fragrances, the scent of which wafts everywhere.
There were various kinds of birds, each chirping in harmony, producing all manner of sounds whose tones were plaintive and elegant. "O Bhikṣus!
In the very center of the city of Śrāvastī, for the sake of the Asura King Vemacitrin, there was established an assembly hall named Saptamukha."
That place was five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, adorned all around with sevenfold railings. It was also surrounded by sevenfold nets of golden and silver bells.

Outside, it was encircled on all four sides by seven rows of *tāla* trees, decorated with various colors and most delightful to behold; they were all composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, crystal, coral, red pearls, *śaṅkha-śilā*, and *musāragalva*.

On each of its four sides there are various gates; every gate is equipped with watchtowers and defensive bulwarks, all likewise composed of the seven treasures, interspersed with diverse colors that are pleasing for the eye to behold.
"The ground there is entirely of deep blue lapis lazuli, soft and smooth; when touched, it is like kācilindika cloth. O Bhikṣus!"

In that assembly hall of the seven heads of the asuras, there is naturally a jeweled pillar in the center, twenty yojanas high; beneath this jeweled pillar, a jeweled throne has been established for the asura king Vemacitra.

It is one yojana in height and half a yojana in width, composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva and aśmagarbha, with various colors intermingled, exceedingly lovely and delightful; it is soft, fine, and smooth, so that touching it is like the touch of kācalindika cloth.

On both sides of that seat, there are sixteen places for the minor asuras to sit, likewise fashioned from the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, and so forth up to agate—which are multicolored and pleasing to behold, soft and smooth to the touch, like kācilindika cloth.

“Monks! At that assembly place of the seven heads of the asuras, on the eastern side is the palace of the asura king Vemacitra. It is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells.

Outside, there are seven rows of *tāla* trees encircling it on all four sides, forming a magnificent and continuous perimeter. Interspersed with various colors, they are exceedingly delightful and are composed of the seven treasures, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
On each of the four sides, there are various gates; at each and every gate, there are watchtowers, battlements, defensive platforms, pavilions, gardens, ponds, and flower-filled pools.
Furthermore, there are various trees; each tree has diverse leaves, diverse flowers, diverse fruits, and diverse fragrances, whose scents pervade everywhere.
There are various kinds of birds, each warbling harmoniously, producing a variety of sounds whose tones are plaintive and elegant. "O Bhikṣus!

To the south, west, and north of that assembly hall of the seven-headed Asuras, there are palaces, all of which are the dwellings of various minor Asura kings. These places are nine hundred yojanas in length and breadth, or eight hundred, seven hundred, six hundred, five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, or two hundred yojanas; even the smallest is still one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. They have sevenfold walls, and so forth, as briefly described, up to various kinds of birds, each warbling harmoniously."
"Furthermore, monks!

On the four sides of that Assembly Hall of the Seven Heads of the Asuras, there are also palaces where all the smallest of the Asuras dwell. These places are ninety yojanas in length and breadth, or eighty, seventy, sixty-five, fifty, forty-three, thirty, or twenty yojanas; even the very smallest is still twelve yojanas in length and breadth. They have sevenfold walls, and to speak briefly, they contain various birds, each chirping in harmony."
"O bhikṣus! To the east of that assembly hall of the seven heads of the asuras, there is a grove belonging to the asura king Vemacitra called the Śāla Forest."
That grove is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells, all composed of the seven treasures such as agate.

On each of the four sides, there are various gates; each and every gate is equipped with watchtowers and defensive bulwarks of variegated colors, beautiful to behold, and likewise accomplished of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to agate.
"O bhikṣus! To the south of that assembly hall of the seven heads of the asuras, there is another park belonging to the asura king Vemacitra, named the Śamālī Forest."
That grove was also one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells, all composed of the seven treasures such as agate and the rest.

On each of the four sides, there are various gates; at every gate, there are watchtowers and battlements of diverse and beautiful colors, all fashioned from the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to agate.
“Monks! To the north of that assembly hall of the seven heads of the asuras, there is also a grove belonging to the asura king Vemacitra called the Nandana Forest.”
That grove was also one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells, all composed of the seven treasures such as agate.

On each of the four sides, there are various gates; each and every gate is fully equipped with watchtowers and defensive parapets, beautiful to behold in their diverse colors, and even entirely composed of such precious substances as musaragalva and agate.
However, regarding these various gates, they lack only the pavilions; all other adornments are identical to those previously described. "O Bhikṣus!
Between the Śāla forest and the Śamālī forest, there is a great lake belonging to the Asura King Vemacitrin, named Nanda."
The pond is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are exceedingly cool, clear, pure, light, and sweet, and are never turbid.

It is paved with bricks made of the seven kinds of jewels interspersed throughout, and it is surrounded on all sides by seven layers of stone slabs, seven layers of railings, and seven layers of bell-nets hanging down.
Outside, sevenfold rows of *tāla* trees encircle it on all four sides; they are of various beautiful colors and are composed entirely of the seven precious substances, such as agate.
On each of the four sides, there are stairways of variegated hues interspersed together, which are pleasing to behold and likewise accomplished from the seven precious substances.
Furthermore, various flowers grow everywhere within the ponds, namely the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers.
Those whose forms are like fire have the color and radiance of fire;
those whose forms are like gold have the color and radiance of gold;
those whose forms are blue have the color and radiance of blue.
Those whose forms were red had red color and red light;
those whose forms were white had white color and white light;
those whose forms were green had green color and green light.
The clusters are like chariot wheels; their floral radiance illuminates one *yojana*.
The fragrance they emit likewise pervades one *yojana*.
From within the pond, immeasurable lotus roots emerge, as large as chariot axles. When cut, sap flows forth, white in color like milk, and its taste is sweet and exquisite, like the finest honey.
“O bhikṣus! Between those two groves, Kūṭāgāra and Nandana, there is a great tree belonging to the asura king Vemacitrin, named Sujātāpāṭala.”

Its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference; its roots extend twenty-one yojanas into the earth, while its trunk rises one hundred yojanas above ground. Its branches and foliage provide shade over fifty yojanas. The surrounding enclosure is five hundred yojanas in circuit, and outside of it there are likewise seven layers of walls, briefly described as being completely encircling, of various beautiful colors, and composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva and agate.

On the four sides there are also gates, all of which are composed of the seven precious substances; each gate is further equipped with watchtowers and defensive parapets, and to speak briefly, even down to various kinds of birds, each chirping in harmony.
The Scripture on the Arising of the World, Scroll Five;
The Scripture on the Arising of the World, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
The Remainder of Chapter Six: The Chapter on the Asuras. "O Bhikṣus!
At that assembly place of the seven heads of the asuras, there are two diverging paths for the sake of allowing that king to travel back and forth for his pastimes."
At the location of the palace of Vemacitrin, the Asura King, there are likewise two diverging paths.
At the locations of the palaces of the various minor Asura kings, there are also two diverging paths;
at the dwelling places of the various minor Asuras, there are also two diverging paths.
In the Śāla grove, there were likewise two branching paths;
in the Śalmali grove, there were likewise two branching paths;
and in the Kovidāra grove, there were likewise two branching paths.
In the Nandanavana grove, there were likewise two forked paths;
by the side of the Nandā pool, there were likewise two forked paths;
beneath the great tree Sūci-dhvaja-pāṭala, there were likewise two forked paths.
In all respects it was as before; they communicated with and traveled back and forth to the place where the Seven Heads assemble. "O Bhikṣus!

If the Asura King Vemacitrin desires to go to those groves—Sāla, Śamālī, Kovidāra, Nandana, and so forth—to bathe, play, wander, and enjoy himself, at that time the king immediately directs his mind toward the various minor Asura kings and the various hosts of minor Asuras."
At that time, the various minor asura kings and the various minor asuras likewise gave rise to this thought:
"The asura king Vemacitra is thinking of us."

Having understood this, they adorned their bodies with various kinds of precious necklaces and ornaments. Once they had each completed their adornments, they mounted various vehicles and together proceeded to the gate outside the palace of Vemacitra, the Asura King. Upon arrival, they dismounted from their vehicles and stood before the hall of Vemacitra, the Asura King.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, seeing these various minor Asura kings and the hosts of minor Asuras arrive before the palace, likewise adorned his own body with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments. Having completed his adornment, he rose and mounted his vehicle.

At that time, the minor asura kings and their various minor asura hosts attended upon him from the left and right, surrounding him on all sides and escorting him from front and rear. Together they proceeded toward the Sāla grove, the Śamālī grove, the Kovidāra grove, and the Nandanavana grove. Having arrived at those places, they first halted their carriage before the Nandana grove to rest.
“Monks! Within the Nanda Garden, there are three wind-circles that blow naturally, adorning that garden.
What are these three?
This refers to opening, purifying, and blowing.
What is meant by "opening"?
A wind-circle comes and opens those various gates; this is called "opening."
What constitutes purification?
A wind-wheel comes and sweeps that grove, making the ground pure; this is called purification.
What constitutes blowing?
A wind-wheel arises and blows through that garden, causing the trees and various flowers to scatter and fall in all directions;
this is called "blowing. Monks!
Within Nanda’s Garden, the wind scatters various kinds of exquisite and sublime flowers, which accumulate up to the knees.
There were various kinds of fragrances, their sweet scents pervading the groves.

At that time, Vemacitra, the Asura King, surrounded by the minor Asura kings and the hosts of minor Asuras, entered the Nandana Grove together to bathe at will and enjoy themselves with sightseeing and play.
The various asuras, within these groves, spend one month, or two or three months, bathing and sporting; each according to their desires, they dwell, roam, and indulge themselves in pleasure at will.
“Monks! There are five asuras who dwell perpetually by the side of Vemacitra, the king of the asuras, for the purpose of warding off and obstructing all evil matters.”
What are these five? First is named Anumoda;
second is named Nitya; third is named Nityamadā; fourth is named Mucilinda; and fifth is named Vaihāyasa.
"O bhikṣus!
The asura king Vemacitra has these five kinds of asuras who constantly remain at his side to guard and protect him."
"O Bhikṣus!
Above the palace of that Asura King Vemacitrin, there is a great body of seawater ten thousand yojanas deep, upon which he dwells."
However, that mass of water is naturally sustained by four kinds of wind-circles. What are these four?
First is named Abiding; second is named Securely Abiding; third is named Non-falling; and fourth is named Firmness.
Sustained by this wind, it remains eternally stable and motionless. "O bhikṣus!
One thousand yojanas to the south of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, beneath the great ocean, lies the palace residence of the Asura King Valāhaka."

That place is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold city walls; in brief, it is like the abode of the asura king Vemacitra, and you should know that everything contained therein is described exactly as there.

Furthermore, even the great masses of water above this royal palace are sustained by four wind-wheels, namely: the wind-wheel of abiding, the wind-wheel of firm abiding, the wind-wheel of non-falling, and the wind-wheel of stability.

"O Bhikṣus! On the western side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, likewise extending for a thousand yojanas beneath the great ocean waters, there is the palace residence of the Asura King Śambara. Its length and breadth are eighty thousand yojanas, and it has sevenfold city walls. In brief, it is just like the residence of the Asura King Vemacitrin; everything that exists there, each and every detail, is as described for him—you should know this."
Furthermore, even all the masses of water above this royal palace are sustained by four kinds of wind-wheels—by means of supporting, stabilizing, preventing falling, and making firm.

“O Bhikṣus! To the north of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a depth of one thousand yojanas beneath the great ocean, there is the palace and dwelling place of Rāhu, the Asura King. That place is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold city walls, gates, towers, pavilions, battlements, and defensive works; it contains gardens, flower ponds, and various kinds of trees, leaves, flowers, fruits, and fragrant incenses. There are various birds, each singing harmoniously together, all as described above.”
“O bhikṣus! Within that city, there is a city inhabited by Rāhu, the Asura King, named Māpadeva; its dimensions and adornments are also as previously described.”
There were sevenfold city walls and sevenfold railings.

Outside, there were seven rows of *tāla* trees and seven layers of bell-nets, encircling it on all sides; they were of various beautiful colors and were composed entirely of the seven treasures, such as *śukti* and *musāragalva*.
The height, depth, and dimensions of these city walls are also as previously described.
On each of the four sides of the city walls there are gates; the height, depth, and dimensions of each individual gate are likewise as previously stated.
Each of these gates is equipped with watchtowers, battlements, and pavilions, as well as gardens, various ponds, and flower pools; there are also many trees.
Each tree possesses various kinds of leaves, various kinds of flowers, various kinds of fruits, and various kinds of fragrant scents.
There were also various kinds of birds, each warbling harmoniously. "O Bhikṣus!
In the city of Māpadevī, where the king resides, there is a gathering place for Rāhu, the Asura King, which likewise has seven heads; its length and breadth are as described above."

There were seven tiers of railings and various networks of bells, surrounded on all sides by rows of *tāla* trees of variegated and beautiful colors; these were likewise adorned with the seven treasures, such as musaragalva and agate.

On each of the four sides there are gates, and each of these gates is also equipped with watchtowers, which are variegated and beautiful to behold, even being composed of the seven precious substances such as musāragalva and agate.
The ground was entirely covered with celestial *śukti* (mother-of-pearl), soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching it was like touching *kācalindika* cloth.
In the center of that place stood a jeweled pillar, its height and dimensions being as previously described.

Beneath this pillar, for the sake of the Asura King Rāhula, a high throne was established; the height and dimensions of this throne, as well as its adornments, were each exactly as before. It was of variegated colors, beautiful to behold, and composed of the seven treasures, namely *śukti*, *musāragalva*, and so forth; it was soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching it was like touching *kācalindika* cloth.
To the left of that seat were sixteen minor asura kings, each provided with a separate, exquisite high throne made of the seven precious gems, variegated and beautiful to behold;
to the right were likewise sixteen minor asura kings, provided with high thrones as described above, soft, fine, and smooth to the touch like kācilindika cloth.

"O bhikṣus! To the east of the assembly hall of seven peaks belonging to that asura king, a separate palace has been established for the asura king Rāhula. Its dimensions in length and breadth are each exactly as previously described; it is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets of bells, and even sevenfold rows of tala trees, forming a pleasing sight of various colors, and is composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva and aśmagarbha."

On each of the four sides there are gates; at each gate there are watchtowers, palatial towers, defensive galleries, multi-storied pavilions, gardens, various ponds, and many flowers, springs, and marshes. There are all kinds of trees, and each tree has various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, and various fragrant scents.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of birds of different species, each warbling in harmony; their voices are plaintive and elegant, most delightful to hear. "O Bhikṣus!

To the southwest and north of that assembly hall of the seven heads of the Asura King, there are the palaces and residences of the minor Asura kings. These palaces are some nine hundred yojanas in length and breadth, some eight hundred, some seven hundred, and even down to six hundred, five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, and two hundred yojanas; the smallest of them is still one hundred yojanas."
Each [of these] has sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings; to speak briefly, they include everything up to various kinds of birds, each chirping in harmony. "O Bhikṣus!

At that assembly place of the seven heads of the Asura King, there are further palace dwellings for the minor Asura hosts on all four sides; these locations are ninety yojanas long and wide, or eighty, seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, or twenty yojanas, with the smallest being at least twelve yojanas long and wide.
There are sevenfold walls; to speak briefly, there are various kinds of birds, each singing in harmony. "O Bhikṣus!

To the east of the Seven-Headed Assembly Place of that Asura King, there is another garden park belonging to the Asura King Rāhula, named the Śāla Forest. Its length and breadth are each as previously described, with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings, even up to being composed of the seven treasures such as agate."

On each of the four sides there are gates, and at each gate there are watchtowers of various beautiful colors, even composed of the seven precious gems such as musāragalva and agate; they are exceedingly lovely and delightful.

“O bhikṣus! To the south of that assembly hall of the seven heads of the asura king, there is also a park belonging to the asura king Rāhu called the Śamālī Forest. Its dimensions and adornments are all as described above; it has seven layers of walls, and so on, up to seven rows of tala trees, which are variegated and beautiful to behold, and are likewise composed of the seven treasures, such as musāragalva, agate, and the rest.”
"On each of the four sides there are gates, and each of those gates has watchtowers made of the seven treasures, such as agate and the rest. O Bhikṣus!"

To the west of that Seven-Headed Assembly Hall of the Asura King, there is also a garden belonging to the Asura King Rāhu called the Kubera-vana Forest; its length and breadth are each as described above, with sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, such as agate and so forth.

On each of the four sides there are various gates, and each of these gates is equipped with watchtowers and battlements of variegated colors that are beautiful to behold; they are even composed of treasures such as *śukti* and *musāragalva*, and are exceedingly delightful.

“Monks! To the north of that assembly hall of the seven heads belonging to the Asura King, there is a park of the Asura King Rāhu named Nandana Grove. Its length and breadth are as previously described, with sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, such as agate and the rest.”

On each of the four sides there are gates; each of these gates is further provided with watchtowers, adorned with various ornaments in diverse colors that are beautiful to behold, even being embellished with precious gems such as musaragalva and agate, and are exceedingly delightful.

"O bhikṣus! Between the two groves of Śamālī and Sāla, Rāhu-rāja, the asura king, has produced a lake named Nanda. This lake is as long and wide as previously described; its waters are cool, soft, light, sweet, pure, and free from turbidity."

It was constructed with seven layers of bricks made of the seven precious substances, adorned with seven layers of precious planks interspersed and arrayed, and seven layers of railings and seven layers of bell-nets.
It was also surrounded on all sides by seven rows of *tāla* trees, beautiful to behold with their variegated colors, composed of the seven precious substances such as agate and the rest.
On the four sides of the pond, there are stairways, each most delightful and adorned with the seven precious jewels.

Various flowers grow in the pond—namely, the *utpala*, the *padma*, the *kumuda*, and the *puṇḍarīka*. These flowers have the shape of fire, the color of fire, and the radiance of fire; briefly described as above, they likewise possess the shape of water, the color of water, and the radiance of water, brilliantly illuminating the four directions. Their fragrance is dense and pervasive, wafting everywhere.
Furthermore, there are lotus roots whose sap is white and sweet in taste; when eaten, they are fragrant and delicious, like the finest honey. "O Bhikṣus!

Between the two groves of Kuvidhara and Nandana, for the sake of Rāhu, the Asura King, there grows a great tree. This tree is also named Sujātapaṭṭala; its form and its various adornments are all as described above."
Extending even to sevenfold walls and courtyards, and sevenfold railings, all are composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva and agate, and are exceedingly delightful.
To speak briefly, there are various kinds of birds, each singing in harmony; their voices are mournful and elegant, bringing joy to those who hear them.
“O bhikṣus! At that assembly place of the seven heads belonging to that asura king, all the adornments are as described above.
There are also branching paths and thoroughfares for coming and going, in order to provide passage for the asura king Rāhula’s travel to his palace.”
Furthermore, for the various minor asura kings and the various minor asura hosts, there are also branching paths through which they may travel to and fro.
Toward the Śālmali and the Kovidāra trees, there are also branching paths;
toward the Nandana grove, the Nandā pool, and the Suvicitrapāṭala trees, there are likewise branching paths through which they may travel to and fro, sporting and enjoying themselves.

“Monks! When the asura king Rāhu wishes to go to the Sālavana grove, the Nandanavana grove, and other such places to bathe, sport, and survey them thoroughly, he then calls to mind the asura king Vemacitra.”
At that time, the asura king Vemacitra thought to himself:
"The asura king Rāhu has set his mind upon me, desiring to sport together with me."
At that time, after the asura king Vemacitra had formed this thought, he further called to mind his various minor asura kings and their hosts of minor asuras.
At that time, those minor asura kings, together with their hosts of minor asuras, all conceived this thought:
"The asura king Vemacitra is showing us his favor; we shall go to him."

They then adorned their bodies with various kinds of precious necklaces and ornaments; having finished adorning themselves, each mounted a vehicle and together proceeded to the abode of the Asura King Vemacitra. Upon arrival, they stood in a line outside the palace gate.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, seeing that all the minor Asura kings and the hosts of minor Asuras had already assembled, [proceeded].

He immediately adorned his body, donned various necklaces and ornaments, and mounted a variety of vehicles; accompanied by minor kings and hosts of asuras, with attendants on his left and right and surrounded by them in front and behind, he proceeded to the abode of Rāhu, the king of the asuras, and having arrived, he halted there.
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, again gave rise to a thought, calling to mind the two Asura Kings, Vala and Śambara.
Then, the two Asura Kings, Vala and Śambara, also had this thought:
"Rāhu, the Asura King, is now thinking of us."
Having known this, they each thought of their respective minor asura kings and their various minor asura hosts.
As they were thus thinking, those [minor kings] all knew it and likewise adorned themselves, gathering together and arriving at the place of the two great kings, Saṃpāti and Śaṃbara, leaping for joy.

Having arrived, they likewise adorned their bodies with necklaces and ornaments, and accompanied by their mounts and retinues surrounding them before and behind, they proceeded toward the abode of Rāhu, the Asura King; each taking his proper place, they stood to one side.

"At that time, the Asura King Rāhu, seeing that the Asura King Vemacitrin and the others had all gathered like clouds, immediately thought of his various minor Asura kings and his various minor Asura hosts."
Once their host had learned this, they too each adorned themselves and arrived riding in their carriages; they stood solemnly before the asura king Rāhula.

At that time, having seen the assembly gathered, Rāhu, the Asura King, adorned his body with various exquisite jewel necklaces and ornaments. Mounted upon various vehicles and surrounded by attendants before and behind, he joined the Asura King Vemacitra, the Asura King Saṃjaya, the Asura King Śabara, along with their subordinate kings and the hosts of asuras. All having assembled like clouds, with those leading and following them before and behind, they proceeded to the Sāla grove, the Śamālī grove, the Kovidāra grove, the Nandana grove, and others. Having arrived, they stood there for a short while, hesitating.
“Monks! Within the Nanda Garden, there are naturally three kinds of wind-circles.
What are these three?
This refers to opening, purifying, and blowing.
Among these, "opening" means that a wind-circle comes to open the various gates of the grove; this is called opening.
"Purifying" means that a wind-circle comes to sweep the ground, making it entirely clean; this is called purifying.
As for "blowing," there comes a wind-circle that blows upon the various flowering trees, causing the flowers to scatter;
this is called "blowing. O monks!

In the Nanda Garden, exquisite and beautiful flowers are scattered everywhere across the ground, piled up to the knees. The fragrance of these flowers perfumes the entire grove, which is fully adorned and possesses every kind of delight.

"At that time, Rāhu the Asura King, along with Vemacitra the Asura King, Valayanta the Asura King, Śabara the Asura King, and others—surrounded by their minor kings, retinues, and followers, as well as the minor Asuras—entered the Nandana Grove together."
Having entered, they bathe, sport, and enjoy themselves, observing various sights; whether walking, standing, lying down, or sitting, they roam at will according to their desires and pleasures.
"O Bhikṣus!
The Asura King Rāhu also has five asuras who constantly attend and guard him, protecting him from all evil matters; their names are as previously stated."
The seawater above Mount Sumeru—its extent, breadth, depth, and thickness—is sustained by four kinds of winds so that it does not fall away; all this is as explained above.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings (*Caturmahārājakāyika*) from the *Sūtra of the Arising of the World* (*Lokotpatti-sūtra*). “O Bhikṣus! [...]”
On the eastern flank of the king of mountains, Sumeru, there is a mountain named Yugandhara; its summit is forty-two thousand yojanas above the ground.

Upon the summit of that mountain is the city and residence of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the city is named Bhadraśreṇī, measuring six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells.

Furthermore, there were seven rows of tāla trees surrounding it on all sides, of various beautiful colors and adorned with the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and emerald.

On each of the four sides, there are various gates; at each gate, there are watchtowers, defensive parapets, and pavilions, as well as gardens and various ponds. There are groves of flowers and many kinds of extraordinary trees, each tree possessing various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, and various fragrances, the scent of which perfumes everywhere.
There are various kinds of birds, each singing in harmony; their voices are plaintive and elegant, most delightful to hear. "O Bhikṣus!

On the southern slope of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, forty-two thousand yojanas down from the surface of the earth, atop the summit of the Yugandhara mountain, lies the city and dwelling place of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka. The city is named Sunirmita; its dimensions and adornments are exactly as described regarding the dwelling place of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"Furthermore, various kinds of birds each sing in harmony, their voices plaintive and elegant, most delightful to hear. 'O Bhikṣus!

On the western flank of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, forty-two thousand yojanas below the summit and above the earth’s surface, on the peak of Mount Yugandhara, is the city and dwelling place of the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa. The city is named Sudarśana; its dimensions and adornments are each exactly as described regarding the dwelling place of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.'"
"Furthermore, various kinds of birds each warble in harmony; their voices are plaintive and elegant, most delightful to hear. 'O Bhikṣus!

On the northern slope of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, forty-two thousand yojanas down from the summit toward the base of the earth, on the peak of Mount Yugandhara, is the dwelling place of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, consisting of three great walled cities.'"
What are these three? The first is named Viśvāvasu, the second is named Ghaṭapāṇi, and the third is named Āṭavaka.
Each is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings; to speak briefly, they are further adorned with various kinds of birds, each chirping in harmony.

“O bhikṣus! With the exception of the palaces of the Moon Devaputra and the seven great palaces of the Sun Devaputra, as well as the palaces of the various devaputras belonging to the retinues and those within the realm of the Four Great Kings, some among them are forty yojanas in length and breadth, some thirty, some twenty, and even down to twelve yojanas; the smallest of these is still six yojanas in length and breadth.”
The residences they inhabit likewise each have sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings; the details are as previously described.
Even down to the various birds, each sings in harmony. "O bhikṣus!

Between the two palaces of Viśvāvasu and Ghaṭotkaca, a pond was produced for the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, named Nandini, forty yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly equal in both dimensions.
The water is well-blended, cool, refreshing, light, and soft; its taste is sweet and delicious, fragrant, pure, and unclouded.
The four sides of the pond are lined with seven tiers of brickwork, interspersed clearly with seven tiers of precious planks.

There are seven tiers of railings and seven tiers of bell-nets, likewise surrounded on all sides by seven rows of *tāla* trees; they are of various beautiful colors and are composed of the seven treasures, such as mother-of-pearl and agate.
On each of the four sides, there are stairways likewise adorned with the seven treasures.

Within the ponds, many *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers grow spontaneously; these flowers possess the forms, colors, and radiance of fire, as well as the forms, colors, and radiance of water.
The size of each flower is like that of a chariot wheel.
The radiance they emit extends for half a yojana,
and the fragrance they waft fills one yojana.
There are various lotus roots as large as chariot axles.
When cut, they exude a sap white in color like milk; when eaten, it is sweet and delicious, its flavor like refined honey.

“O Bhikṣus! Between the two palaces of Ghaṭāpati and Aṭaṇḍa, a park was established for the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; that park is named Kapiñjala, and it is forty yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly square.”

It was surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and even sevenfold rows of *tāla* trees; it was of variegated colors, beautiful to behold, and as briefly described before, was composed of the seven precious substances.
“O bhikṣus! On the roads leading to and from the city of the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s abode, Bhadraśreṣṭha, there are two forked paths;
on the roads leading to and from the city of the Great King Virūḍhaka’s abode, Suprabha, there are likewise two forked paths.”
The abode of the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, where he dwells and through which his city-walls pass, also has two forked paths;
the abode of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the city of Aḍakavatī, also has two forked paths;
and the abodes of the cities of Viśālamati and Ghaṭapāṇi also each have two forked paths.
The various minor deva hosts and their palatial abodes belonging to the retinues of the Four Great Kings likewise have two-branched paths for their coming and going;
the Nandīkāra Lake and the Caitraratha Grove, among others, also each have two-branched paths for their coming and going.
“O Bhikṣus! When the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa wishes to go to the Caitraratha Garden to sport and bathe, he then calls to mind the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.”
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra also had this thought arise in his mind:
"The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa is thinking of me.
Having known this, he then further thought of the various minor heavenly kings and the hosts of minor devas belonging to his own realm.
At that time, the kings of the retinue facing the east, together with their celestial hosts, all thought to themselves:
"The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra has turned his mind toward us."

Having understood this, they each adorned their bodies, donned various necklaces and ornaments, mounted their respective vehicles, and went to where the Great Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was; having arrived, they stood before him to one side.

At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra also adorned himself, donned various necklaces and ornaments, and prepared his carriage and mount. Surrounded before and behind by various minor kings, celestial hosts, and retinues, he went together with them to the place of the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; having arrived, he stood to one side in front of him.
"At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa again thought of the two great heavenly kings, Virūḍhaka and Virūpākṣa.
Then those two kings also had this thought: 'King Vaiśravaṇa is thinking of us.'"
Having known this, each of them immediately thought of the minor deva-kings they respectively commanded, as well as their various retinues of devas.
At that time, those minor kings and their retinues of devas also all thought:
"Our Great Heavenly King is thinking of us; we should go there with all speed."
Having understood this, they each adorned their bodies with necklaces and together proceeded to the abodes of the two great kings, Virūḍhaka and Virūpākṣa.

At that time, the two Heavenly Kings, knowing that all the minor kings and the other hosts of devas had assembled, likewise adorned themselves, donned various necklaces and ornaments, and mounted their vehicles. Surrounded by the multitude, they proceeded together to the abode of the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; having arrived, they halted before him as was appropriate.

"At that time, the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, seeing that the two heavenly kings and their celestial hosts had all assembled, likewise called to mind the minor kings and their celestial hosts whom he himself led."
At that time, the minor kings of the northern quarter and their celestial hosts immediately thought to themselves:
"The Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa is now mindful of us."
Having understood this, they each donned various necklaces of many jewels to adorn their bodies and went together before the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, standing there in silence.

At that time, the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa likewise adorned his body with various precious necklaces and ornaments, mounted upon various vehicles, and together with the four great heavenly kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and others—each leading their respective hosts of heavenly kings as they surrounded him in front and behind, they all went together to the Caitraratha Garden.
Having arrived, they paused for a moment before the gate of the grove.
"O Bhikṣus!
Within that Caitraratha grove, there are naturally three kinds of wind-circles: namely, the Opening, the Purifying, and the Blowing."
"Opening" means opening the gates of that garden;
"purifying" means cleansing the grounds of that garden;
"blowing" means blowing upon the trees of that garden so that the flowers flutter and drift.
"O Bhikṣus!
The various flowers scattered within the Caitraratha Grove have accumulated up to the knees, their manifold fragrances perfuming everywhere."

At that time, the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, surrounded by various minor kings and their retinues, entered the Caitraratha Grove together to bathe, sport, and enjoy all manner of pleasures.

Having finished bathing in that garden, they may sport and enjoy themselves for one month, two months, or three months, wandering at will according to their desires and following whatever pleases their hearts.
“Monks! King Vaiśravaṇa has five yakṣas who constantly follow him, attending to his left and right for the purpose of protection.”
What are the five?
First is named Wuzhang (Five-Fathom), second is named Kuangye (Wilderness), third is named Jinshan (Golden Mountain), fourth is named Changshen (Long Body), and fifth is named Zhenmao (Needle-Hair).
"O Bhikṣus!
When Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, goes out for recreation or comes back, he is always protected by these five yakṣa deities.
Chapter Eight: The Thirty-three Heavens, Part One. 'O Bhikṣus!'"

At the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is the dwelling place of the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; it is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold city walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells.

Outside, there are seven rows of *tāla* trees encircling it on all sides; they are of various beautiful colors and composed of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
The city rises four hundred yojanas in height and is fifty yojanas thick; the four sides of the city walls are each five hundred yojanas apart.
Within this space, a single gate is opened, and each of these gates is thirty yojanas high and ten yojanas wide.
On both sides of the gates, there were watchtowers, defensive parapets, terraces, pavilions, balconies, railings, and carriages.

Furthermore, there were various ponds, flower groves, and fruit trees; each tree possessed various kinds of leaves, various kinds of flowers, various kinds of fruits, and various kinds of fragrances, the scent of which permeated everywhere.
There are various kinds of birds, each singing in harmony; their voices are melodious and refined, most delightful to hear.
Furthermore, at each of those gates, there are five hundred yakṣas who guard the Heaven of the Thirty-three day and night.

"O Bhikṣus! Within that city, for the sake of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, another city was established called Sudarśana. That city was sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold city walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells."

Outside, there are seven rows of *tāla* trees encircling it on all sides; they are of various beautiful colors and are likewise composed of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to agate.
That city was also four hundred yojanas high and fifty yojanas thick; its four sides were each five hundred yojanas apart.

Within it, a single gate was opened; each gate was thirty yojanas high and ten yojanas wide. Each gate was further equipped with watchtowers, defensive parapets, terraces, pavilions, water-pools, flower groves, and various extraordinary trees.
Each of those trees has various kinds of leaves, various kinds of flowers, various kinds of fruits, and various kinds of fragrances, the scent of which perfumes everywhere.
Various birds each sing together in harmony.
In these various gates, each gate has five hundred yakṣas who guard the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven day and night. "O bhikṣus!

Beside the city of Sudarśana in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, a palace was established for the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa. That palace is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings; to speak briefly, it contains all manner of birds, each singing in harmony."

“Monks! Within the city of Sudarśana, there is a place for the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas called the Sudharmā Hall; it is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and is adorned with sevenfold railings and sevenfold networks of bells.”
Outside, there are seven rows of *tāla* trees encircling it on all sides; they are of various beautiful colors and are composed of the seven treasures, including agate.
On each of the four sides, there are gates, and at every gate there are watchtowers, battlements, and palatial pavilions of various colors, all made of the seven treasures.
The ground there is composed entirely of blue lapis lazuli, soft, fine, and smooth, feeling to the touch like kācilindika cloth.
At its center stands a jeweled pillar twenty yojanas in height.

Beneath the jeweled pillar, a separate seat was prepared for Śakra, Lord of the Devas; it was one yojana in height and half a yojana in square, of variegated and beautiful colors, composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva, soft and smooth to the touch, just as described before.

On both sides of that seat, there were sixteen seats for minor celestial kings, attending upon it to the left and right; they were composed of the seven treasures, variegated and beautiful to behold, soft, fine, and smooth, with a touch as described before.
"O Bhikṣus!

This Sudharmā Hall is the assembly place of the devas, where the palace of Śakra is located. That palace is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and even the various birds there sing in harmonious chorus."
“O bhikṣus! In this Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the devas, there are dwelling places for the palaces of the minor deva-kings on all four sides—east, west, south, and north.”

Those palaces are either nine hundred yojanas in extent, or eight hundred yojanas in length and breadth, or seven hundred, six hundred, five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, or two hundred yojanas; even the smallest among them is still one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
There are seven layers of walls, and even the various birds each sing in harmony.

Furthermore, in the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the devas, there are residences for the palaces of the various minor deva hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in the east, west, south, and north. These palaces are either ninety yojanas in extent, or eighty yojanas in length and breadth, or seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty yojanas; even the smallest is still twelve yojanas in length and breadth.
There are sevenfold walls, and even the various birds each sing in harmony. "O Bhikṣus!

In this Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the devas, there is on the eastern side the celestial garden of the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings named Pāruṣyaka. It is exactly one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; briefly described, it has sevenfold walls, all composed of the seven treasures such as agate.

On each of the four sides there are various gates; each gate has its own watchtowers and battlements, which are of variegated colors and beautiful to behold, even being composed of the seven treasures including agate.
"O Bhikṣus!

In the Pārileyyaka Grove, there are two great boulders: one named Bhadra and the other named Subhadra. Both are composed of celestial agate; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching them is like touching a kācilindika cloth."

“Monks! To the south of this Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, there is also a celestial garden belonging to the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings called Citraratha. This garden is also one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, up to being composed of agate.”

On each of the four sides there are gates; each gate is equipped with watchtowers and battlements, variegated and beautiful to behold, and is composed of the seven precious substances, including agate.

Within that grove, there were also two rocks: one named Variegated Color and the other named Well-Variegated Color. They were composed of celestial blue lapis lazuli, each measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth. They were soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching them was like touching kācilindika cloth.

"O Bhikṣus! To the west of this Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, there is another celestial garden belonging to the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings called Citraratha. This garden is also one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, all accomplished of the seven treasures."
At each of the four gates, there are watchtowers, defensive parapets, and pavilions, all fashioned from the seven precious gems.

Within this Garden of Miscellaneous Delights, there are also two stones: the first named Sudarśana and the second named Upasudarśana. Both are composed of celestial crystal and are each fifty yojanas in length and breadth; they are soft, fine, and smooth to the touch, like kācilindika cloth.

“O bhikṣus! To the north of this Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, there is another celestial garden belonging to the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings called Nandana. This garden is also one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, including agate and so forth.”
At each of the gates in the four directions, there are watchtowers, battlements, and defensive galleries, likewise adorned with the seven precious substances. "O Bhikṣus!

Within the Nandana Grove, there are also two stones: one named Nandana and the other named Sunandana. They are composed of celestial silver, each fifty yojanas in length and breadth, soft and lustrous; when touched, they feel like touching kācalindika cloth."

“O bhikṣus! Between the two groves, Pāruṣyaka and Citrapāṭalika, for the sake of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, there is a great lake named Nandana, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, equal in all dimensions.”
The water is cool, light, soft, sweet, and delicious; it is pure and free from turbidity.
It is lined on all four sides with bricks made of the seven treasures, and adorned with seven tiers of precious planks set in alternating patterns.
It was surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings, extending even to seven rows of *tāla* trees, which were of various beautiful colors.
At the four corners of the pond, there were stairways, each adorned with the seven precious substances.

Within it are various flowers, namely the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka; these flowers have the shapes of fire, the colors of fire, and the radiance of fire, and likewise the shapes of water, the colors of water, and the radiance of water.
Its length and breadth are both equal to the size of a chariot wheel.
The light it emits illuminates for one yojana.
When the wind blows, its fragrance perfumes for one yojana.
There are lotus roots as large as chariot axles; when cut, their sap flows out, white in color like milk, and its taste is sweet and delicious, like the finest honey.

“O Bhikṣus! Between the two gardens, Citra and Caitraratha, for the sake of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a great tree named Pārijātaka-kovidāra. At the base of this tree, its circumference is seven yojanas; briefly stated, its branches and leaves extend everywhere to cover the walls and courtyards, measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. It has seven layers of walls, and even the various birds each sing in harmony.”
“O Bhikṣus! Beneath this Pārijāta-kovidāra tree there is a stone named Paṇḍakambala, which is composed of celestial gold.”
That stone is fifty yojanas in length and breadth; it is soft and lustrous, and when touched, it feels like touching kācilindika cloth.
"O Bhikṣus! For what reason is this assembly hall of the devas, the Sudharmā Hall, called 'Sudharmā'?"

"O monks! When the kings of the Thirty-three gather and sit in the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, they discuss therein only subtle, refined, and excellent speech regarding profound meanings; they contemplate them with discernment, weighing and examining them—all of which are the most eminent and essential dharmas of the world, the true and correct principles."
For this reason, the devas call this assembly hall the Sudharmā Hall.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is the Pāruṣyaka Grove named so? "Pāruṣyaka" means "roughness" in the language of the Sui.
"O Bhikṣus!

Once the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has entered the Pāruṣyaka Garden, he sits upon the two rocks named Bhadra and Subhadra, and there they discuss only worldly, coarse, unwholesome, and frivolous talk; for this reason, it is called Pāruṣyaka."
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Citraratha Park? Monks!

Once the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has entered the Citraratha Garden, he sits upon two stones—the Citra and the Sucitra—and discusses only the various worldly phenomena, colors, and speech of diverse kinds.
For this reason, it is called the Grove of Variegated Chariots;
and for what cause and condition is it named the Grove of Confusion? O monks!

In this Garden of Confusion, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of every month, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enters with all his court ladies into this garden, causing them to mingle and sport with the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa devas without any obstruction. They indulge in their pleasures at will, experiencing the five celestial sensual desires and their full merits as they roam about and enjoy themselves.
For this reason, the devas collectively designate this grove as the "Grove of Confusion" (Saṃkīrṇa-udyāna).
*Lokotpatti-sūtra*, fascicle 6;
*Lokotpatti-sūtra*, fascicle 7.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Central India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Part Two. "O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do those devas have a garden named Nandana? Monks!

Once the King of the Thirty-three has entered that Nandana Garden, he sits upon two stones, Nanda and Sunanda; his heart experiences joy, his mind dwells on joy, and as he reflects again and again, he experiences various pleasures. Having experienced delight, he further experiences supreme bliss. For this reason, all the devas collectively designate that garden as "Joy."
"O bhikṣus!
Furthermore, for what reason and by what causes is that celestial tree named Pāriyātra-kovidāra?
O bhikṣus!"

Beneath that Pārijāta-kovidāra tree dwells a devaputra named Manda, who day and night constantly enjoys pleasure through play, fully endowed with the various fivefold sensual qualities of that celestial realm.
For this reason, the devas subsequently named that tree *Pāriyātra-kovidāra*.

Furthermore, monks, even when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are in great haste, they never wish to leave the *Paṇḍakambala* stone; they invariably make offerings to it with reverence and respect before departing as they please.
Why is this so? This rock is the very place where the Tathāgata resided in the past.
For this reason, the devas regard it as a caitya; it should be venerated by all the world, including devas, humans, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
"O Bhikṣus!

There are gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven who can only see the Pāruṣyaka Garden with their eyes, but their bodies cannot enter it. Because their bodies do not enter, they are unable to experience the full enjoyment of the fivefold sensual pleasures there."
Why is this? Because that karma is superior; since their roots of goodness from previous lives were weak and inferior, they were unable to enter.

There are those belonging to the Heaven of the Thirty-three who are able to see the Pāruṣyaka Garden and can also physically enter it. Having entered, they fully experience the various merits of the union of the five sensual pleasures and enjoy happiness therein.
Why is this? Because their roots of goodness are superior and preeminent. O bhikṣus!

There are gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three who cannot see the Garden of Variegated Chariots with their eyes, nor can they enter it; furthermore, they are unable to experience the pleasure derived from the combined excellence of the five sensory desires within that garden.
Why is this? It is because their roots of goodness differ.

There are those among the Trāyastriṃśa devas who, though they can see the Citraratha Garden with their eyes, cannot enter it with their bodies, nor can they experience the pleasure derived from the harmonious merits of the five desires within that garden.
Why is this? It is because their roots of goodness vary in degree of excellence.

There is a Heaven of the Thirty-three where the gods, having seen the Garden of Variegated Chariots with their eyes, also enter it with their bodies; having entered, they fully enjoy the various fivefold sensual pleasures, experiencing happiness in harmonious union as one body.
Why is this? Because their roots of goodness are superior and preeminent. O bhikṣus!
All the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven without exception behold the Garden of Confusion;

they all gain entry into it, and once having entered, they all likewise equally obtain within that grove the various pleasures of the five sensory desires, which are endowed with harmonious merit and experienced as a single unified body.
Why is this? Because their cultivation of practice is equal;
there are no distinct or superior roots of goodness within them.

“Monks! There are certain gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven who are unable to see the Nandana Grove, nor can they enter it. Because they cannot enter, they are unable to experience the bliss of possessing in its entirety the various merits of the five sensual pleasures in union within that place.
Why is this? Because the fruits in that place are superior, due to the distinct nature of the karma created in previous lives.

There are those among the Trāyastriṃśa gods who, though they behold the Nandana Grove, are unable to enter it; nor can they obtain the various fivefold sensual pleasures within the Nandana Grove, nor experience the bliss of being fully endowed with that state of harmonious integration.
Why is this? It is because the karma of those various devas differs.

There are the Trāyastriṃśa devas who, upon seeing the Nandana Grove, their bodies also enter it; having entered, they fully obtain the various merits of the union of the five sensual desires and experience that same essential happiness, all receiving them together.
Why is this? Because the wholesome karma cultivated by those devas in the past is without distinction. "O bhikṣus!
The Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, has two branching paths;
the palace residence of Śakra, King of the Devas, also has two branching paths;
and the palaces of the various minor deva kings and their subordinate officials in the Heaven of the Thirty-three likewise have two branching paths.
At the location of the palace of the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa, there are likewise two branching paths;
at the Pāruṣyaka garden, there are likewise two branching paths;
and at each of the locations—the Citraratha garden, the Miśrakāvana garden, the Nandana garden, the Nandana pool, and so forth—there are respectively two paths.
Beneath the Pārijāta-kovidāra tree, there are likewise two branching paths.

Monks! Whenever Śakra, the King of Devas, desires to go to the Pāruṣyaka Garden, the Citraratha Garden, the Nandana Garden, and so forth, to bathe, sport, and enjoy pleasures, he then calls to mind the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa.
At that time, the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa also had this thought:
"The Heavenly King Śakra is thinking of me.

Having known this, he emerged from his palace and immediately manifested himself with thirty-three heads; each head possessed six tusks, upon each tusk were manifested seven ponds, in each pond were seven lotuses, on each lotus were seven jade maidens, and each jade maiden, in turn, had seven daughters as her attendants.

At that time, having performed such various supernatural transformations, the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa immediately proceeded to where King Śakra was; having arrived, he stood before him with solemn dignity.
At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, further turned his mind toward the thirty-two minor kings of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, as well as the thirty-two assemblies of minor devas.
At that time, those minor kings and the hosts of devas also gave rise to this thought:
"Śakra, King of Devas, now thinks of us.

Having known this, each adorned their bodies with various kinds of exquisite necklaces and ornaments, and each mounting a vehicle, they all went together to the abode of Śakra, Lord of Devas. Upon arrival, they each stood before him.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having seen the various devas, likewise adorned his own body in manifold ways and donned many necklaces and ornaments.
Surrounded on all sides—front, back, left, and right—by the great assembly of devas and accompanied by various minor kings, he ascended together with them upon Airāvaṇa, the king of nāga-elephants.
Śakra, King of Devas, sits directly in the center upon its head.
On each of the left and right sides, there are sixteen minor deva kings, each seated atop one of the transformed heads of the nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa.
Once they had each taken their seats, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, led the host of devas toward the Pāruṣyaka, Citraratha, Miśraka, and Nandana gardens; having arrived, he halted there.

Within each of the four gardens, such as Nandana and the others, there are respectively three kinds of wind-circles—namely, the Opening, the Purifying, and the Blowing; a brief explanation is as before: they open the ground, purify it, and blow away the flowers, and so forth.
"O Bhikṣus!
Within those gardens, flowers are blown about and scattered, covering the ground to a depth reaching the knees; the fragrance of those flowers permeates everywhere."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by the minor deva kings and the assembly of the thirty-two devas, entered the gardens of Variegated Chariots, Joy, and so forth; there they sported and enjoyed themselves, wandering at will, sometimes sitting and sometimes reclining.
At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra, desiring to obtain a necklace (*hāra*), immediately called to mind the devaputra Viśvakarman.
Thereupon, that devaputra manifested various precious necklaces and offered them to the Heavenly King.
If the various retinues of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven require necklaces, Viśvakarman likewise manifests them all to provide for them.
If they wish to hear sounds and music, various birds then produce diverse notes, their voices harmonious and elegant, causing the gods to rejoice as they listen.

At that time, the devas experience such pleasures for one day up to seven days, and for one month up to three months; they enjoy various forms of amusement, bathing and sporting, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, moving freely to the east or west as they please.
“Monks! The celestial king Śakra has ten devaputras who constantly act as his guardians.
What are these ten?
First is named Indrakaka; second, Gopaka; third, Binduka; fourth, Bindubhaka; fifth, Akrūṭaka; sixth, Ṭaṭotka; seventh, Śimbhaka; eighth, Hulugīna; ninth, Naṭaka; tenth, Hulubhaka.
"O Bhikṣus!
Śakra, the King of Devas, has such a host of ten devaputras who constantly follow him on his left and right, never departing from him, for the purpose of guarding him."

“Monks! For the sake of all people in the land of Jambudvīpa, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, supreme, and most delightful—namely, the *utpala*, the *padma*, the *kumuda*, and the *puṇḍarīka*. These various flowers are fragrant, soft, and beautiful.

There are also land-born flowers that are most exquisite—namely, the *atimuktaka*, the *campaka*, the *pāṭala*, the *sumana*, the *bāliśika*, the *mallikā*, the *mātuluṅgikā*, the *sākuṇḍikā*, the *yūthikā*, the *cūṭaśakalika*, and the *dhanuśakarnika*, and so forth.”

“Monks! Among the people of Aparagoyānī, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *utpala*, the *padma*, the *kumuda*, and the *puṇḍarīka*; their fragrance is exquisite, wafting everywhere.

There are also land-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *atimuktaka*, the *campaka*, the *pāṭala*, the *sumana*, the *vārṣika*, the *mallikā*, the *mādhūkadika*, the *sāktika*, the *yūthikā*, the *śukrasārikā*, the *tānuśakarnika*, and so forth.”

“Monks! Among the people of Pūrvavideha, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers; their colors are exceedingly brilliant and their fragrance is most fragrant.

There are also land-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *mādhūkadika*, *sāktika*, *yūthikā*, *śukrasārika*, and *tānuśakarnika* flowers, and so forth.”

“Monks! Among the people of Uttarakuru, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers; their fragrance is soft and pervades everywhere.

There are also land-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *mātuluṅgikā*, *sākuṇḍikā*, *yūthikā*, *śukrasārikā*, and *dhānuṣkāriṇī* flowers, among others.”

“O bhikṣus! In the abodes of all the nāgas and garuḍas, there are various water-born flowers; among them, the most excellent are the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers, which are fragrant, pervasive, soft, and exquisite.

There are also land-born flowers; among them, the most excellent are the atimuktaka, campaka, pāṭala, sumana, vārṣika, mallikā, mādhūkadika, saptaparṇa, yūthikā, śukrasārikā, karkārava, and mahākarkārava flowers.”

“Monks! The asuras also each possess various water-born flowers, the most excellent of which are the blue lotus (utpala), the red lotus (padma), the white lotus (kumuda), and the fragrant water lily (puṇḍarīka); their fragrance wafts everywhere, and they are exceedingly delightful.”

There are flowers that grow on land, the most excellent of which are known as the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *mādhūkadīrghikā*, *sāndīrghikā*, *yūthikā*, *śukticārikā*, *tānuṣkara*, *karkārava*, *mahākarkārava*, *bimbi*, *mahābimbi*, *mandārava*, and *mahāmandārava* flowers.

“O bhikṣus! Among all the devas of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, there are water-born flowers that are most exquisite, upright, and delightful—namely, the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, and the puṇḍarīka. Their fragrance is most intense, and their substance is extremely soft.”

There are flowers that grow on land, among which the most excellent and beautiful are as follows: the *atimuktaka*, the *campaka*, the *pāṭala*, the *sumana*, the *vārṣika*, the *mallikā*, the *mātuluṅgī*, the *sākuṇḍikā*, the *yūthikā*, the *śukrasārikā*, the *tānuśaka*, the *karkārava*, the *mahākarkārava*, the *pundarīka*, and the *mahāpundarīka*.

“Monks! Among the Trāyastriṃśa devas there are water-born flowers that are most exquisite, beautiful, and delightful—namely, the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers—which possess an extremely fragrant scent and are very soft in form.

There are flowers that grow on land; among them, the most excellent and beautiful are as follows: the *atimuktaka*, the *campaka*, the *pāṭala*, the *sumana*, the *vārṣika*, the *mallikā*, the *mātuluṅgī*, the *sugandhikā*, the *yūthikā*, the *śukrasārikā*, the *dhanuṣkāri*, the *karka-ravī*, the *mahākarka-ravī*, the *bimbi*, the *mahābimbi*, the *māndārava*, and the *mahāmāndārava*.

Just as all the flowers possessed by the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are present, so too are they found in each successive realm—Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, and the Māra-devas—each possessing them exactly as such, without any difference.
“Monks! There are seven kinds of colors among the various flowers of the human world.
What are these seven?

That is to say: the color of fire and its flames; the color of gold and its radiance; blue color and blue light; red color and red light; white color and white light; yellow color and yellow light; black color and black light.

For example, O monks, just as the Māras and Brahmās constantly manifest their forms, so too among humans there are these seven kinds of colored flowers; and likewise, the asuras also possess these seven colors.
All the hosts of devas likewise possess these seven kinds of radiant colors, just like the colors constantly manifested by Māra and Brahmā.
"O bhikṣus! All devas have ten distinct qualities."
What are the ten?
Monks! First, when the devas move, their coming and going are boundless;
Second, when the devas travel, they come and go without obstruction;
third, when the devas travel, they have neither slowness nor haste;
fourth, when the devas travel, their feet leave no tracks.
Fifth, the bodies of all devas possess strength and are free from illness or fatigue;
sixth, the bodies of all devas have form but cast no shadow;
seventh, all devas, whether great or small, have neither excrement nor urine.
Eighth, all devas are free from nasal mucus and saliva;
ninth, the bodies of the devas are pure and subtle, lacking skin, flesh, sinews, veins, fat, blood, marrow, and bone;

tenth, as for the bodies of the devas, whether they wish to appear long or short, blue, yellow, red, or white, large or small, coarse or fine, they are able to manifest them all at will, and these forms are all exquisite and magnificent, surpassingly beautiful, and pleasing to all who behold them.
All celestial bodies possess these ten kinds of inconceivable qualities.

O bhikṣus! Furthermore, the bodies of the devas are full and robust; their teeth are white, square, and closely set; their hair is blue-black and neatly trimmed; and they are soft, supple, and lustrous.
Their bodies possess radiance and supernormal powers;
they soar through the void with swift flight, their eyes do not blink,
their jeweled necklaces appear spontaneously, and their garments are free from dust or grease.
“Monks! The people of Jambudvīpa have a lifespan of one hundred years, yet among them there are those who die prematurely;
the people of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of two hundred years, and among them, too, there are those who die prematurely.”
The people of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of three hundred years, though there are also those who die prematurely;
the people of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years, with no untimely deaths;
and the sentient beings in the world of Yama have a lifespan of seventy-two thousand years, though there are also those who die prematurely.
The various nāgas and garuḍas have a lifespan of one kalpa, yet they also die prematurely;
the asuras have a lifespan of a thousand years, the same as that of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, yet they also die prematurely;
the Cāturmahārājika devas have a lifespan of five hundred years, yet they also die prematurely.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have a lifespan of one thousand years;
the gods of the Yāma Heaven have a lifespan of two thousand years;
and the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven have a lifespan of four thousand years.
The gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven have a lifespan of eight thousand years;
the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven has a lifespan of sixteen thousand years;
and the Māra-kāyika Heaven has a lifespan of thirty-two thousand years.
The Brahmakāyika devas have a lifespan of one kalpa;
the Ābhāsvara devas have a lifespan of two kalpas;
and the Śubhakṛtsna devas have a lifespan of four kalpas.
The gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven have a lifespan of eight kalpas;
the gods of the Non-conceptual Heaven have a lifespan of sixteen kalpas;
and the gods of the Not-Coarse Heaven have a lifespan of one thousand kalpas.
The gods of the Heaven Free from Strife have a lifespan of two thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Heaven of Good Vision have a lifespan of three thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Heaven of Good Appearance have a lifespan of four thousand kalpas.
The lifespan in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is five thousand kalpas;
in the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven, it is ten thousand kalpas;
and in the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven, it is twenty-one thousand kalpas.
The gods of the Sphere of Nothingness have a lifespan of forty-two thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception have a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas.
Among these various heavens, there are those who die prematurely.
“O bhikṣus! The people of Jambudvīpa are three and a half cubits tall; their robes are seven cubits long and three and a half cubits wide.
The people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha are equal in body size and clothing to those of Jambudvīpa.”
The people of Uttarakuru are seven cubits tall; their garments are fourteen cubits long and seven cubits wide at the top and bottom.
The bodies of the asuras are one yojana tall; their garments are two yojanas long, one yojana wide, and weigh half a kāliṃśa (translated into Chinese as "half a liang").
The gods of the Four Heavenly Kings are half a yojana tall; their garments are one yojana long, half a yojana wide, and weigh one kāliṃśa.
In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the height of the gods is one yojana; their garments are two yojanas long and one yojana wide, weighing half a karṣa.
In the Yāma Heaven, the height of the gods is two yojanas; their garments are four yojanas long and two yojanas wide, weighing one-quarter of a karṣa.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, the height of the gods is four yojanas; their garments are eight yojanas long and four yojanas wide, weighing one-eighth of a karṣa.
The gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven are eight yojanas in height; their garments are sixteen yojanas long and eight yojanas wide, weighing one-sixteenth of a karṣa.
The gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven are sixteen yojanas in height; their garments are thirty-two yojanas long and sixteen yojanas wide, weighing one-thirty-second of a karṣa.
The gods of the Māra realm are thirty-two yojanas in height; their garments are sixty-four yojanas long and thirty-two yojanas wide, weighing one-sixty-fourth of a karṣa.
From this point upward, the various heavens possess bodily dimensions that are exactly equal to the length of their robes, without any discrepancy. "O bhikṣus!
Regarding all the commercial transactions of the people of Jambudvīpa, they are conducted either with money and treasures, or with grain and silk, or with living beings."
The people of Aparagoyānī engage in trade using either cattle and sheep or maṇi-jewels;
the people of Pūrvavideha engage in trade using either wealth and silk, or the five grains, or maṇi-jewels;
the people of Uttarakuru have no further need for trade, as all that they desire arises spontaneously.
“O bhikṣus! The people of Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, and Pūrvavideha all have the customs of marriage between men and women;
however, the people of Uttarakuru have no sense of ‘self’ or ‘mine. When the branches of trees hang down, men and women unite; they have no further need for marriage.”
"O Bhikṣus!
The various nāgas, garuḍas, asuras, and others all have marriage and the social customs of men and women, which are roughly similar to those of the human world.

The gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Māra-kāyika devas all likewise have marriage and taking wives; a brief explanation is as given before."
From this point upward, all the devas no longer practice marriage, because there is no distinction between male and female. O Bhikṣus!
When the people of Jambudvīpa engage in sexual desire, the two organs meet and impurity is emitted.
The people of Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru are all likewise;
when all the nāgas, garuḍas, and others engage in sexual desire, their two organs also meet, yet they achieve satisfaction merely by emitting a wind-like breath, without any impurity.

When the asuras, the gods of the Four Great Kings, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven engage in sexual desire, their organs meet and they achieve satisfaction, also emitting a wind-like breath, no different from the nāgas and garuḍas.
The gods of the Yāma Heaven fulfill desire by holding hands;
those of the Tuṣita Heaven fulfill desire by mere thought;
and the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven fulfill desire by gazing intently.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, desire is fulfilled through conversation;
among the various heavens of the Māra realm, desire is fulfilled by mutual gazing, whereby they both attain satisfaction and accomplish their sensual purposes.
