“Monks! The light of a firefly possessed by humans does not equal the radiance of a lamp’s flame;
the radiance of a lamp’s flame, in turn, does not equal the light of a torch.”
The brilliance of a torch is not equal to that of a mass of fire;
the brilliance of a mass of fire is not equal to the radiance of the stars and constellations in the heavens;
and the radiance of the stars and constellations is not equal to the brilliance of the lunar palace.
The radiance of the lunar palace is not equal to the radiance of the solar palace;
the light of the solar palace, with its blazing effulgence, is still not equal to the radiance of the walls, palaces, and bodily ornaments of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
and all the light of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is, in turn, not equal to all the light of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The radiance of all the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is not equal to the radiance of the walls, palaces, and necklaces of the gods in the Yāma Heaven;
the various lights within the Yāma Heaven are not equal to the radiance of the Tuṣita Heaven;
and the various lights of the Tuṣita Heaven are not equal to the radiance of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
The radiance of all the gods in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is not equal to the radiance of the gods in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations;
the radiance of the gods in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations is, in turn, not equal to the radiance of the gods in the Heaven of Māra’s Body.
Compared to the lower heavens, the radiance of the walls, palaces, and necklaces of the gods in the Heaven of Māra’s Body is most supreme, most wondrous, and uniquely unsurpassed.
"O monks! Although this light of the gods of the Māra-body heavens, when compared to the light of the Brahma-body heavens, falls far short;
and those Brahma-body heavens, when compared to the Ābhāsvara (Light-Emanation) heavens, likewise fall short."
When the devas of Ābhāsvara are compared to those of Śubhakṛtsna, they fall short;
when the devas of Śubhakṛtsna are compared to those of Bṛhatphala, they likewise fall short.

Thus, in brief, it should be understood that for the gods of the Heaven Free from Affliction (Avṛha), the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana), the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation (Sudṛśa), and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, with the sole exception of their necklaces, everything else is as described above.

"O bhikṣus! Whether in the world of devas, or among māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or humans—whatever light exists in the world, if one were to attempt to compare it with the light of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, even as many as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers, it could not be compared to it."
This light of the Tathāgata is most excellent, most wonderful, extraordinary, and foremost.
Why is this so? O bhikṣus!

The body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable because his ethical conduct is immeasurable; likewise, because his samādhi, prajñā, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, supernormal powers and the exercise of those powers, his teaching and the wheel of teaching, and his places of discourse and the wheel of discourse are all immeasurable.
"O Bhikṣus!
The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable merits, fully endowed with all dharmas. For this reason, the radiance of the Tathāgata is supreme and unsurpassed; you should uphold it thus."
“Monks! All sentient beings have four kinds of nutriment which sustain the great elements, enabling them to maintain themselves, to bring about existence, and to provide mutual support.”
What are the four?
First, coarse and subtle edible food; second, contact-food; third, volition-food; and fourth, consciousness-food.
Which sentient beings should consume coarse and subtle edible food?
"O monks! For the people of Jambudvīpa, meals consisting of parched grain, beans, fish, meat, and the like are called coarse, solid food;
while covering the body, massage, bathing, rubbing with powders, and anointing with oils and unguents are called subtle food."
The people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha have both coarse and subtle food, which are roughly equivalent to those of Jambudvīpa.
The people of Uttarakuru do not cultivate the land; rather, naturally ripened non-glutinous rice serves as their coarse food, while clothing, bathing, and massage serve as their subtle food.
"O bhikṣus!
All the nāgas, garuḍas, and others take various fish, turtles, crocodiles, alligators, frogs, dragons, chimeras, snakes, otters, and kumbhīras as their coarse material food;
they take coverings, bathing, and so forth as their subtle food."
The various asuras take the exquisite flavor of celestial *sudhā* as their coarse food,
while they regard things such as coverings as subtle food.
The Cāturmahārājika devas and all the hosts of devas likewise take that celestial *sudhā* flavor as their coarse food.
For the various beings covered by clouds and so forth, these are considered subtle;
for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the flavor of the *sudhā* nectar of that heaven is considered coarse morsels,
while the various coverings and so forth are considered subtle.
As it is with the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and likewise with the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens, they all take the flavor of the heavenly *sūdā* as their coarse food,
and various coverings and such as their subtle food.

From this point upward, all the devas take the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as their food; they take samādhi as their food and samāpatti as their food, having no further coarse or subtle material food.
"Monks! What kind of beings take contact as their nutriment? Monks!"

Among all sentient beings, those born from eggs—namely geese, wild geese, swans, cranes, chickens, ducks, peacocks, parrots, mynas, pigeons, doves, sparrows, quails, magpies, crows, and other various kinds of creatures born from eggs—all of them, because they obtain their bodies from eggs, take touch as their food.
What kind of sentient beings take volition as their food?

If there are sentient beings who, through mental volition, nourish and moisten their sense faculties and increase their physical life—namely, fish, turtles, snakes, frogs, *kārakūṭas*, and other such beings, as well as other sentient beings who, through mental volition, benefit their sense faculties and prolong their lifespan—all these take volition as their food.
Which sentient beings take consciousness as their nutriment?
They are the sentient beings of the hells, as well as those in the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness and so forth; all these sentient beings take the sustenance of consciousness as their food.
"O bhikṣus!
These four kinds of food sustain the great elements of all sentient beings and maintain the factors of birth.
In this regard, there is an udāna verse:
Flower colors and all phenomena, lifespan and clothing as the fifth,
commerce and marriage, and roots, light, and food make ten. "O Bhikṣus!"
All sentient beings in the world equally possess three kinds of unwholesome conduct.
What are these three?
They are unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind.

"Monks! There are sentient beings who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil destinies and are born in hell."
In that place, at the final moment, consciousness ceases; simultaneously, the consciousness of hell arises in continuous succession.
With the arising of that consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) comes into being; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise.

“Monks! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up at the end of life, they fall into an evil destination and are born among the animals.”
In this place, his final consciousness ceases, and the consciousness of an animal arises in immediate succession.
At the very moment that consciousness arises, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases.

"Monks! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up at the end of life, they fall into an evil destination and are born in the world of Yama."
In that place, his final consciousness ceases, and the consciousness of the world of Yama arises for the first time in succession.
At the very moment that consciousness first arises, it simultaneously co-arises with name-and-form; and conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases come into being.
"Monks! These are called the three kinds of unwholesome conduct;
they should be avoided. Monks!"
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wholesome conduct in the world.
What are these three? They are:
wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind.
"O bhikṣus!

There are some sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds of body, wholesome deeds of speech, and wholesome deeds of mind. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the human realm."
In this place, his final consciousness ceases, and the consciousness of the human realm arises for the first time in succession.

When that consciousness arises, it simultaneously and concurrently arises together with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Because of name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) come to be.

"Monks! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds of body, wholesome deeds of speech, and wholesome deeds of mind. By reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the heavens."
When consciousness ceases here, consciousness first arises in succession in that heavenly realm.
At the moment that consciousness arises, it simultaneously arises together with name-and-form; because there is name-and-form, the six sense bases arise.

"O monks! Among those in the heavens, whether among the sons of gods, or the daughters of gods, or upon their seats, or within their two knees, or between their two thighs, they are born suddenly; at the moment of their first birth, they are like twelve-year-old children of the human world."
If it is a male deva, he is born in one of the places near the knees on the seat of a devaputra;
if it is a female deva, she is born between the two thighs of a female deva.
Once they have been born, those gods immediately claim, "These are my sons and daughters.
Thus it should be understood: "O Bhikṣus!"

There is such a law regarding those born in heaven through the cultivation of merit: namely, when a celestial son or daughter first takes birth, due to the habitual perfuming of their own karmic causes, they attain three kinds of recollection:

first, they know for themselves from which place they died; second, they know for themselves that they have now been born here; and third, they know that this birth is the fruit of such karma and the retribution of such merit.
Furthermore, they think:

"Having had my body and life destroyed in that place, I have been reborn here; it is because I possess these three kinds of karmic fruits, and as the fruits of the three types of karma ripen, that I have obtained birth here."
What are these three? They are namely:
wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind.
Because the retribution of these three types of karma has ripened, at the dissolution of the body after death, they have come to be born in this place.
Again, he formed this thought:
"May I, having died here, be reborn among humans.
Once I have taken birth among humans, may I once more cultivate virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind."
"Because I have cultivated wholesome conduct through body, speech, and mind, after the dissolution of the body, I have returned to this life.
Having formed this thought, he next reflected upon food.
When they think of eating, there appear before them various precious vessels, naturally filled with celestial *sudhā* food of diverse colors.
Among the sons of gods, those with superior karma have *sudhā* that is the purest white;
if a son of gods is one whose karmic fruit is middling, his *sudhā* is somewhat red.
If that deva’s merit is inferior, the color of that divine *sudhā* flavor will be somewhat dark.

Then, that deva takes the divine *sudhā* flavor in his hand and places it in his mouth; once this *sudhā* flavor has entered the mouth, it immediately and gradually dissolves and transforms of its own accord.
For example, if ghee or fresh butter is cast into a fire, it immediately melts away, leaving no further form or shadow.
In just this way, when the celestial flavor of *sūda* is placed in the mouth, it is naturally digested; it is exactly like that.
Having consumed this flavor, if they should feel thirsty, there immediately appears before them a celestial jewel-vessel filled with celestial liquor.
According to the superior, middling, or inferior merit [of the beings], it is white, red, or black in color; a brief description is as given previously.
As it entered their mouths, it was likewise dissolved.

Then, once that deva had finished eating and drinking, his body grew large; in terms of thickness, fineness, height, and breadth, he became no different from the other devas and devīs who had been born there previously.

“O bhikṣus! These devaputras and devakanyās, their bodies being fully satisfied, each follow their own inclinations wherever they wish to go; some proceed to the ponds and enter those pools to bathe and purify themselves, experiencing joy and pleasure.”

Having emerged from the pond, they proceed again to the fragrant trees; the branches of those fragrant trees naturally bend downward, and from within the branches various exquisite perfumes emerge and flow into their hands, which the sons of gods take and smear upon their bodies.

Having finished anointing his body, he proceeded again to the tree of garments; at that time, the tree of garments likewise bent its branches, and from among those branches, various kinds of exquisite and wonderful garments emerged, hanging down to his hands, which he took and put on.
Having finished dressing, he went to the necklace tree; it bent down until it reached his hand, and as before, he wound it around himself from top to bottom, adorning his body.
They then proceed to the Garland Tree (*mālā-vṛkṣa*), which bends low and pours forth various exquisite flower garlands; the devas take them and adorn their heads with them.

They then proceed to the Vessel Tree (*bhājana-vṛkṣa*), from which emerge various vessels made of diverse jewels that fall into their hands according to their wishes. Taking these, they go to the Fruit Grove (*phala-vana*), where they gather various fruits—either eating them whole or taking their juice to drink.

Thus, he further proceeded to the various musical instrument trees; these trees also bent low, spontaneously manifesting all kinds of musical instruments. He took them as he pleased, either plucking, striking, singing, or dancing; the sounds were subtle and exquisite, causing those who heard them to rejoice.

Thereupon, he proceeded again to various groves and gardens; having entered a garden, he immediately beheld immeasurable hundreds, immeasurable thousands, and immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of billions of celestial maidens.
Before these devas had seen the woman, they possessed knowledge and vision regarding the retribution of their past karma, thinking:
"I have come from such-and-such a place to be born in this realm; my body now receives such a fruit of retribution."
Because his karma had ripened, at that moment he clearly and distinctly remembered his past lives as if looking into the palm of his hand.
However, due to seeing the celestial maidens and becoming infatuated with their forms, his right mindfulness and awakened wisdom were immediately extinguished.
Having thus lost the mindfulness of their previous lives, they become attached to present desires and cry out with their mouths:
"Are these all celestial jade maidens!
Are these celestial jade maidens!"
"This is what is called being bound by the craving for sensual desire. Monks!
These are called the three kinds of wholesome conduct; they should be cultivated."

“O Bhikṣus! Within each month, there are six upoṣadhas—translated in the Sui language as ‘increases’—meaning that by observing the rules of the fast, one increases one’s roots of goodness. The bright fortnight consists of fifteen days, and the dark fortnight likewise consists of fifteen days; thus, in both the bright and dark months, there are three fast days.”
What are the three days for observing the fast during the bright fortnight?
They are the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month;
the dark fortnight likewise has three days for observing the fast, corresponding in number to those of the bright fortnight.
For what reason do the fasts (upoṣadha) on the third day of each of the two months—the bright and dark fortnights—observed? O Bhikṣus!
During each of these two months, there are eight days; on these days, the Four Great Kings assemble their retinues and proclaim to them all:

"Go each of you and observe thoroughly the four quarters; within this world, is there perhaps anyone who practices filial piety and makes offerings to their parents, or who shows reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?"
Do you honor and respect your elders and superiors?
Do you practice giving and observe the precepts?
Do you maintain the eightfold abstinences and observe the six fast days?

At that time, after the Four Heavenly Kings had issued these commands, their messengers, having received the kings' orders, immediately descended to survey all the human worlds, seeking out who was practicing filial piety and making offerings to their parents.
Which clansmen revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
Furthermore, in which families do men and women honor their elders and cultivate the virtues of propriety and yielding?
Who practices giving?
Who observes the six fast days?
Who maintains the eight precepts?
"Who observes the precepts?

At that time, the messenger traversed the world in succession to observe it; if he saw among human beings those who were rarely able to be filial and support their parents, rarely able to serve and honor śramaṇas, rarely able to revere elders and virtuous brāhmaṇas, rarely able to show respect to their seniors, whose giving was meager, whose observance of the fasts was infrequent, whose protection of the precepts was incomplete, and whose restraint was full of deficiencies—having seen all this fully, the celestial messenger returned that very day to the abode of the Four Great Kings and addressed them, saying:

"Great King, you should know that among all the people in the world, there are not many who provide filial support and service to their parents; nor are there many who show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; nor are there many who honor the elderly, the virtuous, teachers, and elders; nor are there many who practice giving or observe the six fast days; nor are there many who uphold the prohibitions and guard the eight precepts."

At that time, having heard these words from the celestial messengers, the Four Great Heavenly Kings felt deep sorrow in their hearts and were greatly displeased. They replied to the messengers, saying:
"If it is truly so for the people of the world, it is most unfortunate."
Why is this so? The lifespan of human beings is exceedingly brief;
dwelling in this world for but a short time, one ought to cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds, so that upon passing to the next life, one may attain peace and happiness.

Why is it that these people nowadays do not practice filial piety and support for their parents to any great degree, and are even unable to observe the six fast days or undertake the eight prohibitions to restrain their bodies and speech?
"This will greatly diminish my host of devas and further increase the race of asuras. "O bhikṣus!

If in the world many people practice filial piety and provide offerings to their parents; revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; honor and serve the elderly; cultivate courtesy and yielding; delight in practicing generosity; joyfully observe the six fast days; diligently promote meritorious deeds; and constantly maintain the eight precepts—if they continue to practice in this manner without interruption."
At that time, the celestial messenger, having observed this during his patrol, addressed the Four Great Kings, saying:

"Great Kings, you should know that among the people of the world, there are many who are filial and provide for their parents; many who show reverence to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and their elders; and many who delight in practicing generosity and diligently cultivate the fasts and precepts."
At that time, having heard these words from the celestial messengers, the Four Great Heavenly Kings were filled with immense joy and leaped for joy beyond measure, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
People of the world who are able to practice in this way are exceedingly noble and virtuous. Why is this?
Because those people have short lifespans; before long, they shall inevitably pass on to another world.

Now you are able, among those humans, to provide filial support for your parents, serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, revere the elderly, practice courtesy and yielding, delight greatly in giving, uphold the precepts, and observe the fasts; by doing so, you shall increase the immeasurable retinues of the devas and diminish all the classes of asuras.
“Monks! For what reason are the fourteenth days of both the dark and the bright fortnights called *upavasatha*? Monks!”

On the fourteenth day of both the dark and light fortnights, the Four Great Heavenly Kings likewise each summoned their respective princes as before, dispatching them to descend into the world to observe good and evil; they grieved when goodness was scarce and rejoiced when goodness abounded, with everything else being exactly as described by the celestial messengers, differing only in that the princes descended of their own accord.
“Monks! Both the dark and light fortnights consist of fifteen days; for what reason, moreover, are they called *uposatha*? Monks!”

Today, the Four Great Heavenly Kings descended from their realms to personally inspect the good and evil of the world. Having ascertained the extent of such deeds, they immediately proceeded to the Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), where the various devas gather for deliberation. Standing before the hall and facing Śakra, they fully recounted the matters of good and evil, their frequency and their conformity or opposition, as they occurred among humanity.
At that time, Śakra, hearing that those among humans who cultivate merit were few, became once again sorrowful, despondent, and unhappy, wondering: "How can this be?
The hosts of devas are diminishing, while the hosts of asuras are increasing even further."
If they hear that those who act in accordance with the Dharma among humans are many, their hearts will rejoice and leap for immeasurable joy, saying:
"The hosts of our devas shall gradually increase, while the hosts of asuras shall gradually diminish."
"O Bhikṣus! For these six days, the devas descend to observe the good and evil among humans; one should therefore practice the fast and precepts. For this reason, these days are called Upoṣadha."
The Sūtra on the Arising of the World, Scroll Seven;
The Sūtra on the Arising of the World, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Eight on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Part Three: “Monks!
Furthermore, there may be a time when various non-Buddhists—whether they be Pārivrajakas or others—come to where you are and ask you, saying:”
"Elders, for what cause and by what condition is it that some persons of human form are terrified by non-human beings,
while other persons of human form are not terrified by non-human beings?"
"If those non-Buddhists should ask such a question, you should reply to them as follows:
'Venerable elders, there is a cause and condition for this.'"

Why is this? Within the world, there may be a person of beautiful appearance who practices what is contrary to the Dharma; internally possessing wrong views and inverted views, they are devoted to practicing the ten unwholesome paths of action, speaking of unwholesome things, and dwelling upon unwholesome thoughts. Because of such wrong views and inversions, and due to their commission of these ten unwholesome deeds, the various deities who protect living beings will gradually abandon such a person. Whether there were a hundred or a thousand, they will leave behind only a single deity to provide general protection.
It is like a herd of oxen or a flock of sheep, numbering perhaps a hundred or a thousand, with only a single person stationed nearby to guard and watch over them.
This case is likewise; because the protective deities are few, one is constantly terrified by non-human beings.

There is a person of form who practices the True Dharma, does not engage in wrong views, and does not hold perverted views. Because that person practices these ten wholesome deeds, maintains right view and right speech, and cultivates wholesome karma, each such person is guarded and watched over by immeasurable—whether hundreds or thousands of—divine beings. By this cause and condition, this person is not terrified by non-human beings.
“Just as, for example, a king or a royal minister is protected by hundreds of thousands of deities who guard living beings, so it is with each individual.
“Monks! [It is thus.]”
If there are such names and surnames among human beings, among non-humans (*amanuṣya*) there are likewise all such names and surnames. O monks!

Whatever mountains, forests, rivers, marshes, kingdoms, towns, cities, moats, villages, hamlets, and settlements exist among humans, among non-humans there are likewise the names of such mountains, forests, cities, towns, and dwellings.

"O Bhikṣus! Wherever kings and great ministers sit or rise—whether in all the streets, at crossroads, in winding alleys, in butcher shops, or in various mountain caves—none are empty, for they are all inhabited by various deities and non-human beings.
Furthermore, in charnel grounds where corpses are abandoned, among burial mounds and ravines, and on all paths frequented by ferocious beasts, there dwell non-human beings."
In all forests and groves, where trees reach a height of one fathom and have a circumference of one chi, there are spirits and deities who dwell upon them, making them their abodes.

“Monks! For all men and women in the world, from the moment of birth, various deities constantly follow them wherever they go, never abandoning them; it is only when they habitually practice evil deeds or when their lives are about to end that these deities finally depart, as previously described.”
“Monks! There are five things in Jambudvīpa that surpass Aparagoyānī. What are these five?

First, the courageous and steadfast; second, right mindfulness; third, the place where a Buddha appears in the world; fourth, the ground for cultivating practice; and fifth, the place for practicing the holy life.
In the continent of Aparagoyānī, there are three things that surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, an abundance of cattle; second, an abundance of sheep; and third, an abundance of maṇi jewels.
Jambudvīpa has five matters in which it excels Aparagoyānī; these have been briefly explained as before.
Aparagoyānī has three matters in which it excels Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, it is the most extensive of the continents; second, it universally contains all the sub-continents; third, the continent is exceedingly superior and wondrous.
Regarding Jambudvīpa, there are five matters in which it excels Uttarakuru, as described above.
The continent of Uttarakuru possesses three things that surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, the people there have no sense of "I" or "mine"; second, their lifespan is the longest; and third, those people possess superior conduct.
In Jambudvīpa, there are five matters that surpass those of the world of Yama, as previously described.
Within the world of Yama, there are three matters that surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, a long lifespan; second, a large physical stature; and third, the possession of natural clothing and food.
As previously stated, the people of Jambudvīpa surpass all nāgas, garuḍas, and others in five respects.
The various nāgas and garuḍas possess three things that surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, their lifespan is long; second, their physical forms are large; and third, their palaces are vast and spacious.
Within Jambudvīpa, there are five matters by which it excels the asuras, as previously described.
Among the asuras, there are three matters by which they excel Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, a long lifespan; second, superior physical form; and third, abundant enjoyment of pleasure. These three matters are the most preeminent.
“Monks! The gods of the Four Great Kings possess three things by which they excel:
first, their palaces are lofty; second, their palaces are exquisite; third, their palaces possess superior radiance.”
The Heaven of the Thirty-three possesses three superior qualities. What are these three?
First, long life; second, superior physical form; and third, abundant pleasure.

In this same way, it should be understood that the Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Māra-heaven all possess three kinds of superior qualities, just as those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were described as being superior to Jambudvīpa.
"In Jambudvīpa, there are five matters that surpass those of the devas and nāgas,
as previously described. You should know this, O bhikṣus!"
Within the three realms, there are thirty-eight kinds of sentient beings.
What are these thirty-eight kinds? O Bhikṣus!
There are twelve kinds in the desire realm, twenty-two kinds in the form realm, and furthermore four kinds in the formless realm.
O bhikṣus!
What are the twelve types within the desire realm? They are:

hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, asuras, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, and the Māra-body gods; these are called the twelve.
What are the twenty-two types of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?

They are: the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmapārṣadya, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Vihāra, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha. These are called the twenty-two types.

Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are four types, namely: the Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the Heaven of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); these are called the four types.
“Monks! In this world there are four kinds of clouds: namely, white clouds, black clouds, red clouds, and yellow clouds. Monks!”
Among these four clouds, those that are white contain a predominance of the earth element;
those that are black contain a predominance of the water element;
and those that are red contain a predominance of the fire element.
If it is yellow, there is an abundance of the wind element;
you should recognize it in this way. "O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there are four kinds of great deities in the world. What are these four?
They are the great deity of earth, the great deity of water, the great deity of fire, and the great deity of wind.
"O Bhikṣus!
Once upon a time, the great deity of the earth conceived this evil view and thought to himself:
'Within the earth element, there are no water, fire, or wind elements.'"
"O bhikṣus! At that time, I went to where that deity was and addressed him, saying:
'Great Deity!'"
"Does your mind truly hold such an evil view, claiming that within the earth element there are no other three great elements— water, fire,
and wind? He replied to me,
"It is indeed so."
“World-Honored One!
I replied again,
“Great Deity!
You should not now give rise to such an evil view. Why is this?
Within this earth element, there truly exist all the elements of water, fire, and wind; however, because the earth element is predominant therein, it receives the designation "earth."

"O bhikṣus! I was able to know that the great earth deity had conceived such a thought; I severed his evil views, caused him to give rise to joy, and enabled him to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye amidst all defilements. He realized the fruit and the path of awakening, became free from fetters and delusions, crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, was no longer subject to afflictions, did not follow the teachings of others, and followed the practice of the Dharma in accordance with it."
And he said to me:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."
"Venerable World-Honored One!

From this day forward, until the end of my life, I shall constantly uphold the precepts of an upāsikā; I shall no longer commit killing, stealing, or other unrighteous acts, and I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, maintaining them with purity."
“Monks! On another occasion, the great deity Water also gave rise to a wrong view and thought to himself:
‘Within the water element, there is no earth element, fire element, or wind element.’”
I understood his intention, went to where he was, and asked him:
"Is it truly so? He replied:
"It is indeed so," he replied. I further told him:

"Do not now hold such a wrong view. Within this water element, there are present the earth element as well as the fire and wind elements; it is simply because one is predominant that it receives the name 'water element'."
In this manner, even the Fire Deity and the Wind Deity both held this view; once the Buddha was aware of it, he went to each of them and questioned them, and they both replied to the Buddha, saying:
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One."
The Buddha opened their minds, and they all attained awakening and understanding; they took refuge in the Triple Gem and practiced in accordance with it, as briefly described before.
The great deity Mahāpṛthivī, having severed his doubts and perplexities, came to where I was.
"Monks! These are called the four great divine beings. Monks!"
In the world there are clouds that rise from the earth into the void; some remain at one *krośa*, or two, or three *krośas*, up to six or seven *krośas*.
"Monks! Furthermore, there are clouds that abide in the upper reaches of space at a height of one yojana, or two, three, four, five, six, or seven yojanas. Monks!"
Furthermore, there are clouds that abide in the upper reaches of space at a height of one hundred yojanas, and even at two, three, four, five, six, or seven hundred yojanas.

There are also clouds that abide in the sky above the earth at a height of one thousand yojanas, and at two, three, four, five, six, or seven thousand yojanas, continuing thus until the end of the kalpa.
"O Bhikṣus!
At times, a non-Buddhist named Paribrājaka may come to where you are and ask this question:
'Venerable sirs, by what cause and condition does this sound arise within the clouds in the sky?'"
"O monks, you should answer thus:
'There are three causes and conditions; because they strike against one another, sound issues forth from within the massed clouds.'"
What are these three?
Venerable sirs, at times, when the wind element within the clouds comes into contact with the earth element, a sound is produced.
Why is this so? It is like when the branches of trees rub and grind against one another, fire immediately emerges.
In just this way, Venerable Elders, this is the primary cause and condition for the arising of sound.

Furthermore, Venerable, at another time, when the wind element within the clouds comes into contact with the water element, it immediately produces a sound; this is as described above, and this is the second causal condition for the production of sound.

Furthermore, Venerable, at another time, because the wind element within the clouds comes into contact with the fire element, a sound is produced. Briefly stated, it is like two trees rubbing against each other until fire is produced; this is the third cause and condition for the production of sound.
"One should answer in this way. O bhikṣus!
You too should thus understand through extensive analysis."
“Monks! At times, a non-Buddhist named Pāribhājaka may come to where you are and ask you this question:
‘Venerable sirs, for what cause and by what condition does lightning suddenly flash within the clouds in the sky?’”
"O Bhikṣus! You should answer in this way:
'Venerable Elders, there are two causes and conditions by which lightning flashes are produced within the clouds in the sky.'"
What are these two?

First, there is lightning in the east named Kāṅthou; second, there is lightning in the south named Shunliu; third, there is lightning in the west named Duoguangming; and fourth, there is lightning in the north named Bai shengshu.

Venerable elders, there may be a time when a thick, massive lightning bolt arising from the east encounters, confronts, rubs against, and strikes a falling luminous lightning bolt from the west. Because of this, a great radiance is produced from within that mass of clouds in the sky, called "Lightning Flash. This is the first causal condition for the lightning flash.

Furthermore, Venerable Elders, there is a second case: when the Great Lightning of the Southern Current flows toward and encounters the Great Lightning of a Hundred Births in the North, they strike, clash, grind against, and collide with one another. Because of this, lightning flashes are produced—just as two pieces of wood rubbed together by the wind suddenly produce fire—which then returns to its source. This is the second causal condition for lightning flashes, wherein light emerges from within the mass of clouds.

“Monks! In the sky, there are five causes and conditions that can obstruct the rain, such that the diviners cannot predict or know it, increasing their confusion; they record that it will certainly rain, yet it does not rain. What are these five? First, clouds arise from the east and move toward the west; second, clouds arise from the south and move toward the north; third, clouds arise from the west and move toward the east; fourth, clouds arise from the north and move toward the south; fifth, clouds arise from the four intermediate directions and move toward the four cardinal directions. These are the five causes and conditions in the sky that can obstruct the rain, causing the diviners to fail in their predictions and fall into further delusion.”
What are these five?

Monks, there may be a time when clouds arise and thunder rolls in the sky, producing sounds such as *gaṭa-gaṭa* and *gūchu-gūchu*, or when lightning flashes, or when a wind blows with cold air; these various phenomena are all signs of rain.
All the diviners and astrologers alike predicted that at this very time, rain would surely fall.
At that moment, Rāhu, the Asura King, emerged from his palace and, seizing those rain clouds with both hands, cast them into the ocean.
"O bhikṣus! This is the first cause and condition for the obstruction of rain.
Yet the astronomers and diviners do not see it, nor do they know it; their minds are filled with doubt, and though they record that it will certainly rain, in the end it does not."

“Monks! There may be a time when clouds arise in the sky; within those clouds, the sounds ‘gaṭa gaṭa’ and so forth are made, flashes of lightning are emitted, and winds blowing with cold air come forth.”
At that time, when the astronomers and diviners observed these signs, they determined that it was certain rain would fall at this moment in the heavens.

However, at that very instant, the predominant power of the fire element arose, causing the clouds to be consumed by fire and vanish; this is called the second causal condition for the obstruction of rain.
Those astrologers and diviners did not see or know [the truth], and their minds became confused; they predicted that it would certainly rain, yet it did not rain. "O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there may be times when clouds arise in the sky; within those clouds, sounds such as "gaṭa gaṭa" are produced, flashes of lightning emerge, and winds blowing with cold air also come forth.
At that time, when the astronomers and diviners observe these signs, they record that it will certainly rain at this moment in the heavens.

However, because the wind element arises with superior force, it is able to blow the clouds and cast them away—either onto the Kalinga desert, or onto the Tāṇḍaka desert, or onto the Maṇḍakya desert, or into various wildernesses, or onto the Mālana desert. This is called the third cause and condition for obstructing rain.
Those astrologers and diviners, failing to see or know [the truth], their minds became confused; they recorded that it would certainly rain in the heavens, yet it did not rain.
"O bhikṣus!..."
Furthermore, there may be times when clouds arise in the sky; from within those clouds, sounds such as "gaṭa gaṭa" are produced, flashes of lightning emerge, and winds arise that blow cool breezes.
The various diviners record that it will certainly rain from heaven;

yet, the deities who govern the rain may at times become negligent. Because of this negligence, those clouds are unable to bring down rain according to the proper season. Since the rain does not fall at the right time, the clouds naturally dissipate on their own—this is the fourth causal condition for the obstruction of rain.
For this reason, the celestial scribes and astrologers become confused in their minds; they predict that it will surely rain in the heavens, yet in the end it does not rain. "O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there may be a time when clouds arise in the sky, and within those clouds there are sounds such as 'gaṭa gaṭa,' great flashes of lightning appear, and cold breezes blow forth."
The celestial astronomers have recorded that rain will certainly fall.

However, among all the people of this Jambudvīpa, many act contrary to the Dharma; they are addicted to various sensual desires, are stingy, greedy, and envious, and are entangled by false views. Because of these evil deeds, because they practice what is not the Dharma, because they delight in and cling to desire, and because they compete in greed and envy, the heavens do not send down rain.
"O bhikṣus! This is called the fifth cause and condition for the obstruction of rain.
The celestial astronomers and diviners do not see it, nor do they know it; their minds become deluded, and though they record that it will certainly rain, it does not rain."
"O bhikṣus! These are called the five causes and conditions for the obstruction of rain.
In this regard, there is an udāna verse:
Flowers, dharmas, form, and lifespan; clothing and buying and selling;
marriage, assemblies, and samādhi; as well as the four kinds of food and drink.
The two practices and the poṣadha; the upper and lower are called the three realms.
The clouds, the various devas, and so forth, together with the *krośa*-sounding lightning.
Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Battle. *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra*, Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Battle. "O Bhikṣus!
I recall that in the past, there was a time when the devas and the asuras engaged in a great battle.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Trāyastriṃśa devas under his command, saying:
"O worthy ones, you devas, if you are to engage in combat with the asuras, you should properly adorn yourselves and skillfully take up your weapons."

"If the devas are victorious and the asuras are defeated, you all may join together to seize the asura king Vemacitrin, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him before the assembly of devas at the Sudharma Hall."
Upon hearing the command of Śakra, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven followed his instructions and carried them out.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitrin likewise addressed the asuras, saying:

"When the hosts of devas and the asuras engage in battle, if the devas are defeated, you must immediately seize King Śakra alive, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him to the Seven-Headed Assembly of the asuras, placing him before me."
The hosts of asuras likewise followed these instructions. O bhikṣus!

At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, having achieved victory in battle, immediately seized the Asura King alive, bound him with the fivefold bonds, and led him before the assembly hall of the gods known as Sudharmā, where he stood facing Śakra.
At that time, if Vemacitrin, the Asura King, should think:
"May all the asuras each find peace and well-being; I have no further need for the asuras now."
"I shall remain here and dwell together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, sharing in their pleasures; this is most agreeable to my mind.

As soon as the Asura King Vemacitra conceived this thought, he saw his own body completely released from its fivefold bonds, and all the various merits of the five sensual desires of the gods appeared before him.
Or again, at times, he thinks:
"I have no need for the Heaven of the Thirty-three; may all the devas each abide in peace and well-being."
"I wish to return to the palace of the asuras.
As this thought arose, his body was immediately bound again with the five fetters, and the merits of the five desires suddenly vanished and were extinguished.
“Monks! The asura king Vemacitrin has such subtle fetters as these; the fetters of Māra are even subtler than these.”
Why is this so? Monks! At the very moment of wrong reflection, one is bound by fetters.
At the moment of right mindfulness, one is immediately liberated.
Why is this? O Bhikṣus!
To contemplate that there is a self is wrong thought;
to contemplate that there is no self is also wrong thought;

even to contemplate that the self is permanent, that the self is impermanent, that it has form or is formless, that it has perception or is without perception, or that it is neither with nor without perception—all such thoughts are likewise wrong thought.
"O bhikṣus!
This wrong reflection is an abscess, it is a sore, and it is like a poisoned arrow.

If among them there is one who is learned, noble, and possessed of wisdom, who knows that this wrong reflection is like a disease, like a sore, like an abscess, and like an arrow—having reflected thus, he binds his mind in right mindfulness, does not follow the movement of the mind, and keeps the mind immovable; this brings great benefit."
"O monks! If one conceives of a self, that is a false notion, it is conditioned, and it is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

If one conceives of non-self, that too is conceptual proliferation. This extends to all things: whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all are conceptual proliferation."
"O monks! All conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is entirely a disease, like an abscess, like a sore, and like a poisoned arrow.

Among them, those who are learned, noble, and possessed of wisdom, having understood these faults of conceptual proliferation, delight in the absence of proliferation; they maintain mental tranquility and engage extensively in spiritual practice."
“Monks! I recall that in the past, there was a King Śakra of the Devas who wished to wage war against the asuras.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the gods of the Thirty-three in the four directions, saying these words:”
"O worthy ones, you should well adorn your bodies and weapons, for now the Asuras desire to come and engage in battle.
If the gods are victorious, you may capture the Asura King Vemacitra alive, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him before the assembly place in the Hall of Good Dharma to let him see me."
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven received the command of Śakra and carried it out according to his instructions.
The Asura kings likewise received such instructions. O Bhikṣus!
During that battle, the devas were victorious and bound the Asura King with the fivefold fetters, leading him before the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitrin, having been bound by the five fetters in the presence of the celestial hosts, saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, enter the Hall of Good Dharma and take his seat; he then uttered evil words, reviling and insulting the Heavenly Lord in various ways.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, had a charioteer named Mātali. Seeing the Asura King Vemacitrin addressing the assembly with harsh words and reviling the Lord of Devas, he immediately addressed Śakra in verse:
“Is it out of shame or fear, or because you lack power, that you harbor such patience?
Hearing such coarse and malicious insults, you swallow them and endure them, saying nothing at all.”
At that time, Śakra replied to Mātali with a verse:
"It is not out of shame or fear that I harbor patience, nor is it because I lack the power to overcome the Asuras.
Who else possesses such divine strategy as I do? How could I be equated with those who are devoid of wisdom?"
Then Mātali again addressed the Lord of Devas in verse:
"If you do not strictly reprimand him with harsh words, The fire of his folly will grow even more intense.
If you were to subdue this ignorant man, He would flee like an ox terrified by a staff."
If one were now to let them go so that they might find pleasure, they would become even more arrogant once they reached their own abodes;
therefore, the wise should employ majesty, manifesting valor and strength to restrain the foolish and the deluded.
At that time, Śakra again answered Mātali in verse:

“I have long known such matters as these; it is for the sake of subduing the ignorance of the multitude that they revile me with anger and hatred, yet when I hear them, I endure it and restrain my own mind.”
Then Mātali again addressed Śakra in verse, saying:
"O Śakra, King of Devas, pray consider this well: such forbearance has one drawback.
When that foolish person utters such abuse, one might give rise to cowardice and fear, not daring to respond."
At that time, Śakra again answered Mātali in verse:
“Those foolish folk act according to their own whims; thinking ‘he remains silent out of fear of me,’ they provoke him.
If one seeks personal benefit, lasting welfare, and peace, one should always maintain patience toward them.”
As it seems to me, when seeing another revile you, you should not give rise to anger in response to their anger;
for if one meets anger with anger, it is difficult to achieve victory in such a battle.
If one is harassed and distressed by others, to have the resolve to endure it is extremely difficult;
know that such endurance is a powerful strength, and one who endures in this way should be praised.
Whether for oneself or for others, whenever a thought arises, one should seek only to distance oneself from great fear;
since another has already reviled me with anger, I should not give rise to resentment toward them in turn.
Whether toward oneself or toward others, one should act for the benefit of both;
once it is known that one has been reviled by another, one should cause one's own anger to be extinguished.
Thus, in these two instances, the mind that seeks benefit—whether for oneself or for others—is accomplished;
yet the mental intentions of those people are deluded, all because they do not understand the Dharma.
If there are powerful men who, for the sake of those who are weak, are able to practice forbearance;
if they endure the weak without anger—such forbearance as this is praised by others.
Those people lack the power of wisdom; they take only the power of delusion as their strength.
Because of their deluded minds, they abandon the Dharma; such persons possess no correct practice.
He seeks victory over me through folly, Hating and reviling with coarse words;
If one can endure his wickedness, one is always victorious— The supremacy of this patience is difficult to describe in full.
One does not speak out of fear when addressing those superior to oneself; one endures out of fear of provoking enmity with equals;
but he who can endure the words of those inferior to him—this patience is praised by all the wise.
"O bhikṣus! You should know that at that time, Śakra was none other than myself. At that time, I was the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

I ruled with sovereign power, received superior karmic rewards, and enjoyed unrestrained happiness. Yet I always maintained patience and praised patience; I delighted in practicing gentleness and was free from anger, and I also constantly praised those who were free from anger."
"O bhikṣus!
You yourselves declare that, in the course of your practice, you possess a mind of faith and understanding, have renounced worldly life to go forth, and are diligent and tireless.

If you wish, toward other sentient beings, to practice patience in bodily action, to praise patience, to be disciplined and compassionate, to always act for their peace and happiness, to eliminate anger, and to praise those who are free from anger, you should likewise train yourselves in this way."
“Monks! I recall that in the past, the hosts of devas and the asuras, each having arrayed their weapons, were about to engage in battle.
At that time, Śakra addressed the devas, saying:”
"O virtuous ones!
If the asuras should fight with the devas and the devas gain the victory, you must bind them with the fivefold fetters.
As previously stated, the devas carried out these instructions.
The Asura King did likewise, commanding his host of troops.
Monks! At that time, in the battle, the Asuras were victorious, and Śakra, the Heavenly King, was defeated and retreated.
At that time, the charioteer turned the noble, well-tamed chariot with its thousand-spoked wheels, intending to head toward the celestial palace.
There was a *kūṭaśālmali* tree upon which a king of the garuḍas had built a nest, in which eggs had already been laid.
Having seen this, Śakra addressed Mātali, his charioteer, saying:
"Mātali, there is an egg upon the tree; turn the chariot and avoid it from afar to protect it.
It would be better to lose one's life to the asuras than to let this bird’s nest be destroyed."

Then Mātali, the skilled charioteer, having heard this command from the King of the Śakras, immediately turned the divine, thousand-spoked wheel of the noble and well-governed chariot to the right and once again pointed it directly toward the palace of the Asuras.
"O Bhikṣus!
At that time, when the hosts of asuras saw Śakra’s chariot suddenly turn back, they all thought that Śakra had some extraordinary stratagem and was coming again to join battle;
consequently, the asura hosts retreated in great numbers, each returning to his own palace."
"Monks! At that time, by virtue of the cause and condition of his loving-kindness, Śakra and the devas prevailed once more, while the asuras were defeated. Monks!"
If you wish to know who the Lord Śakra was at that time, it was none other than myself. Monks!

At that time, as the Great Heavenly King, I ruled over the Heaven of the Thirty-three with sovereign authority; yet even while receiving such superior karmic rewards, I still felt compassion for all sentient beings, acting for their benefit regarding their lifespans and giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness and pity.
"O bhikṣus, having left the home life out of faith, you should benefit all sentient beings. Bhikṣus,
I recall that in the past, the devas and asuras were about to engage in battle."
At that time, Śakra addressed the Asura King Vemacitrin, saying:
"O Benevolent One!
Let us first gather our various weapons."

Among both the devas and the asuras, there are those who possess clear wisdom; they are all able to discern the meaning of the teachings spoken by our two families, whether they be good or evil, yet it is only through superior and virtuous speech that one achieves victory.
Thereupon, the Lord of the Devas and the Asura vied with one another to speak first.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra immediately came forward and addressed the Deva Śakra in verse:
"One who is possessed of fierce ignorance must be severely rebuked."
To subdue those lacking wisdom, one is like an ox that flees from the fear of a whip.
Being foolish and devoid of knowledge, they are difficult to discipline wherever they may be;
therefore, using the strict staff, one swiftly cuts through their delusion and pride.

At that time, after Vemacitrin, the Asura King, had spoken these verses to Śakra, the Lord of Devas, the host of Asuras along with their retinues were all greatly delighted, praising him with exultation;
Śakra and the various devas, together with their retinues, remained silent.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitrin addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Great Heavenly King!
You may now recite the verse."
At that time, the Heavenly King spoke these verses to the asuras:
"I clearly see this matter; I do not wish to be the same as the deluded.
The fool gives rise to anger within himself; who would a wise person quarrel with?"
When Śakra, King of the Devas, had spoken these verses, the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens and their retinues all likewise praised them, leaping for joy with great delight;
the asuras and their retinues remained silent.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Asura King Vemacitrin, saying:
"O Benevolent One!
Please speak further words of virtue."
At that time, the asura again addressed the Lord of Devas with these verses:
"O Śakra, I too know your mind of tranquil forbearance;
yet when the foolish prevail, you say, 'I endure out of fear.'"
At that time, after Vemacitrin, the Asura King, had spoken these verses, all the asuras and their retinues leaped for joy, praising him with great delight;
Śakra and the devas, along with their retinues, remained silent.
At that time, the Asura King also addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Benevolent Lord of Devas!
You may further expound well-spoken words in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the host of asuras and spoke again in verse:
"The fool acts according to his own whims, Claiming that patience is out of fear of others."
Seeking one's own benefit by this means brings no advantage to the other.
When I perceive another committing an evil act, I should not respond with anger to their anger;
he who can remain silent in the face of anger will always be the victor in such a conflict.
If one is troubled by others, yet possesses the strength to endure it,
know that such patience is the most supreme among all forms of endurance.
Whether it concerns oneself or another, all seek a place free from fear.
If you know that another dislikes you, you should not feel anger toward them.
This brings benefit to both parties— namely, yourself and the other—
for if the other person becomes angry or reviles you, it is your own anger that can destroy you.
Whether toward oneself or toward others, both benefit is achieved;
yet others harbor thoughts of folly because they do not understand the Dharma.
If there is a person of great strength who practices patience toward those who are weak, [he shall attain peace].
This patience is supreme; no other patience surpasses it.
They lack the nature of wisdom and possess only the power of delusion.
Because they abandon the Dharma through delusion, they naturally lose their right conduct.
The fool boasts of his own superiority; when anger arises, he utters harsh words.
If one can endure such provocation, one is always truly superior.
The superior man endures out of fear; the equal fears the birth of enmity.
"One who can endure what is below [the lower realms], this endurance is praised by the wise.
When Śakra, King of the Devas, had spoken this verse, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and their retinues praised it with joy, leaping for immeasurable delight;
the hosts of asuras, however, all remained silent.

At that time, those among the devas who possessed wisdom and those among the asuras who possessed wisdom each gathered in one place. They all deliberated together upon these verses, examining them with careful reflection, observing and investigating them, and having praised them in unison, they spoke thus:

"O worthy ones, today Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has skillfully explained the meaning of his words. In that which he governs and transforms, there is entirely no use of weapons, staves, or whips; nor is there strife, insult, or enmity, nor are there legal disputes or the seeking of retribution."

Furthermore, within the midst of birth and death, there is that which is to be weary of and afflicted by; one seeks liberation from desire for the sake of cessation, for the sake of tranquility, for the sake of attaining supernormal powers, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the śramaṇa, and for the sake of accomplishing right awakening and attaining nirvāṇa.
"O virtuous ones, the verses spoken by the asura king Vemacitrin contain no such words of excellence and subtlety.

All of them consist only of swords, staves, whips, beatings, afflictions, destruction, insults, strife, litigation, enmity, and the seeking of retribution; they foster birth and death without weariness, and are characterized by attachment to all desires."
They do not contemplate the practice of tranquility and cessation; they do not aspire to supernatural powers or the fruits of the śramaṇa;
they do not seek perfect enlightenment or great nirvāṇa. O worthy ones, the verses spoken by Śakra, King of Devas, are well-spoken;
the verses spoken by Vemacitrin, King of Asuras, are not well-spoken.
"O virtuous ones, the verses spoken by Śakra, King of the Devas, are well-spoken, truly well-spoken;
the verses spoken by Vemacitrin, the Asura King, are not well-spoken, truly not well-spoken."
"O bhikṣus! You should know that at that time, Śakra was none other than myself.
O bhikṣus!"

At that time, I was the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, ruling and transforming with sovereign power and enjoying meritorious bliss; yet even then, I spoke virtuous words as my instruments of war, and by virtue of those virtuous words, I was always victorious in battle.
"You, bhikṣus, having been able to renounce worldly life with a pure mind within my well-expounded teaching, have left the home-life to practice the path of diligent exertion.
If you seek to grasp the meaning within this well-expounded teaching—whether it be well-spoken or ill-spoken—you should understand it in this way."
“Monks! I recall that in the past, the various celestial kings and others engaged in battle with the asuras. At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, defeated the asuras;
having won the battle, he constructed a Palace of Victory measuring five hundred yojanas from east to west and two hundred and fifty yojanas from north to south.”
"O Bhikṣus!
Outside the Palace of Victory, there are one hundred defensive towers.
Between each pair of towers, there are seven pavilions, all fashioned from the seven precious substances."
Within each story, seven rooms were established;
in each room, seven couches were arranged;
and upon each couch, there were seven jade maidens.
Each of these jade maidens, in turn, has seven other maidens as her attendants.
Śakra, King of Devas, together with the jade maidens and their attendants, has nothing else to do but to experience supreme bliss.
Whatever food, drink, incense, flowers, garments, playthings, and all objects of enjoyment he requires are obtained according to his past karma, as he receives their karmic rewards.
O Bhikṣus!
Within this trichiliocosm, among all the celestial palaces, there is none that can compare to this supreme hall of Śakra, King of Devas.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitra had this thought:

"I possess such majestic spiritual power and virtue; although the palaces of the sun and moon and the Heaven of the Thirty-three revolve and circulate above me, by my power I could take them to fashion earrings, and I could travel everywhere without being hindered."
Once, on one occasion, the asura king Rāhu, his mind filled with fierce anger and burning resentment, being displeased in spirit, thought of the asura king Vemacitra.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitra had this thought:
"The asura king Rāhu is now thinking of me."
He then further thought of the minor Asura kings under his command and their retinues of minor Asuras.

At that time, those minor kings and the various Asuras, having perceived the thoughts of King Vemacitra, immediately each equipped themselves with various weapons and went to where he was; having arrived, they stood silently before him.

At that time, the asura king Vemacitra donned his armor, took up his weapons, and prepared his chariot; surrounded by his subordinate kings and the various hosts of his army, he proceeded to the abode of the asura king Rāhu.
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, again thought of the two Asura Kings, Saṃkoca and Māyāvin.

When those two kings perceived his thought, they returned to the thoughts of Vemacitra, the Asura King, and likewise thought of their subordinate kings and all their respective divisions. Having each become aware of this, they equipped themselves with weapons and armor, went to where their king was, and upon arrival, all together approached the place of Rāhu, the Asura King.

At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, donned various ornaments and weapons for his body and, accompanied by the three Asura Kings Vemacitra, Vala, and Māyāvin, along with their subordinate kings and retinues surrounding him before and behind, emerged from the Asura city in a grand procession, intending to engage in a great battle with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, the two great dragon kings, Nanda and Upananda, emerged from their palace and each encircled Mount Sumeru with their bodies seven times. They shook it all at once; having shaken it, they shook it again; they shook it greatly and shook it everywhere. Having caused it to tremble, they trembled again; they trembled greatly and trembled everywhere. Having caused it to surge, they surged again; they surged greatly and surged everywhere. Then, striking the ocean with their tails, they caused a single mass of water to rise into the air above the summit of Mount Sumeru.
"O Bhikṣus!
At that very time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
'O virtuous ones, do you see this great earth shaking in such a manner?'"
"The sky is overcast like clouds and rain, resembling a thick mist; I now know for certain that the asuras wish to battle with the devas.

Thereupon, the various nāgas dwelling within the ocean each emerged from their own palaces, taking up diverse weapons and arraying themselves in full armor to stand before the asuras and engage them in combat.
If they were victorious, they pursued them back as far as their palace;
if they were defeated, they fled in terror.
They then went together to see the terrestrial yakṣas, and having arrived, they addressed them, saying:
"You all should know that the asuras wish to fight with the devas; you may now accompany me to them to assist in breaking their ranks.
Having heard this, the yakṣas again equipped themselves with weapons and, following the nāgas, joined the asuras in battle.
If they prevailed, they pursued them;
if they were not successful, they retreated and fled in terror.
They went together again to see the yakṣa Pāṇi, and upon arriving, they said to him:
“O Yakṣa Pāñcika, do you not know?
The asuras wish to fight with the devas.
You should come and assist me, going out to strike them down.”
Upon hearing this, Patthaka also prepared his weapons and followed along until they were forced to retreat.
They then went together to inform the Mālādhāra yakṣa, recounting everything as before regarding their retreat.
He went to inform the yakṣa Nityamada, who likewise equipped himself with weapons; together they took up garlands and other gear, joining their forces to fight.
If they were victorious, they would pursue him to his palace;
if they were defeated, they would retreat in terror.
They then went together to see the Four Great Heavenly Kings; having arrived, they addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"O Four Kings, you should know that the asuras now wish to come and fight with the devas. You kings ought to assist us in striking them down and dispersing them."

At that time, hearing the words of Chang-zui (Constantly Drunk), the Four Heavenly Kings immediately prepared various kinds of weapons and set out on their mounts; yet they were eventually forced to retreat and flee, unable to subdue him.
At that time, the Four Kings ascended together to the Hall of Good Dharma, the place where the devas assemble for deliberation, and addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Heavenly King, you should know that the asuras have now gathered with the intent to fight the devas; you ought to go there and engage them in battle."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard these words from the Four Heavenly Kings, opened his mind and granted permission. He immediately summoned a celestial *māṇava* and addressed him, saying:

"Come, you son of heaven! You should now go to the Suyāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Upon arrival, speak thus to the various heavenly kings on my behalf:
'O you gods, you yourselves should know this: the Asuras now desire to fight with the devas.'"
"O benevolent Heavenly Kings, you ought to assist one another and go together to that place to engage in battle.
When the māṇava had heard the words of Śakra, he immediately went to the Suyāma Heaven and reported these matters in detail.

At that time, having heard these words from the young brahmin Māṇava, the messenger of Śakra, the King of the Suyāma Heaven immediately gave rise to a thought directed toward all the celestial hosts within the Suyāma realm.

At that time, having known what was in the mind of the celestial king, those hosts of devas each donned various kinds of armor and weaponry and mounted their respective celestial vehicles; they all came together to the place where the celestial king was, and upon arrival, stood solemnly before him.

At that time, the King of the Suyāma Heaven also donned various celestial armor adorned with many jewels and, holding a multitude of precious weapons, descended surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devaputras. Arriving at the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, he hoisted a pure blue banner difficult to subdue on its eastern face and stood upon the peak.
At that time, the celestial messenger, the māṇava, ascended once more to the Tuṣita Heaven; having arrived, he returned to report to the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, speaking thus:
"Your Majesty should know that Śakra, the King of Devas, has made this report:
'The asuras desire to fight with the devas.'"
"I only pray that all the devas will come to my aid, exerting their strength together in battle to cause him to retreat and flee.
Having heard these words, the Tuṣita Heaven immediately called to mind its own great assembly of devas.

Having learned this, those devas all assembled at the abode of the Great Heavenly King. Upon arrival, each of them equipped themselves with weapons and mounted various vehicles; leading one another, they descended and gathered like clouds upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings. On its southern face, they erected a pure yellow banner difficult to subdue and stood there, leaning against the peak.
"At that time, the celestial messenger Māṇava again went to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and addressed the deva there, saying:
'O Heavenly King, you should know that Śakra’s messenger has arrived with these words:
"The asuras desire to fight with the devas. "

He recounted everything as before, until it was said that the deva, together with a host of hundreds of thousands of millions of sons of gods, each adorned with weapons and mounted on various vehicles, all descended together to the summit of Mount Sumeru. On its western side, they erected a banner of pure crimson, difficult to subdue, and stood there leaning against the peak.
Thus he addressed the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, as previously described.

At that time, that host of devas, arrayed with weapons and surpassing those of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven in splendor, descended surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of devaputras, immeasurable thousands of devaputras, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras. Upon reaching Mount Sumeru, they stood upon its northern face, hoisting pure white banners difficult to subdue and remaining there, resting against the peaks.
"At that time, Śakra, seeing that the various devas had all gathered like clouds, again gave rise to a thought directed toward the yakṣas of the void.
Thereupon, the assembly of yakṣas in the void all spoke these words:
'The Heavenly King Śakra is thinking of us.'"

Having understood this, they immediately exhorted one another, donned their armor, took up their weapons, and put on all their various accoutrements; mounting their respective vehicles, they proceeded before Śakra and stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again called to mind the minor deva kings and all the retinues of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
As he thought of them in this way, they each donned their armor, solemnly took up their weapons, mounted various vehicles, and went before the Heavenly King.

Thereupon Śakra, having donned various kinds of armor and weaponry and mounted various vehicles, emerged from his celestial palace surrounded by the aerial yakṣas, the minor kings, and the thirty-three devas, both before and behind him, intending to engage in a great battle with the asuras.

“Monks! When these hosts of devas engage in battle with the asuras, they possess such various types of weapons as follows: namely, swords, arrows, spears, clubs, mallets, vajras, scimitars, face-arrows, chisel-arrows, barb-arrows, calf-tooth-arrows, kalinga-leaf-barbed-arrows, fine-pointed-arrows, and straight-arrows. These weapons are of diverse and lovely colors, all fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, ruby, musaragalva, and agate.”

With these weapons, they hurl them from afar at the bodies of the asuras; none fail to pierce through them, yet no harm is done. Upon their bodies, not even a trace of a wound is seen, yet due solely to the causal condition of contact, they experience painful sensation.
"O Bhikṣus!

All the weapons possessed by the asuras, when they fight with the devas, are similar in appearance and are likewise fashioned from the seven treasures. Though they pierce the bodies of the devas and pass completely through them, there are no scars; yet, solely due to the causal condition of contact, they experience suffering."
"O bhikṣus!
When the devas of the desire realm and the asuras engage in battle, they still possess such various weapons; how much more so, then, the weapons of the people of the world?"
The Sūtra on the Arising of the World, Scroll Eight;
The Sūtra on the Arising of the World, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Duration of the Kalpa "O bhikṣus!
There are three distinct kinds of intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) in the world."
What are these three?
First, weapons; second, famine; and third, pestilence.
What is meant by the intermediate kalpa of weapons?
"O Bhikṣus!

As for the kalpa of weapons, at that time the multitude of people will lack right conduct, speak contrary to the Dharma, hold perverted and inverted views, and fully engage in the ten unwholesome courses of action."
At that time, sentient beings will have a lifespan of only ten years. Monks!
When people have such a lifespan of ten years, girls will marry at five months of age, just as today girls of fifteen or sixteen years of age go to their husbands' homes.
At present, the products of the earth’s power—namely clarified butter, fresh butter, honey, granulated sugar, and non-glutinous rice—all these will perish and no longer appear at that time.

Furthermore, when the lifespan of those people is ten years, they wear clothing made solely of coarse woolen cloth (*kambala*), just as today the *kāśika-kauśeya*, *kṣauma*, *dukūla*, *korumba*, *kārpāsa*, and *kambala* precious garments are considered the most excellent and sublime; that woolen clothing is likewise so.
At that time, they will eat only millet, just as people today consider rice and the like to be fine food.

Furthermore, they will be cherished and loved by their parents, who will wish for them to live to ten years of age, considering that to be a long life, just as people today wish to live to a hundred years.
"O Bhikṣus!

At that time, when they were ten years old, all sentient beings were unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and disrespectful toward their elders; yet they still received offerings, service, praise, and respect from others, just as those who practice the Dharma and instruct others do now, with no difference in their reputation."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of karma.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!
At that time, people will have no reputation for virtue, nor will they practice the ten paths of wholesome action; instead, they will mostly perform unwholesome deeds.

When sentient beings see one another, each will give rise to thoughts of malice and slaughter, devoid of any compassion, just as hunters in the empty mountains and marshes encounter various birds and beasts and conceive only thoughts of malice and slaughter.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

At that time, all the ornaments for adorning the bodies of the people will be weapons; just as people today adorn their bodies with flower garlands, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, rings, hairpins, and tweezers, so too will they use weapons to adorn themselves.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!

At that time, toward the end of the intermediate kalpa, within seven days, everything that people touch with their hands—whether grass, wood, clods of earth, tiles, or stones—all becomes weapons. Their blades are exceedingly sharp, surpassing anything crafted by humans. Each person competes to seize them and they slaughter one another. Within those seven days, they nearly exterminate one another through mutual killing; having thus met their end, they all fall into the evil realms and undergo the sufferings of hell.
Why is this? Because they face one another with minds of killing, turbid minds, evil minds, unbeneficial minds, minds devoid of compassion, and impure minds.
