"Monks! These are called the intermediate kalpa of weapons. Monks!"
What is called the intermediate kalpa of famine? O bhikṣus!
During the kalpa of famine, all people lack practice in accordance with the Dharma; their views are perverted and inverted, and they fully engage in the ten unwholesome courses of action.

Due to these causes and conditions, the heavens do not send down rain; because there is no rain, the world suffers from famine, and there are no longer any seeds. People take white bones as their sustenance and live by means of various hides.
What is meant by "using white bones as sustenance"? Monks!

During times of famine, those people go everywhere—whether to crossroads, streets, alleys, city walls, or pathways—to collect white bones. They boil them in water to extract the broth, drinking it to sustain their lives; therefore, it is called "using white bones as sustenance."
What is meant by "those who live by tree bark"? Monks!

During the kalpa of famine, because those people were driven by the urgency of hunger, they would take the bark of various trees, boil it to drink its juice, and thereby sustain their lives; for this reason, they are called "those who live by tree bark."
"O bhikṣus!

At that time, when those beings have died of hunger, they shall all descend to be reborn in the evil destinies; that is to say, they fall into the world of Yama and receive the bodies of hungry ghosts (preta), because those beings were stingy, greedy, and envious, and because they feared their food would run out and scrambled to hoard it."
"Monks! These are called the intermediate kalpas of famine. Monks!"
What is called the intermediate kalpa of pestilence? O bhikṣus!

At that time, the people desire to practice the True Dharma, desire to speak according to the Dharma, also desire to practice non-perverted views, and further desire to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action.

However, at that time, because those who follow the Dharma lacked the superior karmic fruit of the ten wholesome deeds in their past lives, non-human beings were consequently incited to release their calamitous vapors, causing pestilence to spread and leading many people to fall ill and die.
"O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, during such an age of pestilence, there will be immeasurable non-human beings from other worlds who come to inflict various epidemics upon all the people here."
Why is this? Because they practice non-Dharma through negligence.
Those non-human spirits seize their vital essence and inflict harmful contact, causing their minds to become distressed and confused; among them, many people of meager merit die from illness.

For example, suppose a king or a royal minister, for the sake of protecting the people, stationed guards at the borders of his realm. At some time, bandits from another region might suddenly arrive; because those guards were not diligent and were negligent, they were all slaughtered by the host of thieves at once, or their families were exterminated, or their villages destroyed, or their towns butchered, or their capital cities ruined.

In this way, and in this very manner, because of their negligence, non-human beings from other regions will come to inflict pestilence, and they shall all perish at the end of their lives; it shall be just so.
Or again, at that time, non-human beings from other regions will come to spread diseases.

At that time, although the sentient beings were free from heedless conduct, those ghosts—possessing great power and force—oppressed and tormented them, seizing their vital spirits and inflicting harmful contact that caused their minds to become confused and distressed; among them, many met with illness and passed away.

For example, suppose a king or a royal minister, for the sake of protecting various settlements, establishes defensive outposts; and later, when bandits from other regions come to invade and harass them, those outposts remain vigilant and diligently provide protection.

However, those bandits, being of great strength and power, may oppress and harass them, and they are even capable of slaughtering all the people at once, or destroying their villages, households, and settlements; this is briefly described as above.
"In this way, monks, it is so!
During an age of pestilence, when people encounter disease and their lives are cut short by its intensity, it is likewise:
once their bodies have died, they all ascend and are reborn among the devas."

Why is this? Because those people possess no intent to harm, no mind of affliction or disturbance, but rather a mind of benefit, a mind of loving-kindness, and a pure mind; thus, at the time of their death, they will each ask one another:
"Is your illness bearable? Have you experienced some relief?"
"Is there anyone who has been liberated? Is there anyone who has arisen [from illness]? Is there anyone whose disease has completely recovered?
"O monks! By such causes and conditions, one attains birth in the heavens."
These are called the intermediate kalpas of pestilence.
Monks! These are known as the three types of intermediate kalpas in the world.
11. Chapter on the Abiding of the World, *Qishi jing*, Chapter Eleven: "O bhikṣus!
Within the world-system, there are four immeasurables that cannot be measured, cannot be weighed, and are inconceivable."

Whether among gods or humans, if one were to attempt to calculate its measure within this world—counting for several years, several hundred years, several thousand years, several hundred thousand years, several *koṭi* years, several hundred *koṭi* years, several thousand *koṭi* years, or several hundred thousand *koṭi* years—one would ultimately never be able to reach it.
What are these four? Monks!

If one were to attempt to calculate the duration of the world’s persistence, it could not be known as being so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many *koṭi* years, so many hundreds of *koṭi* years, so many thousands of *koṭi* years, or so many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi* years.
"O bhikṣus!

If the world, having remained, were to be destroyed, it could not be calculated or known as lasting for so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many koṭis of years, so many hundreds of koṭis of years, so many thousands of koṭis of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years."

"O monks! When the world has been destroyed and arises again, this too cannot be calculated or known—whether it be for some years, some hundreds of years, some thousands of years, some hundreds of thousands of years, some koṭis of years, some hundreds of koṭis of years, some thousands of koṭis of years, or some hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years."

"O monks! When the world has been formed and remains so, this duration cannot be calculated as being so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many koṭis of years, so many hundreds of koṭis of years, so many thousands of koṭis of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years."
"O monks! These are called the four immeasurables—unmeasurable, incomparable, and inconceivable.

Whether among gods or humans, there is no one who can calculate or know them by numbering them as 'so many hundreds of thousands of millions of years' or 'so many hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis of years.'"

“Monks! In all the worlds here in the eastern direction, there is no interval of time when they are not either evolving or dissolving; some are evolving into formation, while others are evolving into destruction.”
"Monks! All the worlds in the southern, western, and northern directions that undergo transformation, subsistence, and destruction are likewise thus. Monks!"
Just as a five-part wheel, once its axle is removed, continues to spin without ceasing and finds no moment of rest, so too, in brief, is the nature of the world.

Furthermore, just as summer rain falls in large drops, pouring down in succession without interruption, so too it is with the formation, abiding, destruction, and transformation of the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions; there is no time when they remain stationary.
“Monks! Within that interval, there are further three calamities.
What are the three?
First is the calamity of fire, second is the calamity of water, and third is the calamity of wind.
During the calamity of fire, the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven are the first to escape its destruction;
during the calamity of water, the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven are the first to escape its destruction.
At the time of the calamity of wind, the gods of the Bṛhatphala heaven are the first to be spared from that disaster.
What is the calamity of fire? Monks!

When the fire arises, all sentient beings will possess virtuous conduct; their speech will accord with the Dharma, they will be endowed with right view, and will be free from delusion. They will fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action, attaining the dhyāna of non-discursive thought and non-examination effortlessly, without the need for strenuous cultivation.

At that time, those sentient beings, by means of their supernormal powers, abide in the void; they abide in the paths of the sages, in the paths of the devas, and in the paths of Brahmā. Having thus abided, they experience the bliss of the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought.
Having realized this and attained full accomplishment, at the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

Beings from the hells, beings from the animal realm, the world of Yama, the world of the asuras, the world of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Suyāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and even the gods of Māra’s realm, down to all beings in the Brahma-world who are born in the human realm—all of them attain the state of being without vitarka and without vicāra, realize bliss, and at the dissolution of the body are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; thus all six realms of existence are completely severed, and this is called the total exhaustion of the world.
“Monks, how does the world,
having remained for a long time, undergo destruction?
Monks, [it is as follows:]”

At that time, after an immeasurable and exceedingly long period, a great drought occurred throughout the world such that no rain fell; all grasses and trees were completely parched and withered, leaving nothing behind.
It is just as when reeds and rushes are cut while still green; deprived of rain and water, they wither, dry up, and rot away until nothing remains.
In this very way, O bhikṣus!
When it has not rained for a long time in the heavens, all grasses and trees wither and dry up;
it is just so with this. O Bhikṣus!

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise: they are entirely impermanent, not enduring for long, not solid, and not autonomous; they are of a nature to disintegrate. You should cultivate weary detachment toward them and swiftly seek liberation.
"Furthermore, monks!

At that time, there arises the great wind named Kālika, which blows upon the waters of the great ocean for eighty-four thousand yojanas, causing them all to scatter in the four directions. Beneath [the water] is the great celestial palace of the sun; the wind then blows that single sun out onto the sea and places it midway up the side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a distance of forty-two thousand yojanas from the earth, within the path of the sun's course."
"O monks! This is called the second sun appearing in the world.
All small ponds, pools, ditches, and rivers will completely dry up, leaving nothing behind."
"O Bhikṣus!
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely impermanent; as briefly explained above, you should seek liberation from them.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!"

To speak briefly as before: the Kālika wind blows upon the waters of the great ocean and brings forth the solar palace, placing it within the sun’s path; this is called the third sun appearing in the world.
All great ponds, large lakes, vast canals, and mighty rivers, including the Ganges and all other such streams, have entirely dried up, leaving nothing behind.
All conditioned phenomena are likewise thus; all are impermanent.
Following this sequence, a fourth sun shall arise in the world.

At that time, all great waters and great lakes—namely, the Great Lake Sudarśana, the Great Lake Anavatapta, the Great Lake Mandākinī, the Great Lake Sarpadatta, and so forth—all shall utterly dry up and vanish without remainder.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise thus: all are impermanent.

Following this sequence, a fifth sun shall appear in the world. At that time, the waters of this great ocean will gradually dry up and be exhausted; first they diminish slightly until they are level with the ankles, and then they decrease further until they reach the knees, then half the body, then one person’s height, two, three, four, five, six, and seven persons’ heights, until they have dried up completely to this extent.
"O Bhikṣus!

When five suns appear, the waters of the great ocean gradually diminish by the height of half a tāla tree, and so on, down to one tāla tree; or two, three, four, five, six, or seven tāla trees. Gradually, they further diminish to half a krośa, one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven krośas; they dry up and are exhausted until they reach half a yojana, one yojana, two, three, four, five, six, or seven yojanas, diminishing step by step until they reach one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three, four, five, six, or seven hundred yojanas, diminishing gradually."
"O Bhikṣus!
When five suns appear, the waters of the great ocean gradually diminish further by one thousand yojanas, two thousand yojanas, and even up to three, four, five, six, and seven thousand yojanas."

"O Bhikṣus! When the five suns appear in the world, of that great ocean water, what remains—briefly stated—is as follows: it may be seven thousand yojanas deep, or six, five, four, three, two, or one thousand yojanas; likewise, it may remain at seven hundred yojanas, six hundred, five, four, three, two, or one hundred yojanas; and so on until there are seven yojanas, six, five, four, three, two, or one yojana remaining; or even reduced further until there are seven krośas, six, five, four, three, two, or one krośa of water remaining."
"O Bhikṣus!
When five suns appear in the world, of that great ocean water which remains, its depth will be seven tāla trees, or six tāla trees, or five, four, three, two, or one tāla tree;

or again, the remaining water will be as deep as seven men, or six, five, four, three, two, or one man, even down to half a man, or below the knees, or reaching only to the ankles—the residual water will remain at this level."
Furthermore, when five suns appear, there may remain a small portion of water in the great ocean, like the small amount of water found in a cow's footprint during the autumn rains.
In this way, as the five suns arise, even the small amount of water remaining within the great ocean becomes likewise diminished.
Furthermore, O monks!
When the five suns arise, that great ocean will, in every place, become completely parched until not a single drop of water remains, like a smear of oil.

"O bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise thus: impermanent and not long-lasting, existing only for a brief moment. In short, they are to be reviled and abandoned; one should seek liberation from them."
"Furthermore, monks!

To speak briefly as before, up until the time when six suns appear in the world, those four great continents, the eighty-four thousand small islands, all the great mountains, and even Sumeru, the king of mountains, will all emit smoke; rising again and again, just like when a potter fires his vessels, the flames on the vessels rise all at once, rising again and again until the fire becomes intense, filling and pervading everywhere."

In this very way, and in no other, the four great continents and all the great mountains likewise give rise to fierce and powerful smoke; in brief, up to the point that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, one should seek liberation from them.
"Furthermore, monks!

To speak briefly as before, when the seven suns arise, those four great continents, the eighty-four thousand minor islands, all the great mountains, and even Sumeru, the king of mountains, will all be completely ablaze; the subterranean waters at the very bottom of the earth will likewise all dry up and vanish."

Once the mass of water has been exhausted, the mass of wind also subsides; thus, at the time when the flames blaze most fiercely, the upper portion of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, extending for seven hundred *yojanas*, collapses all at once. The fire grows even more intense, and driven by the wind, it burns upward into the palaces of the Brahmā heavens, yet it cannot reach the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

At that time, among those gods, there were certain newly born sons of the Ābhāsvara Heaven who did not yet know that the world undergoes dissolution and formation, or that it has already undergone dissolution and formation and is now in the period of abiding; consequently, they all became terrified, struck with alarm, and trembling, saying to one another:
"Could it be that a mass of flames is spreading here to burn this palace of the Ābhāsvara Heaven?"
At that time, the long-resident devaputras of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, who were well-versed in the destruction, formation, and abiding of the world’s kalpas, comforted the newly born devaputras, saying:
"O noble ones, do not be startled; do not be afraid!"
"You worthy ones, do not be startled and do not be afraid!
Why is this? You worthy ones should know that in the past, a mass of flames also reached this place."

At that time, having heard these words, the assembly of devas immediately recollected the fires of the past; because they recollected those lights without letting them leave their minds, they received this name, namely, the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven).

"Monks, that fire is thus: it blazes with such extreme intensity, its fierce flames so vast and brilliant that they consume everything to ashes and charcoal, leaving nothing behind that can be identified."
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are thus; briefly stated, they may even be sought for liberation and escape.
"O monks, how does the world, having been destroyed, come to be formed again?"
"O Bhikṣus!

At that time, after the passage of immeasurable, long, and incalculable eons of days, months, seasons, and years, a great mass of heavy clouds arose, spreading until they completely covered the world-system of the Brahmā heavens. Once it had completely covered it, a great torrential rain poured down, with drops so coarse that some were like chariot axles and others like pestles. This continued for many years, even hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, until that accumulation of rainwater gradually increased and reached the world-system where the Brahmās dwell, filling it entirely."
However, that mass of water is sustained by four wind-circles.
What are these four?
The first is named Abiding; the second is named Secure Abiding; the third is named Non-falling; and the fourth is named Firm Lord.
At that time, after the rain of that mass of water had ceased, it receded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yojanas.

At that moment, great winds arose simultaneously from the four directions; these winds were named Anāvilas. They blew upon that mass of water, causing the waves and surges to boil and surge in chaotic, unceasing turmoil, and large masses of foam spontaneously formed within the water.

At that time, the great wind Anāvilā blew those masses of foam and cast them into the air; from above, they constructed the various Brahma palaces, which were subtle, exquisite, and lovely, adorned with the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
"Monks! By this cause and condition, there arise these sublime palaces and walls, and the Brahmakāyika devas are born into the world. Monks!"

Having done this, that great mass of water receded further by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *yojanas*. To speak briefly, as described before, winds arose from the four directions called Anābhiras; driven by these great winds, the water-foam was cast up and formed palaces named the Heaven of the Māra-body (*Māra-kāya-deva*), which were dwelling places with walls no different from those of the Brahma-body heavens (*Brahma-kāya-deva*), differing only slightly in the coarseness or fineness of their precious colors.

In this manner, he fashioned the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas and the Nirmāṇarati devas; next, he fashioned the palaces of the Tuṣita devas, followed by the palaces of the Yāma devas. Thus, they were produced in succession until they were complete, all resembling the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, though their precious colors gradually became less refined and somewhat different.
"O bhikṣus!
At that time, that mass of water further diminishes, even receding by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yojanas, until it remains still and tranquil."
Within the mass of water, froth naturally arises on all four sides, floating upon the surface; it is sixty-eight billion yojanas in thickness and immeasurable in its circumference.
It is just as in springs, pools, and lakes, where on all four sides there are floating froths that completely cover the surface of the water and remain there motionless. Even so, O bhikṣus!
Within that mass of water, on all four sides, a layer of floating foam rests upon it, sixty-eight billion yojanas thick and immeasurably wide; it is likewise so.

“O Bhikṣus! At that time, the great wind Anābhiḷa blew upon those water-bubbles, which immediately formed Sumeru, the King of Mountains. Next, it fashioned city walls and moats, variegated and lovely, composed of the four jewels—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.”
"Monks! By this cause and condition, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, comes into being and appears in the world. Monks!"

Furthermore, at that time, the great wind Vīra blew upon those water-foams and fashioned mountain peaks on the upper portion of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, in the four directions. Each peak was seven hundred *yojanas* high, variegated and exquisite, composed of the seven precious gems—namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to musāragalva and aśmagarbha. By this cause and condition, the four great mountain peaks appeared in the world.

That wind, proceeding in this sequence, further blows upon the floating foam on the water to construct palaces for the Trāyastriṃśa devas. Next, at a distance of forty-two thousand yojanas from the mid-slopes of Mount Sumeru in the east, west, south, and north, it constructs palaces for the Four Great Heavenly Kings; their city walls and enclosures are all made of the seven precious gems, magnificent and exquisite, with variegated colors worthy of admiration.

When this was completed, that wind again blew upon the water-foam; at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas on the mid-slope of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, it fashioned a palace for the Moon Devaputra, with high and great city walls, accomplished of the seven treasures and adorned with various colors.

Having done this, he again blew upon the water-foam to create for the Sun Deity seven great palaces, complete with city walls, watchtowers, and battlements all fashioned from the seven precious gems; they were adorned in various ways, their diverse colors beautiful to behold.
By these causes and conditions, there come to be palaces of the seven suns in the world, abiding in the present.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

That wind blows upon that mass of water-foam and further constructs three cities upon Mount Sumeru, adorned with the seven treasures, variegated and exquisite—namely, the jewels of gold, silver, and so forth, up to musāragalva and aśmagarbha. By these causes and conditions, such cities arise in the world.
Furthermore, monks!

At that time, the great wind Anābhirā again blows these foam-bubbles upon the surface of the ocean to a height of ten thousand yojanas, forming crystal palaces for the sky-dwelling yakṣas; their city walls, towers, and battlements are likewise all made of crystal.
"Monks! By this cause and condition, there arise in the world the palaces and city walls of the yakṣas who dwell in the air, complete in all their parts.
Furthermore, monks!"

At that time, the great wind Anāpila again blew upon the foam of the waters, and to the east, south, west, and north of Sumeru, the King of Mountains—each at a distance of one thousand yojanas from the mountain—it fashioned four-sided Asura cities beneath the great ocean. Adorned with the seven precious jewels, they were exquisite and lovely; indeed, it was in this manner that these four-sided Asura cities came into existence within the world.

"Furthermore, the great wind Anāvilā blows those water-foams and casts them beyond Sumeru, the King of Mountains; there, it constructs another great mountain named Khadiraka. This mountain is forty-two thousand yojanas in both height and breadth, perfectly adorned with the seven treasures, exquisite and beautiful to behold."
"O bhikṣus!
By this cause and condition, there further arises in the world the mountain Khadiraka, produced in this manner.

Furthermore, the great wind Anabhiḷa blows those water-foams and casts them outside the Khadiraka mountain, where it further constructs another mountain named Īṣādhara. This mountain is twenty-one thousand yojanas in height and breadth; it is of various lovely colors, composed of the seven treasures, including even *śukti* and *musāragalva*.
"O Bhikṣus!
By this cause and condition, the mountain named Īṣādhāra came into being in the world in such a manner.

Furthermore, the great wind Anabhiḷa blew upon those water-bubbles and cast them further outside the Īṣādhāra mountain, where it fashioned another mountain called Yugandhara. This mountain is twelve thousand yojanas in height and breadth; it is of various lovely colors and is composed of the seven treasures, including *śukti* and *musāragalva*."
"O Bhikṣus!
By this cause and condition, there appeared in the world the King of Mountains, Yugandhara.
Following this sequence, Mount Sumanas was formed, six thousand yojanas in height, breadth, and circumference."
Next, he further fashioned Mount Aśvakarṇa (formerly called Bāndhuma), which is three thousand yojanas in height and breadth, being perfectly equal in both dimensions.
Next, he further fashioned Mount Nimindhara, which is one thousand two hundred yojanas in height and breadth, being perfectly equal in both dimensions.
Next, he further constructed Mount Vinataka, equal in height and breadth at six hundred yojanas.

Next, he further constructed Mount Khadiraka, equal in height and breadth at three hundred yojanas; it was of various lovely colors, entirely composed of the seven kinds of exquisite jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—as described above, being no different from the construction of Mount Kakudika.
"O Bhikṣus! By this cause and condition, the Cakravāḍa Mountains and so forth come into being in the world in this manner.

Furthermore, the great wind Anabhiḷa blows upon those water-foams and scatters and casts them outside the Cakravāḍa Mountains, forming the four great continents in the four directions, as well as eighty thousand small islands and other great mountains; in this way, through successive stages, they are fashioned and brought to completion."
"O Bhikṣus!
By this causal condition, the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, the various great mountains, and so forth, appeared in succession within the world."

Furthermore, the great wind Anābhila blows those water-foams beyond the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, Sumeru the king of mountains, and all other great mountains, where it arranges them in a circular perimeter called the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains. They are six hundred and eighty million *yojanas* in height and breadth, equal in all dimensions; they are solid and real, composed of diamond (*vajra*), and difficult to destroy.
"O Bhikṣus! By these causes and conditions, the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains appeared in the world.
Furthermore, the great wind Anāvila blew and excavated the great earth, gradually penetrating deep within until it deposited a vast mass of water there, which remained still and accumulated."
"Monks! By these causes and conditions, there further arises in this world a great ocean, produced in such a manner.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is the water of this great ocean so salty and bitter that it is unfit for drinking or eating?"
"O bhikṣus!
You should know that this matter has three causes and conditions.
What are these three?"

First, after the calamity of fire has passed and an immeasurable period of vast duration has elapsed, great heavy clouds arise, spreading and remaining dense as far as the Brahma-heaven; thereafter, rain falls, its drops being exceedingly large, as described in detail previously.

That great rain of liquid washes all the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas; next, it thoroughly washes the palaces of the Māra devas, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, the Tuṣita devas, and the Yāma devas. Washing again and again, thus performing such a great washing, as it cleanses those palaces, all salty, bitter, and pungent flavors flow downward.

Next, he further washed Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, as well as the four great continents, the eighty thousand minor islands, all other great mountains, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth. As he washed them in this manner, immersing and rinsing them, all the salty, bitter, and pungent flavors therein were simultaneously cast down into the great ocean.
"O bhikṣus!
This is the first cause and condition by which the waters of the great ocean are salty and unfit for drinking.
Furthermore, these waters of the great ocean are the dwelling place of various great deities and beings with massive bodies."
What are those of large bodies?

They are namely fish, turtles, dragons, otters, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, frogs, *kumbhīras*, *timayas*, *timi-mīlas*, *timi-tūlas*, *tūlakīras*, and so forth. Among them, some have bodies of one hundred *yojanas*, two hundred *yojanas*, or three, four, five, six, seven, or eight hundred *yojanas*. There are such beings of immense body who dwell therein.
All the excrement and urine that flow from them all enter the ocean; for this reason, its water is salty and bitter, unfit for drinking or eating.
O Bhikṣus!
This is the second cause and condition for its saltiness and bitterness.
Furthermore, it is because in ancient times various seers once made a pronouncement regarding this great ocean water.
The seers’ pronouncement was as follows:
"May you become salty in taste, unfit for drinking! May you become salty in taste, unfit for drinking!
Monks, this is the third cause and condition that makes the waters of the great ocean salty and unfit for drinking.
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does the world of Great Heat and Scorching arise? Monks!

When this world was first evolving at the beginning of the kalpa and was just being formed, the great wind Anāvilā blew those six great palaces of the Sun Deity and placed them all beneath the waters of the great ocean. At the place where they were situated, the masses of great water within that region were immediately consumed and dried up, so that they could no longer flow or overflow."

"Monks! By this cause and condition, there arises in the world this great heat and parched wasteland, manifesting its birth; this is called the world having undergone destruction and remaining in a state of stability."
"Furthermore, what is meant by the world’s dissolution, formation, and subsistence? Monks!
Just as it is now, when the world has been formed and thus stands established, there occurs a fire disaster."
How, furthermore, does the calamity of water arise? Monks!

During the kalpa of the calamity of water, all people act in accordance with the Dharma, speak words in accordance with the Dharma, are accomplished in right view, and are free from inversion; they maintain the ten wholesome courses of action. Those people shall attain the third dhyāna, which is without joy, without exerting effort, and without fatigue, attaining it spontaneously.

At that time, those beings dwell within the path of practice for the various seers, devas, and Brahmās who abide in space; having attained this state, they become free from joy and experience bliss, exclaiming to one another:
"O noble ones, bliss! Bliss! Such is the bliss of this third dhyāna."
At that time, all the sentient beings there together questioned this being who had attained dhyāna, and he replied:
"Excellent, worthy ones! This is the third dhyāna path, which is free from joy; it should be understood in this way."

Once those beings have gained this knowledge, they further accomplish such a third dhyāna path free from joy; having accomplished it, they realize it; having realized it, they contemplate it; and having contemplated it, they abide in it. At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in the Heaven of Universal Purity.

In this way, from the hells below, through the world of Yama, the world of asuras, and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, up to the Brahma-world and the Ābhāsvara deities—everything beneath this, including all sentient beings, all locations, and all modes of existence, is completely severed and exhausted.
"O monks! This is called the turning of the world.
Furthermore, how does the world, having turned, undergo destruction?
"O Bhikṣus!
After an immeasurable and long period of time, a great cloud spread everywhere, even filling the Ābhāsvara devas.
From that point on, it rained down boiling ash-water for immeasurable many years, briefly described as lasting even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of years."
"O bhikṣus!
When that rain of boiling lye falls, it completely destroys all the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, so that not even a trace of form, a particle of dust, or an image can be perceived."
For example, if ghee is thrown into a fire, it is consumed and burned away until nothing remains that can be perceived or verified by its form.
In this very way, when the rain of boiling ash-water falls, it consumes the palaces and other dwellings of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; likewise, they become devoid of any perceivable characteristics.

"O Bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent; they are subject to destruction and dispersion, to wandering and decay, never remaining still for even a moment. It is likewise with these [phenomena]: they are to be loathed and regarded as a source of suffering; one should seek liberation from them."

"O monks! In this way, the celestial palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, the Māras, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Paranirmita-vaśavartins, the Tuṣitas, and the Yāmas—these and others—are washed away and extinguished by a rain of boiling ashes. To speak briefly, it is as described before: just as when butter is thrown into a fire, it melts, dissipates, and vanishes without leaving any trace, so too is it with all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which are impermanent; one should seek liberation from them."
"O bhikṣus!

When that rain of boiling caustic water falls, it rains down upon the four great continents, the eighty thousand small continents, and all other great and small Sumeru kings of mountains, dissolving and utterly destroying them until no form or characteristic remains by which they can be identified or recorded. As explained extensively before, this should be viewed with weariness and revulsion."
Such transformations can only be believed by those who witness them;
this is called the world’s turning and subsequent destruction.
Furthermore, how does that which has already turned and been destroyed come into being?
"O bhikṣus!

At that time, clouds arise and pour down great torrents of rain for many years; winds then arise and blow the foam upward, forming celestial palaces. As explained at length, this is like the event of the fire calamity; this is the water calamity."
Furthermore, what is the calamity of wind?

Monks! When the time of the wind calamity arrives, all sentient beings practice according to the Dharma and achieve right mindfulness, and are reborn in the Abṛha Heaven (the "Vast Fruit" Heaven) within the Fourth Dhyāna.
It is likewise for beings in the hells who, having cast off their hellish bodies, are reborn in the human realm, cultivate pure conduct, and achieve the four dhyānas.

The same applies to those in the animal realm, the world of Yama, the world of asuras, and the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Māra-heaven, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heavens; all of them practice and achieve the four dhyānas, as explained in detail above.
"O bhikṣus! This is called the turning of the world.
How does it turn and disintegrate?"
"O Bhikṣus!
After the passage of immeasurable, long-distant aeons, a great wind arose; that wind was named Saṃghāta.
O Bhikṣus!"

That wind first blows upon all the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, causing them to rub against one another until they are utterly destroyed and annihilated, leaving no residue remaining that can be identified.

For example, suppose a strong man takes two copper vessels, grasps them with both hands, and rubs them together incessantly until they are broken and destroyed, leaving no form or appearance such that nothing remains recognizable.
In the same way, that harmonious wind blows and utterly destroys the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Monks! All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they break apart and disperse, lasting but a brief moment before passing away. They are even worthy of revulsion; one should seek liberation from them.

"In this successive manner, he blows away all the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, and all the palaces of the Mārakāyika, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Nirmāṇarati, and Yāma devas; they collide, strike against one another, rub, and grind until each is rendered formless, signless, shadowless, and dustless, yet still recognizable."

"O Bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise thus: they are subject to decay and lack solidity; they possess no reality. You should cultivate weary detachment and seek early liberation from them."
"O Bhikṣus!
That wind further blows upon the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, and all other great mountains, including Sumeru, the king of mountains.
It may lift them up one krośa and scatter and destroy them, or two, three, four, five, six, or seven krośas, having scattered and destroyed them."

Or they are blown up to a height of one yojana, two, three, four, five, six, or seven yojanas; or they are blown up to a height of one hundred yojanas, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight hundred yojanas, being scattered and destroyed.
Or it may blow them up to a height of one thousand yojanas, two, three, four, five, six, or seven thousand yojanas, or even up to a hundred thousand yojanas, dispersing and destroying them.
That wind blows in such a manner, shattering and destroying everything until it is rendered formless and signless, with not even a trace of a minute particle remaining visible.
It is like a strong man who takes a handful of parched barley, crushes it into fine powder, and hurls it toward the sky; dispersed by the whirling winds, it becomes formless and shadowless.
In this way, in this manner, that wind blows and shatters the various continents and mountains; it is just like this.
Only those who have seen it can believe it.
This is called the destruction of the world’s revolving abode.
"Furthermore, how does the world, having been destroyed, undergo transformation? Monks!
Thus, after the passage of immeasurable years and an exceedingly long period of time, a great black cloud arises, covering the world entirely, even up to the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven."
Once it had completely covered [the world], it then sent down a great rain; the drops were coarse and large, some like carriage axles and others like pestles, pouring down in continuous succession.
After many years, even hundreds of thousands of millions of years, the waters accumulated to a great depth until they filled all the way up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.

Sustained by the four kinds of wind-wheels as previously described, they were blown into foam, which formed the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, variegated with the seven treasures; their manifestation and arising are each explained in sequence according to the fire and water calamities.
"Monks! This is called the world having been destroyed and undergoing reformation.
How does the world, once reformed, remain?
"O bhikṣus!
Just as now, the world of gods and humans has been transformed and established.
O bhikṣus!"
In this sequence, all are driven by wind; these are called the three calamities of the world.
Chapter Twelve: The Most Excellent. *Qishi jing*, Chapter Twelve, Part One: "Furthermore, monks!
When the world has thus evolved and reached its formation, many sentient beings are born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

When these beings are born in that heaven, their bodies and minds are joyful; they take delight as their food, possess natural radiance, and have supernormal powers by which they travel through the air. They attain a most excellent form, enjoy long lifespans, and dwell in peace and happiness.

"O monks! At that time, when the world had undergone destruction and become empty, devoid of all things, and while there were yet no beings within the Brahma palaces, those from the Ābhāsvara Heaven whose merit and karma were exhausted descended to be born within the Brahma palaces.

They were not born from a womb, but appeared suddenly through transformation. This first Brahmā was named Sahampati; 'Saha' is the name of the world, and 'pati' means lord. It is for this reason that he received such a name at birth."

"O monks! At that time, there were other sentient beings whose merit and lifespan had come to an end; having cast off their bodies and lives from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they were also born here in this world. Their physical forms were upright and handsome; they dwelt in joy, taking it as their sustenance; they possessed natural radiance and supernormal powers, traveling by soaring through the air; their bodily color was most excellent, and they remained there for a long period of time."

When those sentient beings dwell in that state, there are no males or females, and no distinction between the noble and the lowly; there exists only this designation, which is called "sentient being, sentient being."
Furthermore, monks!
At such a time as this, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) arises upon this great earth and remains spread everywhere, coagulated and pervasive.
It is, for example, like a person who boils milk until it is thick; a thin film then forms and remains on its surface, just as a film of water rests upon the surface of water.
In this very way, O monks!

Furthermore, at a later time, the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) produced upon this great earth solidified and remained still; it gradually became like curdled milk, achieving the state of fresh butter (*navanīta*). It possessed such forms, colors, and characteristics, and its taste was sweet and delicious, like the finest honey.
At that time, among those beings, there was suddenly one of a greedy disposition who thought to himself:
"I too might now take some of this with my finger and try to taste it, so that I may know what this thing is."
Then, having formed this thought, those beings immediately used their fingers, dipping them to the depth of one joint, to take up some of the essence of the earth, sucking and tasting it.
Having tasted it, his mind was filled with joy; thus he dipped and sucked at it once, then twice and even thrice, until he gave rise to craving and attachment.
Next, he began to scoop it up with his hand, gradually gathering it in handfuls, and finally, scooping up large quantities, he ate it to his heart's content.

At that time, while those sentient beings were thus scooping up and eating as much as they desired, there were again immeasurable other people who, seeing those beings eating in such a manner, likewise imitated them, vying with one another to seize and eat.
"O bhikṣus!

Those sentient beings, having taken up this essence of the earth and eating it incessantly, found their bodies naturally becoming gradually coarse and foul; their skin became rough and thick, their complexion grew turbid and dark, their physical appearance changed, they no longer possessed radiance, and they could no longer fly through the air."
Because the earth has become infertile, their supernormal powers have vanished. O bhikṣus!
As was said previously, it shall be the same hereafter.
At that time, the world became shrouded in darkness. Monks!
It was for this reason that great darkness first arose in the world.

Furthermore, how is it that at such a time, the sun, moon, and various constellations suddenly arise in the world, whereby the designations of day and night, month and half-month, year, season, and so forth come into being?
"O Bhikṣus!
At that time, the magnificent and great palace of the Sun Deity rises from the east, travels around the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, and sets in the west."
Having set in the west, it emerges again from the east.
At that time, sentient beings again see the supreme and magnificent palace of the Sun Deity emerging from the east, and they say to one another:
"O virtuous ones, this is indeed the radiant palace of the Sun Deity emerging once more from the east; it shall circumambulate Mount Sumeru to the right and set in the west."
Having seen this for the third time, they also said to one another:
"O virtuous ones, this is the radiance of that celestial realm flowing forth; this is the radiance of that celestial realm flowing forth."
For this reason, the sun is called *sūrya*. *Sūrya* is translated in the Sui language as "this is that," and thus such a name came into being.
The Scripture on the Arising of the World, Scroll Nine;
The Scripture on the Arising of the World, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
The Remainder of Chapter Twelve: The Most Excellent.

"Furthermore, monks, you should know that the palace of the Sun Deity is exactly fifty-one yojanas in length and breadth, and the same from top to bottom; it has seven layers of walls and seven layers of railings."
The rows of *tāla* trees are likewise sevenfold, encircling it on all sides; they are adorned with a variegated intermingling of colors.
Those walls are all composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
On all four sides there are gates, and each gate is equipped with watchtowers, battlements, and defensive platforms, as well as groves of trees, ponds, and gardens.

Within it grow various kinds of diverse trees; each tree possesses various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, and various fragrances, which spread everywhere with the wind. Furthermore, various birds sing together in harmony.
"Monks! Furthermore, that Sun Deity constructs his palace from two kinds of substances; it is square like a house, appearing round when viewed from afar. Monks!"
What are these two?
They are gold and crystal.
This solar palace is composed of many celestial golds and celestial crystals joined together to form it.
One side is divided into two parts, both made of celestial gold; they are pure and stainless, free from all impurities, and radiantly bright.
One part of the other side is made of celestial crystal; it is clean and luminous, well-polished and well-refined, without blemish or defilement.
"O bhikṣus!
Furthermore, that great and magnificent palace of the Sun God moves as it is driven by five kinds of winds.
What are these five?"

The first is called "holding" (dhāraṇa), the second is called "abiding" (sthiti), the third is called "conforming progression" (anuvartana), the fourth is called "the turning point" (parāvarta), and the fifth is called "about to proceed" (prasthāna).
"Furthermore, O monks!"

Before that palace of the Sun God, there were immeasurable devas who preceded him—immeasurable hundreds of devas, immeasurable thousands of devas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas walking ahead. As they walked, each constantly experienced peace and happiness; they were all named "Firm Walkers" (Dṛḍhacara), and it is from these Firm Walker devas that this name is derived.
Furthermore, monks!

Within the solar palace, there is a magnificent carriage made of Jāmbūnada gold, sixteen yojanas in height and eight yojanas in width, exquisitely adorned and most sublime; it is for the person of the Sun Devaputra and his inner retinue.
Within that palanquin, they experience joy and delight, fully endowed with the harmonious qualities of the five celestial sensual pleasures. Monks!
The life span of the Sun Deity is five hundred years; his descendants succeed one another, all governing there, and they maintain their residence in the palace for the full duration of a kalpa.
"Furthermore, monks!

From within the joints and members of the body of the Sun Deva-son, light issues forth and illuminates the Jāmbūnada chariot; from the light of the Jāmbūnada chariot, light again issues forth and illuminates that palace."
From that great palace of the Sun Deity, rays of light issued forth in continuous succession, illuminating the four great continents and all the worlds.
O bhikṣus!
The body, carriage, and palace of the Sun Deity are all fully endowed with one thousand rays of light; five hundred rays of light shine horizontally, and five hundred rays of light shine downward.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does the magnificent great palace where the Sun Deity dwells illuminate the four continents and all worlds? O monks!
There is a certain kind of person who is able to practice generosity.

When practicing generosity, they give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, and those who have come from afar seeking aid—namely, food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flower garlands, necklaces, ointments and perfumes, bedding, dwellings, lamps and oil, and whatever else is required to sustain life. At the time of giving, they bestow these things swiftly and without guile or crookedness.

Furthermore, by making various offerings and serving those sages who uphold the precepts, who are endowed with merit, and who practice the wholesome Dharma, one will, as a result of these causes, experience immeasurable kinds of physical and mental peace and happiness.
It is like a vast marsh, a desolate mountain forest, or a wide and distant desert plain where, suddenly, a pool of water appears—its water cool, clear, pure, light, and sweet.
There are several strong men who, having traveled a great distance, are exhausted, tormented by heat, and parched with thirst; they have been without food or drink for a long time.

Upon reaching that pond, they drink and bathe, thereby eliminating all thirst, exhaustion, and the torment of feverish distress. Emerging from the pond, their bodies and minds are tranquil and joyful; they experience immeasurable bliss and give rise to great gladness.
In this way, because his mind was pure at the time of giving, when his body dissolved and his life ended, he was reborn as a son of heaven within the solar palace.
Having been born therein, they obtain as a karmic reward such swift, mind-pleasing celestial palaces for flight.
By this cause and condition, the palace of the Sun Deity illuminates the four great continents and other worlds.

“Monks! There is another kind of person who does not kill, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not drink intoxicants, and is not negligent; who honors the seers and the noble ones who are endowed with the merit of observing the precepts; and who associates with those who practice the straight and wholesome Dharma—explained at length as before.”
When the body perishes and life ends, one proceeds according to one's vows to be reborn in the celestial palace of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva).
There, one immediately experiences swift karmic fruition; therefore, these are called the paths of wholesome action.
By these causes and conditions, this solar palace illuminates the four great continents as well as other worlds.

Furthermore, there is another kind of person who practices non-killing up to right view, who has also made offerings to various sages endowed with the merit of observing the precepts, and who has associated with those of pure, upright, and virtuous conduct.
By encountering those pure causes and conditions, one obtains the retribution of birth in the celestial palace of the Sun Deity and experiences its swift fruit.
For this reason, the celestial palace of the Sun Deity illuminates the four great continents and other worlds, as explained in detail above.
“Monks! Sixty kṣaṇas are called one lava; thirty lavas are called one muhūrta. Monks!”
For a certain number of kṣaṇas, a certain number of lava-s, and a certain number of muhūrta-s, the celestial palace of the Sun God constantly moves without ceasing.
For six months it travels northward; during this period, within a single day, it gradually shifts six krośas toward the north, never for a moment departing from its solar path.
For six months it travels southward; likewise, within a single day, it gradually shifts six krośas toward the south, without deviating from its solar path.
"O Bhikṣus!
When the celestial palace of the Sun God travels for six months, the celestial palace of the Moon God also travels for that same duration during fifteen days.
Furthermore, by what cause and condition do various heat-afflictions arise constantly during the summer season?"
"O Bhikṣus!
When the celestial palace of the Sun-god travels northward for six months, it travels six krośas each day, never departing from its designated path."
However, within that state, there are ten causes and conditions by which feverish distress arises.
What are these ten? O bhikṣus!

Outside Mount Sumeru, there is another mountain named Khadiraka, equal in height and breadth at forty-two thousand yojanas; it is of variegated colors, beautiful to behold, and composed of the seven treasures.

At that time, the light from the celestial palace of the Sun God strikes that mountain, causing it to become hot; therefore, at that time, there arises this heat-affliction, which constitutes the first condition for the arising of heat-affliction.
Furthermore, monks!
Outside of Mount Khadiraka, there is another mountain named Īṣādhara, equal in height and breadth at twenty-one thousand yojanas.
At that time, the light from the celestial palace of the Sun God strikes that mountain, producing a sensation of heat; this is the second condition for the arising of thermal affliction.
Next is Mount Yugandhara, equal in height and breadth at twelve thousand yojanas; this is the third range.
Next is Mount Sudarśana, equal in height and breadth at six thousand yojanas; this is the fourth range.
Next is the mountain Aśvakarṇa, three thousand yojanas in height and breadth, which is the fifth range.
Next is Mount Nimindhara, one thousand two hundred yojanas in height and breadth, which is the sixth range.
Next is Mount Vinataka, equal in height and breadth at six hundred yojanas; this is the seventh range.
Next is Mount Cakravāḍa, equal in height and breadth at three hundred yojanas; this is the eighth range.
Next, ten thousand yojanas above this great earth, in that space, there are dwellings in the form of palaces belonging to various yakṣas, made of crystal; this is the ninth condition.

Next, there are the four great continents and eighty thousand minor continents; the various other great mountains within those continents, such as Sumeru, the king of mountains, constitute the tenth condition.

The details should be understood as fully explained in the *Khadiraka* [Sūtra]. These are the ten types of causes for the heat and affliction experienced by the celestial palace of the Sun God as it travels along the northern path during the six months.
"Furthermore, for what reason and by what causes do there come to be various colds? Monks!
After six months have passed, the celestial palace of the Sun Deity gradually moves toward the south."
At that time, there were further twelve links of dependent origination capable of producing cold.
What are these twelve? O monks!
Between Mount Sumeru and Mount Khadiraka, there is the Sumeru Sea, eighty-four thousand yojanas wide and immeasurable in circumference.
Within it, there were many *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, all of which filled it completely, their fragrance being most intense.
The light from the celestial palace of the Sun God passes through that space and strikes that ocean; this is the first cause and condition for its coldness.
Following this sequence, Mount Īṣādhara is the second cause;
Mount Gandhamādana is the third cause.
Mount Sudarśana is the fourth condition;
Mount Aśvakarṇa is the fifth condition;
Mount Nimindhara is the sixth condition.
Mount Vinataka is the seventh causal condition;
the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains are the eighth causal condition.
Regarding all the flowers within those oceans, they are fully present in their proper order, as should be explained in detail concerning Mount Khadiraka.

"Furthermore, wherever the various rivers flow within Jambudvīpa, they become cold because the light from the celestial palace of the Sun God shines upon them; briefly stated, this is the ninth cause and condition for cold."
Furthermore, just as the rivers flow throughout Jambudvīpa, those flowing through Aparagoyānī are twice as many.
When the light from the sun’s celestial palace shines upon them, they become even more cold; this is the tenth cause and condition for cold.
Furthermore, just as the rivers flow in the continent of Aparagodānīya, the rivers flowing in the continent of Pūrvavideha are twice as numerous; this is the eleventh causal condition for cold.
Furthermore, as the rivers flow through the continent of Pūrvavideha, those flowing through the continent of Uttarakuru are twice as many.
When the light from the celestial palace of the Sun God touches them, it produces cold; this is the twelfth causal condition for cold.
"O bhikṣus!
When the palace of the Sun Deity travels southward for six months, it proceeds every day for six krośas, without deviating from its path."
It is because of such factors as these twelve links of dependent origination that it is cold. "Furthermore, monks,
by what causes and conditions are nights long and days short during the winter season?"
"O monks! After six months have passed, the celestial palace of the Sun God gradually proceeds toward the south, moving six *krośas* each day without fail."
At that time, the celestial palace of the Sun God was at the southernmost extremity of Jambudvīpa; because the terrain there was narrow and small, the sun passed through it with great speed.
O Bhikṣus!
For this reason, during the winter season, the days are short and the nights are long.
Furthermore, bhikṣus,
for what reason are the days long and the nights short during the spring and summer seasons?
"O Bhikṣus!

After six months have passed, the celestial palace of the Sun God gradually proceeds toward the north; each day it shifts by six krośas without deviation, following a path distinct from its usual course."
At that time, as the sun moves toward the center of Jambudvīpa, the ground is wide and its path long; therefore, the days are long.
Monks, by this cause and condition, during the spring and summer the days are long and the nights are short.
"Furthermore, monks! When it is midday in Jambudvīpa,
the sun has just set in Pūrvavideha;
When the sun first rises over Aparagoyānī,
it is midnight in Uttarakuru;
when it is midday in Aparagoyānī, it is then setting in Jambudvīpa, rising in Uttarakuru, and it is midnight in Pūrvavideha.
When it is midday in Uttarakuru, the sun is just setting in Aparagoyānī, just rising in Pūrvavideha, and it is exactly midnight in Jambudvīpa;
when it is midday in Pūrvavideha, the sun is just setting in Uttarakuru, just rising in Jambudvīpa, and it is exactly midnight in Aparagoyānī.
"O Bhikṣus!
What the people of Jambudvīpa call the west, the people of Aparagoyānī regard as the east;
what the people of Aparagoyānī call the west, the people of Uttarakuru regard as the east."
What the people of Uttarakuru call the west, the people of Pūrvavideha consider to be the east;
what the people of Pūrvavideha call the west, the people of Jambudvīpa consider to be the east.
"It is the same for the two directions, north and south.
At this, the World-Honored One spoke these udāna verses:
"Revolution and dissolution, The emergence of heavens and the thin covering."
Twelve layers of winds blow as the various devas pass before them;
with watchtowers and parapets swept by the wind, their bodies shine with radiance.
Through the karma of generosity and upholding the precepts, they pass through kṣaṇas and lava-s.
In heat there are ten conditions, and in cold there are twelve kinds;
by day and night, and at midday, the four directions—east and west—are explained.
"O Bhikṣus!"

The palace of the Moon Deva-son is forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal. On all four sides it is surrounded by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells; furthermore, it is encircled on all sides by seven rows of *tāla* trees of various beautiful colors.
Those walls are all composed of the seven treasures, from gold and silver up to agate.

At each of the four gates, there are watchtowers and battlements adorned in various ways; even the birds each sing in harmony, as described at length previously regarding the celestial palace of the Sun Deity.
"O Bhikṣus!

The celestial palace of the Moon Deity is composed entirely of celestial silver and celestial blue lapis lazuli, interspersed with one another; two parts are celestial silver, pure and stainless, free from all dross and impurities."
Its substance is pure and bright, its radiance exceedingly brilliant;
the remaining portion, made of celestial blue lapis lazuli, is likewise extremely clear and pure, translucent throughout from both sides, with light shining afar.
“Monks! That palace of the Moon Devaputra, most excellent, is sustained and moved by five kinds of winds.
What are these five?
First, upholding; second, abiding; third, conforming; fourth, gathering;
and fifth, moving. Because it is sustained and supported by these five winds, the celestial palace of the Moon Deity travels through space.
"O Bhikṣus!

Before the lunar palace, there are also immeasurable celestial palaces of various devas that proceed ahead; likewise, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of sons of gods also proceed ahead. As they travel forward, they constantly experience immeasurable and manifold pleasures. Those sons of gods all have individual names."
"O Bhikṣus!

Within this great celestial palace of the Moon God, there is a magnificent carriage made of blue lapis lazuli. This carriage is sixteen yojanas in height and eight yojanas in width. The Moon Devaputra and his celestial maidens reside within this carriage, experiencing pleasure in union through the various divine qualities of the five sensual desires; they enjoy themselves with joy and delight, moving about as they please."
"O Bhikṣus!
That Moon Devaputra has a lifespan of five hundred years according to the reckoning of the devas; his descendants succeed one another, all ruling there, yet his palace remains for an entire kalpa."
"O Bhikṣus!

From within the joints and limbs of the body of the Moon Devaputra, light issues forth and illuminates that sapphire chariot on all sides; the light of that chariot illuminates the moon palace, and the light of the moon palace illuminates the four great continents."
"O Bhikṣus!
That Moon Deva has five hundred rays that shine downward, and five hundred rays that shine sideways; for this reason, the Moon Deva is named 'Thousand Rays' and is also called 'Cool Radiance.'"
“Monks! For what reason and by what cause does the celestial palace of the Moon God illuminate the four great continents?

It is because in the past he gave alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, to the poor, the solitary, and those who came from afar to beg—namely, food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flower garlands, various perfumes, beds, seats, dwellings, and all other necessities of life.”
When practicing giving, one should bestow gifts promptly and according to the proper time, with a mind free from flattery or crookedness.
Alternatively, one may make offerings to various sages who maintain the precepts and possess merit, being upright, pure, and virtuous.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they experience immeasurable kinds of physical and mental bliss.
It is like a pool of water in a secluded mountain, marsh, wilderness, or desert, which is cool, refreshing, light, and delicious, free from all turbidity and impurity.

At that time, there was a person who, exhausted from a long journey and oppressed by hunger, thirst, and heat, entered this pond to bathe and drink water, thereby eliminating all suffering and experiencing immeasurable bliss.
In this way, and by these causes and conditions, one is born within the celestial palace of the Moon Deity and experiences the retribution of pleasure;
it is likewise so for all bhikṣus.

Furthermore, there may be some who abstain from taking life, up to and including abstaining from alcohol and heedless conduct, and who honor and serve sages of virtue; they shall be born within the lunar palaces to illuminate the four continents.
Alternatively, there may be some who abstain from taking life, up to and including holding right view; by reason of this, they shall obtain swift-moving celestial palaces that travel through the sky.
These are called the various paths of wholesome action.
And for what reason and by what causes does the celestial palace of the Moon God gradually appear? O monks!
There are three causes and conditions for this. What are the three?
First, turning away from appearances to emerge;

Second, there are the blue-bodied devas, whose forms, garments, and ornaments are all entirely blue; they constantly conceal their palaces during the half-month, and because of this concealment, the lunar disk gradually appears at that time.
Third, from the celestial palace of the Sun God, sixty rays of light simultaneously stream forth, obstructing the lunar disk; by reason of this, it gradually appears.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does this lunar palace appear so perfectly round,
pure, and full? Monks,
it is due to three causes and conditions that it appears thus.
First, at that time, the palaces of the Moon Deity (Candradeva) emerge from their faces; for this reason, they appear perfectly full.

Furthermore, the blue-colored devas wear garments and ornaments that are entirely blue, and they constantly remain hidden within the moon palace during the half-moon. However, on the fifteenth day of the Puṣya month, the form of this moon palace becomes most perfectly full, and its radiance blazes intensely.
For example, when a great, blazing torch is lit amidst many oils, the light of all small lamps is completely eclipsed.
In the same way, the celestial palace of the Moon Deity on the fifteenth day is likewise able to outshine all other lights.

Furthermore, sixty rays of light simultaneously stream forth from the celestial palace of the Sun God, which obstructs the lunar disk. When this lunar palace reaches its full perfection on the fifteenth day of the *puṣya* month, it is entirely free from obscuration in all respects; at that time, the sunlight cannot conceal or cover it.
Furthermore, for what reason and by what causes does the celestial palace of the Moon Deity not appear at all on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight?
O Bhikṣus!
This lunar palace, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, comes closest to the solar palace; because it is then obscured by the sunlight of that [sun], it does not appear at all.
Furthermore, for what reason is the celestial palace of the Moon Deity named "Moon"? O Bhikṣus!
During the dark fortnight, from the first day until the end of the month, the radiance and majestic power of this lunar palace gradually diminish; for this reason, it is called the "Moon."
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do various reflections appear within the lunar palace? O monks!
In this great continent there is a Jambu tree; because of this tree, it is named Jambudvīpa.
Those trees are tall and large, and their reflections appear as lunar discs; for this reason, various reflections arise.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do the various rivers flow through the world?

"O bhikṣus! Because there is the sun, there is heat; because there is heat, there is scorching; because there is scorching, there is steaming; because there is steaming, there is perspiration and moisture. Due to this perspiration and moisture, the juices from all the mountains flow as water, forming the various rivers."
"Monks! For this reason, rivers appear in the world.
Furthermore, for what reason do the five kinds of seeds appear in the world?"
"O Bhikṣus!

In the eastern direction, there are various worlds—some already formed and then destroyed, some already destroyed and then formed, and some already formed and remaining; the same applies to the southern, western, and northern directions regarding their formation, destruction, and abiding."

At that time, the great wind Anābila, blowing from another world-system where it had been formed and established, scattered five kinds of seeds into this realm; having scattered them, it scattered them again, even scattering them extensively—namely, root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, graft-seeds, and seed-seeds; these constitute the five seeds.
"O Bhikṣus!

The fruits of the Jambū tree are as large as a one-hu measure jar from the kingdom of Magadha. When these fruits are plucked, juice flows out following them; their color is white like milk, and their taste is sweet like honey."
"O Bhikṣus!
The fruit of the Jambū tree, wherever it may arise, possesses five benefits: namely, those in the east, south, and west, as well as the two directions of above and below."
Those born in the eastern portion are all eaten together by the gandharvas.
Those born in the southern portion are eaten by the people of seven great settlements. What are these seven?

The first is named *A-samyak-kranda* (Improper Crying), the second *Raurava* (Wailing), the third *Asamyaktva* (Improper Body), the fourth *Bhadra* (Worthy), the fifth *Sādhu* (Good), the sixth *Dṛḍha* (Firm), and the seventh *Jaya* (Victorious).

Within these seven great villages, there are seven black mountains: the first is named *Pārśva* (Side), the second *Eka-piṇḍa* (Single Lump), the third *Kṣudra-kola* (Small Jujube), the fourth *Keśa* (Hair), the fifth *Pañca-pārśva* (Five Sides), the sixth *Abhibhū* (Overpowering), and the seventh *Abhyudgata-jaya* (Supreme Victory).

Within those seven mountains, there are seven caves inhabited by brahmin seers: first, Fine Eyes; second, Good Sage; third, Small; fourth, Crooked Head; fifth, Pool of Putrid Things; sixth, Black Entry; and seventh, Increasing.
At that time, those born in the western portion were eaten together by the garuḍas and other beings;
those born in the upper portion were all eaten together by the space-dwelling yakṣas.
"As for those born in the lower realms, the various insects in the ocean all come to devour them.
Regarding this, there is an udāna verse:
First, the amount of rain is described; Then, manifestations are shown within the palaces.
In these two matters there is much wind, which precedes the movements of the various devas.
Their palanquins and their lifespans, as well as the radiance of their bodies, result from the karma of generosity and the observance of precepts;
these qualities pervade and fulfill the wheel [of sovereignty].
"The moon being eclipsed and its non-appearance; the presence of a shadow and its causes and conditions;
the various rivers and seeds; and lastly, the Jambu tree. O monks!"
At the beginning of the eon, when sentient beings consumed the essence of the earth, they were greatly nourished and remained in the world for a long time.
Among those people, those who ate much became inferior in complexion,
while those who ate little possessed superior radiance.
At that time, because physical forms appeared, people began to deceive one another and compete over who was superior or inferior; those who were superior gave rise to pride.
Due to this pride, the flavor of the earth then vanished.

The skin of the ground reappears, endowed with both color and flavor; its color is like that of a fully blossomed *karṇikāra* flower, and its flavor is like that of pure honey from which the beeswax has been removed.
All those sentient beings gathered together, filled with sorrow and distress, beating their breasts and crying out, bewildered and exhausted, uttered these words: "Alas!"
‘Oh, the taste of the earth! Alas, the taste of the earth!
It is just as when there are various superior flavors today; once one has tasted and known them, one cries out: ‘Alas!’”
"This is my flavor.
Clinging to its former name, they do not know its true meaning.
Those sentient beings are also just like this.
At that time, those sentient beings subsisted on the earth’s crust and remained in the world for a long duration.

Because they ate much of the coarse-colored [portion] and little of the superior-shaped [portion], and due to this distinction between superior and inferior, they began to treat one another with pride and arrogance; consequently, the earth’s crust disappeared once more.

Then a forest creeper sprouted, its form and color fully developed and its fragrance and flavor complete, like the perfected *kālāmbukā* flower which possesses such a hue; when cut, its sap flows like pure honey. Even as described before, they gathered together in mutual grief and distress.
In this sequence, once the forest creepers had disappeared, non-glutinous rice appeared; it was grown neither by plowing nor by sowing, arising spontaneously.
It was without awns or husks, the grains were pure, and they were fully endowed with fragrance and flavor.

At that time, after those sentient beings had eaten this rice, their bodies immediately came to possess fat, marrow, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, pus, and blood, which circulated through the channels; furthermore, the physical characteristics of male and female sexual organs became manifest.
Once the characteristics of the sense organs have arisen, a defiled mind immediately emerges.
Because of this defilement, they gaze at one another repeatedly; having gazed at each other repeatedly, they consequently give rise to lustful desire.
Driven by sensual desire, they engage in unchaste conduct and impure sexual practices in private.
At that time, there are other sentient beings who have not yet practiced this; seeing them, they say: "Hey!..."
"You sentient beings have committed very evil deeds; how can you be like this?

At that time, those sentient beings immediately felt shame and remorse. Having fallen into various unwholesome and evil states, they then received the name *pāṭi*—*pāṭi* being translated in the Sui language as "falling"—which is to say, "husband."
At that time, because those sentient beings had fallen into such evil dharmas, those who shared their lustful desires brought food and drink to present to them, saying to the woman:
"You have committed a transgression!"
"You have fallen!
For this reason, she was given the name Pāriyā, which in the Sui language means "meal-eater";
she was his wife. O Bhikṣus!

For this reason, when the various superior beings who had previously descended [to earth] saw such matters of husband and wife appearing in the world, they felt revulsion and contempt; seizing them with their left hands and pushing them away with their right, they caused them to leave that place.
Then, after two or three months had passed, that couple would return and strike and pelt him with sticks, wooden clubs, clods of earth, tiles, and stones, saying:
"Hide yourself well!"
"May you hide yourself well!

For this reason, when daughters are married today, they either scatter various flowers or scatter gold, silver, clothing, and *rājika*—the Sanskrit term for which refers to the flower made from parched rice—and utter these words of blessing:
"May you, our new bride, be peaceful, secure, and happy."
"O bhikṣus! In this same sequence,
what was considered evil by people in the past is now considered good by people today."
For these reasons, all sentient beings engage in unwholesome conduct within the worldly dharmas.
Following this sequence, they even construct various dwellings for the purpose of concealing those evil karmas.
The verse says:
First he built the city of Campā, then Vārāṇasī;
at the end of the final remnants of the kalpa, he planned and measured out Rājagṛha.

"Monks! By this cause and condition, the ancient and preeminent beings constructed villages, towns, settlements, kingdoms, cities, royal capitals, palaces, and other dwellings, thereby adorning the world; these were produced in succession."

"O monks! When sentient beings in this way further and gradually increase in their practice of unrighteousness, there are other sentient beings whose merit, lifespan, and karma are exhausted; they fall from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, casting off their bodies, and descend to receive a womb-born body within a mother's womb."
Due to these causes and conditions, the number of worldly people gradually increased, and unrighteousness gradually grew. Monks!

Those ancient superior beings who were first born into the world—by the power of the remaining merit of those sentient beings—there was no need for cultivation, and non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously.
If there is need for it, taking it during the first part of the day, it will immediately grow back again by the latter part of the day;
taking it during the latter part of the day, it grows back again by the first part of the next day, maturing without any difference.
If not taken, it remains as it was, ever-present.
In later times, because the merit of sentient beings gradually diminished, they became indolent and lazy, and a spirit of greed and stinginess arose within them. They thought to themselves:
"Since this non-glutinous rice is obtained without the need for cultivation, why should we endure such hardship by going separately at different times—once at dawn and once at dusk—to gather it?"
"It would merely exhaust me in vain.
