I had better take both meals' worth of rice at once.
Thereupon, he took the non-glutinous rice for two meals all at once.
There were other sentient beings who called out to that person, saying:
"The time for eating is approaching; you should come with us to gather non-glutinous rice.
That person replied:
"I have already gathered it all at once; I have brought it here in a single moment during the latter part of the day.
You who wish to depart may know for yourself the proper time.
That person then thought:

"This person has acted skillfully; he has attained great peace and happiness by taking all at once during the latter part of the day. I, too, may now take the food for two or three days at a single time."
He immediately went and gathered it.
At that time, there were other sentient beings who called out to that man, saying,
"We should gather the non-glutinous rice together."
He replied: "I have already taken my portion for three days.
You yourself know the proper time."
Having heard this, that person thought again:
"This man is very skillful; I too should now take the portions for four or five days at once to serve as a store."

For this reason, at that time, the non-glutinous rice gradually developed husks and chaff; once the grain was harvested and bundled up, it would no longer grow in those places, while the unharvested areas remained as they were. Thus, the rice stalks became segmented and grew in clusters.
"At that time, the sentient beings gathered together, filled with grief and lamentation, and said to one another:
'I recall my former body: it took joy as its food, possessed natural radiance, moved freely through the air, had the most excellent appearance, and enjoyed an exceedingly long lifespan.'"
Then, for us, the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) suddenly appeared, complete with color, fragrance, and taste; by eating it, we also lived for a long time.
Those who ate much became coarse in appearance, while those who were able to eat little remained superior in complexion.
Because they contended over superiority and inferiority, prideful minds arose, and thus distinctions were formed.

Due to this, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) vanished; next, the skin of the earth appeared; then forest creepers grew; then non-glutinous rice emerged, eventually reaching the stage where it possessed husks and bran.
"When it is harvested, it does not grow back; when left unharvested, it remains as it was. For this reason, these distinct sections have formed, growing in dense clusters.
We should now divide our territories and establish boundaries between them."
"That is your portion; this is my portion," they said, "and let us establish a covenant that whoever violates it shall be punished.
Monks! Through these causes and conditions, there arose in the world the names of boundaries and punishments.
"At that time, there was a being among the multitude who, out of attachment to his own rice, stole another's rice.
When others saw this, they immediately addressed him, saying: 'Hey!'"
"You sentient beings have committed most evil deeds; you have committed most evil deeds!
How can you, possessing [wealth] yourselves, further steal the property of others!
Having rebuked them thus, he released them and spoke to them, saying:
"Do not do this again.
However, these sentient beings committed it yet again; he scolded them and let them go, and though he did so two or three times, they still did not repent or reform.
He reviled him with coarse words, struck him on the head with his hand, and, seizing him by the arm, led him before a crowd of people, declaring to them:
"This man is a thief!"
Then this thief, in the presence of the assembly, denied the charge and engaged in a dispute, saying to the people:
"This being here has used coarse and evil words to insult me, and has struck my head with his hand."
At that time, the multitude gathered together, sorrowful and weeping, saying to one another:
"Today we have come together to this place of suffering and misery."
"We have already given rise to evil and unwholesome states, engendering various afflictions that increase the fruits of future birth and old age, and lead us toward the evil realms.
Yet now we see before our eyes [the consequences]: striking one another with hands, pulling, pushing, driving away, reviling, and insulting."
"We should now seek out a righteous person and establish him as our leader for the sake of protection.

He shall properly reprimand those who deserve reprimand, properly punish those who deserve punishment, and properly expel those who deserve expulsion. As for all the rice in our respective fields, let each of us take his own share."
"If there is anything required by the guardian, we, the multitude, shall collectively contribute to provide it.
Having thus deliberated with great care, the assembly then sought out a worthy person to serve as the guardian.

At that time, within that great assembly, there was but a single person whose body was the tallest and largest, perfectly full and dignified, with a countenance and deportment exceptionally superior, marvelous and worthy of being beheld; his physical form and majestic radiance were complete in every respect.
Then the great assembly went to that person and spoke these words:
"Excellent, O worthy one! May you provide us with true protection."
Each of us has our own field boundaries; you should manage them so that they do not encroach upon one another.

Where there is a need for reprimand, you must reprimand properly; where there is a need for censure, you must censure properly; where there is a need for punishment, you must duly administer punishment; and where there is a need for expulsion, you must duly carry out expulsion.
"We shall divide the rice harvest gathered by us and give it to you, so that you will not suffer from want.

Having heard this, those people immediately gave their consent; they provided protection for him, reprimanding and punishing wrongdoers, and driving out those who were unjust, so that no one would commit acts of aggression.
The multitude gathered up the rice grain and provided for him, ensuring there was no lack or deficiency.
Thus, acting as their rightful leader according to the law by taking a portion of the land from among the people’s rice fields, he was therefore named Kṣatriya (in the Sui language, "Field Lord").
At that time, all sentient beings rejoiced and followed the teachings with devotion.
Among all affairs, that Kṣatriya was skillful in wisdom; dwelling among the multitude, his radiant appearance was most preeminent. For this reason, he was further named *Araja* (Sui: "King").
The great assembly established him as King Mahāsamata; for this reason, he was also called Mahāsamata, which in the Sui language means "Great Equality. O Bhikṣus!
During the reign of that King Mahāsamata, all people first began to be designated by the name *sattva*, which in the Sui language means "sentient beings."
"O monks! King Mahāsammata had a son named Hu-lu-che (Huluṣa), which in the language of Sui means 'Joyful Intention' (Manoratha). O monks!"
When Puluṣa was reigning as king, people collectively called him Haimaka (translated in the Sui language as "the Abandoner").
Monks! King Puluṣa had a son named Kāliyaṇa (translated in the Sui language as "The Truly Righteous").
"O monks! When that Kāliyaṇa reigned as king, all people collectively called him Tilasandha, which in the language of Sui means 'sesame-born. O monks!"
King Kāliyaṇa had a son named Varakāliyaṇa (translated into Chinese as *zuì zhèng zhēn zhě*, "Most Righteous and True"). O bhikṣus!
During the reign of that King Varakāliyaṇa, all people collectively called him Avadāra-khaṇḍa (translated into Chinese as *yún piàn*, "Cloud Shards").
"O bhikṣus!
That King Megha-vatsa had a son named Upoṣadha (translated in the Sui language as 'Fasting and Precepts').
O bhikṣus!"
During the reign of King Śīlavrata, all people collectively called him Tālajaṅgha (in the language of Sui, "Wooden Shanks").

O Bhikṣus! From the crown of King Śīlavrata’s head, a fleshy tumor spontaneously emerged; as that tumor opened, a boy was born, exceptionally handsome and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Immediately upon birth, he cried out: "Mātāta" (in the language of Sui, "Sustain me").
That King Māndhātṛ possessed supernormal powers and great majesty; he ruled over the four great continents, governing them with sovereign authority. Monks!
These six kings possessed immeasurable lifespans.
"O Bhikṣus!

From the right thigh of King Mūrdhaja, a blister arose, from which was born a boy, exceptionally handsome and distinguished, his body likewise endowed with the thirty-two marks. He was named Dakṣiṇa-ja (Born of the Right Thigh); he possessed great majesty and power, and ruled over the four great continents."

From his right thigh and the king’s left thigh, blisters emerged, from which a boy was born; he too was endowed with the thirty-two marks and was named Left-Thigh-Born (Vāmapārśvajāta). Possessing majestic power and authority, he ruled over three great continents.
On the left thigh of the King of the Right Knee, a fleshy bubble arose, from which was born a boy whose majestic appearance was as described before; he ruled over two great continents.
On the right knee of the King of the Left Thigh, a fleshy bubble arose, from which was born a boy whose majestic appearance was as described before; he governed one great continent.
“Monks! From this time forward, there have been wheel-turning kings, each ruling over a single continent;
you should know this, monks! Monks!”
In this successive order, first the multitude established King Mahāsamata;
next, King Manu; next, King Samyama; next, King Samyamatattva; next, King Upoṣadha; next, King Māndhātṛ;
next, King Dakṣiṇajaṅgha; next, King Vāmajaṅgha; next, King Dakṣiṇajānu; and next, King Vāmajānu.
Next is King Vimukta; next is King Vimuktatara; next is King Śarīra; next is King Rasāgra;
next is King Phalārtha-ratha; next is King Sāgara; next is King Mahāsāgara;
next is King Śakulī; next is King Mahāśakulī; next is King Kuśa; next is King Vikuśa.
Next was King Subhadra; next, King Mahāsubhadra; next, King Priya; next, King Mahāpriya;
next, King Rāvaṇa; next, King Mahārāvaṇa; next, King Nīlaka;
next, King Nākuśa; next, King Vṛka; next, King Sāgarabhāga; next, King Vajrabhuja.
King Śayana, followed by King Siṃhacandra, followed by King Nayati, followed by King Vyatireka,
followed by King Subhadra, followed by King Tapana, followed by King Prabhākara,
followed by King Āṭavika, followed by King Parvata, followed by King Parvatika, followed by King Arciṣmat, followed by King Jvalana.
"O bhikṣus! The descendants of King Jvalana succeeded one another for one hundred and one generations, all of whom ruled over the world from the city of Puṇḍravardhana."
The last of these kings was named Śatrujit; because he was able to subdue all enemies, he was called Śatrujit. "O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of King Śatrujit succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Ayodhyā; there were fifty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Durjaya."
"O bhikṣus!
That King Durdharṣa’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the realm from the city of Vārāṇasī; there were sixty-three thousand kings, the last of whom was named Durmanas."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Dṛḍhadhanu, his descendants succeeding one another, ruled and transformed the city of Kapilavastu; there were eighty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Brahmadatta."
"O Bhikṣus!

That King Brahmadatta’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the realm from the city of Śvetahastinapura. There were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Gajamukha."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Gajagandha had his descendants succeed one another, ruling and transforming the city of Kuśinagara. There were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Karpūra."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King of Tagara had descendants who succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the land from the city of Ullarasā. There were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Nāganandi."
"O bhikṣus!

That King Nāganaśī had descendants who succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the realm from the city of Durdharṣa. There were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Parantapa."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Parantapa’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the realm from the city of Kanyakubja; there were twelve thousand kings, the last of whom was named Jayasena."
"O Bhikṣus!
King Jayasena’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Pāṭaliputra; there were eighteen thousand kings, the last of whom was named Devendra."
"O Bhikṣus!
That celestial dragon king’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Tāmalipta; there were twenty-five thousand kings, the last of whom was named Sāgaradeva."
"O bhikṣus!

That Sea Heavenly King’s descendants succeeded one another, continuing to rule and transform the people in the city of Tāmalipta. There were ten thousand kings, and the last of these was also named Sea Heaven."
"O Bhikṣus!

That Sea Heavenly King’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the people in the city of Dantapura; there were eighteen thousand kings, the last of whom was named Sumati. His descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the people in the great city of Rājagṛha; there were twenty-five thousand kings, the last of whom was named Suśāsana."
"O Bhikṣus!

The kings who ruled through virtuous governance had their lineage passed down from father to son, continuing to rule in the city of Vārāṇasī. There were one thousand and one hundred such kings, the last of whom was named Mahādeva."
"O Bhikṣus!

A great imperial sovereign, his descendants succeeding one another, ruled and transformed the realm from the capital city of Māyāpurī. There were eighty-four thousand kings, and the last of these kings was named Sāgaradeva."
"O Bhikṣus!
That Deva-king Sāgara’s descendants succeeded one another, continuing to rule and transform the city of Puṇḍravardhana; there were fifteen hundred kings, the last of whom was named Duṣkaracaryā."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Duṣprasaha’s descendants succeeded one another, continuing to rule and transform the great city of Kuśāvatī; there were eighty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Bhūmipati."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Bhūmipati’s descendants succeeded one another, continuing to rule and transform the people from the city of Ayodhyā; there were a thousand kings, the last of whom was named Dharaṇīdhara."
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Dharaṇīdhara’s descendants succeeded one another, continuing to rule and transform the great city of Vārāṇasī; there were eighty thousand kings, the last of whom was named Bhūmipati."
"O bhikṣus!
That King Bhūmipati’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the realm from the city of Mithilā; there were eighty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Mahādeva."

"Monks! That Great King Mahādeva’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming from the great city of Mithilā. There were eighty-four thousand kings, all of whom resided in the great city of Mithilā and practiced the holy life within the Āmra Grove."
The last of them was named King Nimi; next, King Mṛta; next, King Sthitajaṅgha;
next, King Hana; next, King Upa; next, King Numā; next, King Sudarśana; next, King Candradarśana;
next, King Śrutabala; next, King Dharmabala; next, King Vinīyaka; and next—
Mahāvinīta-rāja, followed by Vinīta-rāja, followed by Aśoka-rāja, followed by Vigataśoka-rāja,
followed by Skandha-rāja, followed by Parvata-rāja, followed by Malla-rāja, followed by Lona-rāja,
followed by Janapada-rāja, followed by Reṇu-rāja, followed by Kāla-rāja, followed by Nanda-rāja, and then...
King Mirror-Surface, King Born-Next, King Measure-Neck,
King Food-and-Drink, King Abundant-Food, King Hard-to-Conquer, King Hard-to-Vanquish, King Peacefully-Abiding,
King Well-Abiding, King Great-Power, King Power-Virtue, and King Upright-Walk.
"O bhikṣus!

Those kings of the Urdhvaga dynasty, succeeding one another through their descendants, ruled and governed from the city of Kāśyapa; there were seventy-five thousand kings, the last of whom was named Ambaṣṭha."
"Monks! That King Ambaṭṭha had a son named Suppatiṭṭhita. Monks!"
That King Śūradatta’s descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the great city of Pāṭaliputra; there were one thousand one hundred kings, the last of whom was named Kīlīki.
“O bhikṣus! At that time, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; the Bodhisattva practiced the holy life under him and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.”

King Kīliki had a son named Śaṅkara; his descendants succeeded one another, continuing to rule and transform the kingdom from the city of Puṇḍravardhana for one hundred and one generations, the last of whom was named Karṇin.
That King Karṇa had two sons: the elder was named Gautama, and the younger was named Bharadvāja.
That King Gautama had a son named Ikṣvāku.
"O bhikṣus!
The Ikṣvāku kings, their descendants succeeding one another, continued to rule and govern from the city of Potalaka. There were one hundred and one Ikṣvāku kings, the last of whom was named Aśoka."
"O bhikṣus!
King Dīrghāyu begot four sons: the first was named Ummaka, the second Suvarṇa, the third Hastin, and the fourth Pāduka."
That King Pāda had a son named Devapura; Devapura had a son named Go-pura. That King Go-pura’s descendants succeeded one another in ruling and transforming the city of Kapilavastu.

There were seventy-seven thousand kings, the last of whom was named Vipula-ratha. Next was Viśeṣa-ratha, then Dṛḍha-ratha, then Sthira-ratha, then Daśa-ratha, then Śata-ratha, then Navati-ratha, then Citra-ratha, then Jñāna-ratha, then Vipula-dhanus, then Bahu-dhanus, then Abhīkṣṇa-dhanus, then Sthira-dhanus, then Daśa-dhanus, then Śata-dhanus, then Navati-dhanus, then Citra-dhanus, and finally Jñāna-dhanus.
"O Bhikṣus!
That King Jñānabāhu fathered two sons: the first was named Siṃhahanu, and the second was named Siṃhapāda.
King Siṃhahanu succeeded to the throne and fathered four sons: the first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, the third Droṇodana, and the fourth Amṛtodana."
Furthermore, he gave birth to a daughter named Amṛtā. O Bhikṣus!
King Śuddhodana had two sons: the first was named Siddhārtha, and the second was named Nanda.
Śuklodana had two sons: the first was named Tiṣya and the second Nandika;
Droṇodana had two sons: the first was Aniruddha and the second Bhadrika;
Amṛtodana had two sons: the first was Ānanda and the second Devadatta.
That woman Amṛtā had only one son, named Śepha. O bhikṣus!
The Bodhisattva’s only son was named Rāhula.

“O bhikṣus! In this manner, from King Mahāsamata onwards, the lineage was passed down through successive descendants of that most excellent clan until it reached the youth Rāhula, who attained arhatship, severed all afflictions, brought an end to birth and death, and will have no further existence.”
“Monks! For this reason, in times past, there arose in the world a preeminent kṣatriya who acted in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma.”
"Monks! Because of this dharma, the kṣatriyas of the world constitute the most excellent birth.
At that time, there were other sentient beings who thought as follows:"
"Worldly conditioned phenomena are a disease, an abscess, and a great poisoned arrow.
Having reflected deeply thus, he renounced all conditioned things and, within the mountain wilderness, constructed a thatched hut where he sat in stillness to cultivate dhyāna.
If they had any need—whether in the forenoon or in the afternoon—they would briefly leave their grass huts to enter the village for alms.
When people saw them, they would give whatever was required and even build dwellings for them, saying together in praise:
"These beings cultivate the most virtuous karma; having abandoned the worldly, samsaric, unwholesome, and evil dharmas, they are true brahmins."
For these reasons, the Brahmin caste arose in the world.

Among them, some were unable to achieve meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and, dwelling in villages, taught many incantations and arts; for this reason, they were further called "Teachers" (*śāstṛ*).
Furthermore, because such a person enters a village dwelling, they are called "one who is heading toward a settlement.
Moreover, because they seek to accomplish the various dharmas of sensual desire, they are called "one who accomplishes desire."
For this reason, in times past, a preeminent brahmin of noble lineage was born into the world; he acted in accordance with the Dharma and never otherwise.

Furthermore, there is another class of sentient beings who engage in various livelihoods such as seeking profit, performing crafts, technical skills, and the arts; by reason of this, they are called Vaiśyas.
Therefore, when those of the Vaiśya caste appeared in the world in the past, they also acted in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to it. "O Bhikṣus!
After these three castes had arisen in the world, there subsequently arose a fourth caste in the world."

"Monks! There is a certain kind of person who, having disparaged the traditional laws of their own family, shaves off their hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, renounces the world, leaves the home life to practice the Way, and declares with their own mouth:
'I am a śramaṇa.'"
Having made this proclamation, he immediately fulfilled his vow;
the same applies to those of the Brahmin caste and the Vaiśya caste as well.
There is a type of person who, having previously reviled [others], likewise renounces the world and goes forth, declaring with his own mouth:
"I shall become a śramaṇa," he thought,
and thus he immediately formed a right vow.
It is for that reason that there exists the category of right vows.
"O Bhikṣus!

There are certain Kṣatriyas who practice unwholesome conduct through their actions of body, speech, and mind; because of these unwholesome deeds, when their bodies dissolve at the end of life, they experience nothing but suffering.
It is the same for Brahmins and Vaiśyas as well."

Furthermore, there are kṣatriyas who practice wholesome conduct through the actions of body, speech, and mind; because of these wholesome deeds, when their bodies perish at the end of life, they experience nothing but happiness.
The same is true for brahmins and vaiśyas.
"O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there are kṣatriyas who perform two kinds of conduct through their bodily, verbal, and mental actions; because of these two kinds of conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, they shall experience both suffering and pleasure.
The same is true for brahmins and vaiśyas."
"O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there are kṣatriyas who, having left the household life out of right faith, cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they are able to exhaust all outflows, attain liberation of mind, attain liberation by wisdom, realize the Dharma in the present life, and acquire the various supernormal powers."
Having realized this, he declared aloud: "Birth has been exhausted;
the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence."
The same applies to the Brahmins and the Vaiśyas. O Bhikṣus!
Among these three castes, those who in future lives are able to accomplish the perfection of knowledge and conduct (vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna) and attain Arhatship are called the most excellent.
“Monks! In the past, before me, the Brahmā King Sahampati spoke these verses:
‘The Kṣatriya is the most excellent birth; If one emerges from among the various castes, ...’”
"Endowed with the perfection of knowledge and conduct, he surpasses all devas and humans. "O bhikṣus!
This verse well-recited by Brahmā Sahampati is not ill-spoken; I have approved it."
"O monks! I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, also teach this meaning. O monks!"
In this sequence, I have fully explained how the world evolves, how it dissolves, and how it remains stable. Monks!
Whatever is to be done by a Teacher out of compassion for his disciples, seeking their welfare and acting with loving-kindness, that I have now completed; you should rely upon it.

“Monks! Whether in a wilderness or an empty place, at the foot of a mountain or under a tree, in a quiet room or a secluded chamber, in a cave, a cliff, or a grotto, or among graves in the open air—far removed from all villages—one may construct a hut using grass, wood, and other materials.”
"You, bhikṣus, should practice meditative concentration in this place; do not fall into negligence, lest you come to regret it later.
This is my instruction to you, bhikṣus."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Qishi jing*, Scroll Ten.
